items.title: Seasonal habitat dynamics and anthropogenic exposure of loggerhead turtles at a global scale.
items.abstract: Loggerhead turtles (Caretta caretta) are highly migratory marine reptiles whose seasonal habitat shifts can alter their exposure to fisheries, vessel traffic, and plastic pollution. We combined global occurrence records with seasonal environmental predictors to build species distribution models (SDMs), mapped potential habitats for four seasons, and overlaid these habitats with fishing, shipping, and floating-plastic layers. We then compared cumulative exposure with the global marine protection network to identify conservation gaps. Potential habitats varied strongly among seasons and were associated mainly with sea surface temperature, mixed layer depth, and distance from shore. Fisheries exposure was concentrated in nearshore and continental shelf waters, shipping exposure followed major traffic corridors, and plastic pollution produced broader areal exposure. Multiple-pressure hotspots occurred consistently in the Mediterranean Sea, the northwestern Pacific, and the northwestern Atlantic. Existing marine protection covered only 11.2%-13.7% of cumulative exposure across seasons, indicating that the majority of cumulative exposure occurred outside the current marine protection network. These results show that seasonal habitat dynamics can substantially reshape anthropogenic exposure for a wide-ranging marine vertebrate. Integrating seasonal SDMs with pressure-specific exposure layers can help prioritize dynamic ocean management and transboundary conservation for loggerhead turtles.

items.title: Ecosystem restructuring of subtidal oyster reefs responding to a dredged material disposal disturbance revealed by ecological network analysis.
items.abstract: Understanding how coastal ecosystems reorganize after abrupt anthropogenic disturbances is fundamental for predicting ecosystem resilience and informing adaptive management strategies. Here, we examined the temporal reorganization of an oyster reef ecosystem responding to an unexpected dredged material dumping event using a before-after assessment framework. Four annual Ecopath models (2017-2020) were constructed to characterize temporal variations in ecosystem structure, energy pathways, trophic organization, and functional resilience. Ecosystem-level indicators displayed strong temporal fluctuations (p 2020 > 2019 > 2018. Following extensive mortality of oysters and macroalgae, the ecosystem experienced substantial functional reorganization in 2018, characterized by reduced ascendency/development capacity ratio and connectance index, together with increased system omnivory and total primary production/total respiration ratio (p < 0.001). These shifts suggested enhanced trophic flexibility accompanied by reduced ecosystem maturity. Following the disturbance, Finn's cycling index, Finn's mean path length, and the detritivory/herbivory ratio increased and reached their maximum values in 2019, indicating enhanced detritus-based energy pathway. Keystone functional groups gradually shifted from fish-dominated regulation toward invertebrate-mediated control, while oysters consistently remained among the dominant functional groups. Redundancy/ascendency index analysis revealed that top predators played important roles in maintaining ecosystem stability under disturbance, whereas zooplankton functioned as key mediators of trophic connectivity. Collectively, these results demonstrated that ecosystem stability depends on higher functional diversity, trophic connectivity, and ecological redundancy. Maintaining ecosystem engineers and preserving diverse energy pathways may therefore represent essential strategies for sustaining ecosystem resilience and long-term ecological stability.

items.title: Chemical Ecology and Management of Imported Fire Ants.
items.abstract: Imported fire ants ( Solenopsis invicta and S. richteri ) are invasive pests that were introduced into the United States via Mobile, Alabama, in the early twentieth century. As these species spread, interbreeding led to the emergence of hybrid populations. Their rapid expansion and ecological dominance prompted extensive control efforts, including chemical eradication campaigns and biologically informed strategies. Today, fire ants infest over 140 million hectares across the southern United States, affecting public health, agriculture, and ecosystems. Despite decades of research, many fire ant semiochemicals remain unidentified because of the ants' complex social behavior and because multicomponent chemical signals occur in trace amounts and are difficult to isolate, especially those involved in aerial mating. Additionally, components often lack activity unless presented in specific combinations. These challenges limit traditional bioassay-guided structure elucidation. This review summarizes advances in fire ant chemical ecology, highlights persistent knowledge gaps, and proposes innovative strategies to accelerate pheromone discovery and improve management.

items.title: Dams not to blame for all reservoir carbon emissions from retained organic carbon.
items.abstract: Dams trap organic carbon (OC) and create carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) and methane (CH 4 ) emission hotspots within reservoirs, underlying the ongoing debate over their role in carbon emissions. However, even without dams, this labile OC would still decompose and emit CO 2 or CH 4 during downstream transport and after deposition in estuaries. Thus, relying solely on dammed reservoir observations to assess these emissions may introduce considerable bias. Here, we simulated both dammed and non-dammed scenarios for 5346 global reservoir dams to assess their impact on carbon emissions from retained OC. The results show that reservoir-only approaches overestimate dam-induced carbon emissions by neglecting baseline emissions under no-dam conditions. After baseline correction, dams increase carbon emissions by an average of 21.5% in CO 2 -equivalent (CO 2 -eq), which represents only 18.6% of the emissions estimated using the conventional reservoir-based accounting approach. XGBoost identified reservoir depth and hydraulic residence time as the primary controls on dam-induced carbon emissions.

items.title: Cultural norms of exogamy and mobility shape genetic evolution of Central African hunter-gatherers.
items.abstract: Through a hunting and gathering lifestyle, humans have managed to thrive across all terrestrial ecosystems. A key adaptive feature enabling this ecological success is the ability of hunter-gatherer societies to maintain high levels of genetic diversity despite ecological and demographic shocks, but the mechanisms underlying this resilience are poorly understood. Here, we integrate genomic, demographic, mobility, and ethnographic data from two Central African hunter-gatherer populations to show that genetic diversity emerges from interacting effects of population size, mobility, and cultural norms governing marriage. We first demonstrate direct selection against background homozygosity: Even modest increases in runs of homozygosity, in the near absence of close-kin marriages, are associated with reduced reproductive success. Despite regional differences in effective population size, clustering of relatives, sedentism, and exogamy rules, overall levels of homozygosity are similarly low in both populations. These shared genetic outcomes are achieved through distinct strategies: In one region, strict exogamy combined with high lifetime mobility limits local relatedness, whereas in the other, more relaxed exogamy norms are offset by increased male mate-search distances that reduce offspring homozygosity. Together, our results show that human populations flexibly adjust mobility and social norms to demographic constraints to preserve genetic diversity and avoid fitness costs, revealing culture as a central component of human adaptation.

items.title: Broad-scale evaluations of biodiversity change need reference comparisons.
items.abstract: Assessments of broad-scale biodiversity change commonly aggregate communities that differ in their initial impacts and their total degree of change (differing "impact trajectories"). Biodiversity responses may depend on the impact trajectory of a given community; thus, not controlling for these differences could produce a misleading mixture of trends even if all communities degraded or recovered. To evaluate this dependency, we related biodiversity trends for 4062 river invertebrate time series (1971 to 2024) from 23 European countries to impact trajectories for each community, quantified through comparison to least-impacted references. Trends were typically stronger and more consistent in initially more impacted communities that also exhibited more extreme total change. However, responses were weaker when initial impacts were lower and highly inconsistent with lesser total change. Our results show that biodiversity trends should be compared among communities with similar impacts, determined relative to appropriate references. Improving trend comparability is essential to accurately determine how biodiversity generally responds to anthropogenic impacts and conservation actions.

items.title: Dissolved organic matter uptake balances carbon budgets of Red Sea bivalves and ascidians.
items.abstract: Benthic suspension feeders have long been thought to depend solely on particulate organic matter (POM) for their nutritional needs. Our research, conducted in the Gulf of Aqaba (Red Sea), shows that the available concentration of planktonic carbon in the reef water is too low to meet the metabolic demands (measured through in situ oxygen uptake) of common bivalves ( Spondylus sp. and Chama pacifica ) and ascidians ( Polycarpa mytiligera and Halocynthia spinosa ). In situ measurements confirmed a concentration-dependent uptake of bulk dissolved organic carbon (DOC) and protein-like dissolved organic compounds (fDOM, analyzed via spectrofluorometry) by Spondylus sp. and P. mytiligera , suggesting that DOC uptake may balance their carbon budgets. Stable isotope (δ 13 C) mixing models indicate that reef-derived DOC (mean δ 13 C = -18.4 ± 0.7‰) emerges as the primary carbon source for bivalves (57% of their body composition), far surpassing contributions from particulate sources (26% from POC > 100 µm and 14% from POC < 100 µm). While ascidians still rely primarily on POM (60 to 71%), DOC plays an essential role as a supplementary food source (23 to 29%). These results challenge the prevailing assumption that POM is the exclusive food source for these organisms. Given the widespread presence of bivalves and ascidians in benthic habitats, our findings highlight their ability to bypass the microbial loop and directly utilize dissolved organic compounds, prompting a reevaluation of current benthic carbon budgets.

items.title: Recombination rate and efficiency of linked selection in small and large stickleback populations.
items.abstract: Population genetic theory predicts that natural selection will be more efficient in large than small populations because genetic drift reduces the efficiency of selection in small populations. Small populations adapting to new environments can also be expected to evolve higher recombination rates to facilitate adaptation as well as to dissociate and purge harmful mutations. We tested these hypotheses (1) by investigating differences in the strength of association between nucleotide diversity (π) and recombination rate across the genomes of nine-spined sticklebacks (Pungitius pungitius) from four small freshwater (mean Ne ≈ 7 096) and four large marine (mean Ne = 376 828) populations, as well as (2) by comparing recombination rates between small and large populations using population specific linkage maps. We found the predicted positive correlation of π with recombination rate from all but the smallest freshwater populations, suggesting prevalent linked selection even after accounting for variation in GC/CpG content, and gene density. Mean recombination rates did not differ between freshwater and marine populations, except that the smallest Ne freshwater population exhibited significantly elevated recombination rate. Exploratory GWAS analyses suggested a possible polygenic basis for recombination rate. These results suggest an important role for linked selection in reducing π in low recombination regions especially in large populations. Moreover, as predicted by theory, at least one of the small freshwater populations appears to have evolved a higher recombination rate than its marine ancestors.

items.title: Microbiome plasticity during the early life-stage of the angelshark (Squatina squatina) in Las Teresitas (Canary Islands).
items.abstract: Shark microbiome studies offer acute insights into host health, immunity, and ecological interactions, yet remain poorly studied compared to other marine vertebrates. Shark-associated microbial communities, despite being species-specific, are influenced by environmental conditions and feeding ecology. In this study, we aimed to characterize shifts in the microbiome of the Critically Endangered angelshark (Squatina squatina) during the early stages of development and to assess how environmental factors contribute to the shaping of a specific microbiota. Samples from thirty-nine juvenile angelsharks were collected from Las Teresitas nursery area in the Canary Islands over one year. Skin, oral and cloacal microbiomes were analysed using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. The sizes of individuals ranged between 24 and 42 cm in length. The shark microbiome was clearly distinct from the surrounding environment, indicating a unique composition from early life stages. Dominant bacteria present in the shark microbiomes included Vibrionaceae (up to 96%), Pseudoalteromonas (up to 63%), Rhodobacteraceae (up to 57%) and Alteromonadaceae (up to 20%). Seawater had a greater influence than sediment on the external skin microbiome, especially in younger individuals. This was not expected due to the burial behaviour of the species. Notably, the abundance of Pseudoalteromonadaceae (assessed by qPCR) was positively correlated with shark growth but was independent of the skin mucus. This suggests a protective role of this phylotype in younger individuals and may help in the adaptation to habitat conditions. This is the first comprehensive microbiome study in angelsharks, highlighting the importance of environmental preservation for microbial integrity and juvenile fitness.

items.title: An Empirical Snapshot of Local Nutrition Governance Capacity in the Rasuwa District of Nepal Before the Flood Surge of August 2026.
items.abstract: On August 26, 2026, flash floods swept through the Rasuwa district of Nepal, causing mass casualties and severe destruction. Research on disasters has led to valuable recommendations on how governments can be more attentive to warning signs and react more rapidly, and how tapping into local capacity and know-how can lead to more effective responses. However, in most crises not much is known about individual or institutional capacities that predated a shock or what resources donors and governments subsequently should bolster to support emergency responses and build resilience. In this Commentary, we draw on the self-reported data of civil servants and other local professionals tasked with implementing the national multisectoral nutrition strategy in Rasuwa. Data collection in 2024 predated the flood by roughly 2 years. The survey measured routine governance capacity, not disaster-response capacity specifically, and yet such data offer some insights into local capacity before the latest disaster and help our understanding of which elements were already under strain. The aim of this Commentary is not to report full survey findings but to highlight observations most relevant to the 2026 Rasuwa flood. Broadly, we suggest that routine governance research on nutrition and other technical topics of relevance can serve as a baseline for disaster recovery and that global calls for the localization of aid require much deeper understanding and measurement of local capacity to act.

items.title: Modern Himalayan marmot faeces analyses: Implications for palaeodietary, palaeoecological, and palaeoclimate analysis.
items.abstract: Pollen and nutrient analyses of the faeces of the Himalayan marmot (Marmota himalayana) were made to understand its preferred dietary plants and ecology. Pollen preserved in the faeces accurately reflected its diet as a mixed feeder including Artemisia, Caryophyllaceae, Asteroideae, and Ephedra, characteristic plants of the Alpine steppe vegetation under a cold and arid climate in the higher Himalaya. Pollen ratio values between Artemisia/Chenopodiaceae, Artemisia/Cyperaceae, and Artemisia/Ephedra are identified from the Pensilla Pass and Rimkhim regions, as useful tools that characterize the Alpine steppe vegetation and climate in the higher Himalaya. Principal Component Analysis of the pollen taxa indicated only a slight difference in the relative abundance between the two localities sampled, Pensila Pass and Rimkhim areas. Coprophilous fungal spores, Sporormiella and Saccobolus, were abundant and considered useful for understanding the interrelationship between vegetation and the marmot's preferred habitat. Fifteen nutritional elements were recorded, and the high concentration of carbon, nitrogen, calcium, silicon, and, phosphorous is considered significant with a direct dietary relationship with the preferred plants consumed. This study provides a modern analogue and a baseline for coprolite and palaeoecological analyses in marmot inhabited regions and to observe the species future response to vegetation and climate change resulting shifts in altitude in the higher Himalaya.

items.title: Unraveling the role of surface structure and a generalized coordination number descriptor in H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> decomposition: insights for green Fenton systems.
items.abstract: The electrocatalytic green Fenton process has attracted increasing attention for wastewater treatment due to its mild operating conditions. However, the influence of surface structure and metal properties on this process remains poorly understood. In this work, density functional theory (DFT) calculations, combined with free energy calculations, were performed to systematically investigate the H 2 O 2 decomposition on various Pt surface structures and other metal surfaces. The catalytic behavior depends on the Pt facets, with Pt(112) being the most active. Step and vacancy sites also substantially lower the activation barriers for H 2 O 2 decomposition compared to flat surfaces. For example, the decomposition barrier becomes barrierless (0.004 eV) on a Pt(120) step surface. Among other transition metals studied (Pd, Ni, Au, Ag, Ir and Co), Co and Ir are promising cathode materials, whereas Au(111) shows the highest activation barrier (0.249 ± 0.005 eV). Although a Brønsted-Evans-Polanyi (BEP) relationship exists between the activation energy and the dissociative adsorption energy on flat surfaces across different metals, we identify a unified and simple descriptor-the local generalized coordination number (GCN)-that directly determines the activation energy for a given metal ( e.g. Pt), regardless of surface structure or site type. These findings provide a theoretical framework for understanding H 2 O 2 decomposition on metal catalysts and rationally designing cathode materials for electrocatalytic green Fenton systems.

items.title: Salmonid science on the move: Twenty years of research through the lens of early career researchers
items.abstract: Salmonids are among the most studied fish species worldwide, owing to their wide geographic distribution, diversity of life-history strategies, ecological and socioeconomic importance, and vulnerability to global change. In this review, we take advantage of two decades of the International Workshop of PhDs and Post-doctoral Fellows on Anadromous Salmonids (NoWPaS) conference series to track the evolution of salmonid science through the lens of early-career researchers (ECRs). From all abstracts presented at NoWPaS meetings between 2005 and 2025, we extracted structured qualitative and quantitative information to characterize major trends and shifts in the field. Our results show a strong research bias toward Atlantic salmon and brown trout, concentrated in Europe and Atlantic Canada, and a persistent mismatch between the life stages and habitats studied. In particular, the marine phase remains understudied in comparison to fresh and coastal waters. Over the study period, salmonid research shifted markedly from hydro-geomorphological and habitat-based approaches toward genetic and genomic methods, alongside the rise of advanced telemetry methods for reconstructing individual life histories. Research orientation, measured as a gradient from fundamental to applied research, was on average intermediate but varied among countries and disciplines, with the UK and Norway showing shifts to more applied research, as well as the discipline of Ecology becoming more applied. Additionally, we identified a significant increase in Climate change and Aquaculture as research drivers, with some drivers well-represented in some species (e.g., Hydropower and dams for landlocked Atlantic salmon and Climate change for Arctic char). These trends should be interpreted in context of the composition of the NoWPaS network: participation is primarily ECRs in the Northern Hemisphere, with research from Asia, South America, and western North America largely absent from this synthesis. Despite this lens, our analysis identifies clear knowledge gaps, particularly around marine life stages and species other than Atlantic salmon and brown trout, and highlights opportunities for broadening taxonomic, geographic, and life-history coverage in future salmonid research. We also present a roadmap, identifying combinations of life stages, disciplines and taxa which have been under-represented and constitute potential knowledge gaps, while also flagging those combinations that have already been well studied. Overall, we advocate for a continued shift toward integrative and holistic approaches, bridging distinct research disciplines, to better understand, manage, and conserve salmonids under increasingly uncertain future environmental conditions.

items.title: Multicellularity and virulence in the budding yeast, Saccharomyces cerevisiae
items.abstract: In the real world, microbes must cope with environmental fluctuations, compete for scarce resources, and avoid predation. One adaptation to survive this tangled web is the formation of multicellular aggregates, such as biofilms, which are known to be associated with pathogenicity. Despite the importance of the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae to biomedical research, little is known about the natural variation in its multicellular, biofilm-related traits. We investigated five multicellular phenotypes in a diverse, worldwide panel of ~1000 isolates. We found that all traits varied significantly and ~2/3 of the isolates expressed at least one multicellular trait. Both recent ecology and evolutionary history explained some of this variation, with clinical isolates exhibiting increased levels of three biofilm-related traits. When tested against wax moth larvae, hyper-multicellular isolates tended to be more virulent than non-multicellular isolates. Genome-wide association analysis on each trait suggested a genetic architecture of many small effect loci, compatible with polygenic adaptation. Only four genes, SLN1 , ECM5 , MLP2 , and ECM9 , were shared among the traits; deletion of MLP2 and ECM9 verified their association with multicellularity. Our results show that this yeast expresses far more multicellularity than previously appreciated and suggest that the aggregative phenotypes are likely evolving independently.

items.title: Durophagous adaptations in a new crocodyliform from the Santonian of Hungary and a systematic reassessment of European Cretaceous atoposaurids
items.abstract: Atoposauridae comprises a group of diminutive, semiterrestrial, brevirostrine neosuchian crocodyliforms that represents a characteristic component of European Jurassic-Cretaceous tetrapod faunas. Although frequently evaluated within the context of crown-group Crocodylia origins, their highly contested phylogenetic relationships continue to obscure their precise role in crocodylomorph evolutionary history. Particular ambiguity surrounds the monophyly of the genus Theriosuchus - with some hypotheses inferring long-term persistence of the lineage in Mesozoic Europe, whereas others interpreting select Cretaceous species as representatives of separate, even non-atoposaurid clades (e.g. Sabresuchus spp). We describe a new, stratigraphically intermediate taxon from the Santonian of Hungary based on isolated cranial elements, consistently placed as the sister taxon of Sabresuchus (Theriosuchus) sympiestodon from the Maastrichtian of Romania by our comprehensive set of phylogenetic analyses using three separate datasets. Sabresuchus tribodon sp. nov. is either recovered within Atoposauridae (global datasets) or Paralligatoridae (ingroup analysis) and can be distinguished from all other representatives of these groups by a specialized morphology consisting of massive, thick-enameled bulbous posterior maxillary teeth ornamented with apicobasal ridges, an extremely short rostrum with a reduced number of maxillary and dentary teeth, and the significantly upturned dorsal margin of the posterior dentary and surangular. Comparable anatomical adaptations are present in ecomorphologically convergent extinct crocodyliforms whose inferred feeding ecology included durophagy. However, this complete suite of characters has not been previously documented in either atoposaurids or paralligatorids. Our systematic reassessment results in an up-to-date taxonomy of Cretaceous European atoposaurids and tentatively confirms the polyphyly of Theriosuchus, though more definitive conclusions require combining individual, differently focused datasets. We reinterpret Aprosuchus ghirai from the Maastrichtian of Romania as a junior synonym of Sabresuchus sympiestodon and the putative European notosuchian Ogresuchus furatus from the Maastrichtian of Spain as an indeterminate atoposaurid.

items.title: A 47% decline in wind speed shapes phenology and selection on mismatching in Tree Swallows across a quarter century
items.abstract: Studies of the effects of climate change on birds typically focus on how temperature affects the average timing of breeding, often neglecting other climate variables such as wind or precipitation and their ultimate effects on reproductive success. Here, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of Tree Swallow (Tachycineta bicolor) breeding ecology in southeastern Wisconsin, USA, over a 26 year period (1997-2023). During this period there was no significant change in mean annual laying date or air temperature. Wind speed was the only weather variable that changed, slowing by 47% during the laying and hatching periods. This decline in wind speed increased food availability (Nematoceran flies), leading to larger clutches, heavier nestlings, and greater fledging success over time. It also allowed later-nesting birds to advance their laying dates. In contrast, earlier-laying birds did not advance their laying date. A changepoint analysis revealed consistently lower food availability and colder temperatures at the end of April than in early May when laying starts. This change in breeding conditions has not shifted during the study and likely acts as a constraint against earlier breeding. Over the years, the distribution of laying dates has been compressed against this early-season wall, which has resulted in a dramatic decrease in the variance of laying dates, but relatively little change in the population mean. Slowing wind speed has also relaxed selection against individuals that mistime egg laying relative to peak food abundance (i.e., phenological mismatching). Mismatching exerted relatively weak effects on reproductive success, which was driven mainly by food and weather conditions early in the season, prior to and during laying. This pattern contrasts with other Tree Swallow populations in which reproductive success is primarily influenced by temperature, particularly cold snaps, later in the season during the nestling period. Our study demonstrates that more comprehensive analyses of the effects of climate change are needed because temperature, food and wind speed can interact to produce different effects at the beginning and end of the breeding season, and this can reshape long-term trends in phenology and selection, even before eggs are laid.

items.title: Considering more complex covariate responses improves predictive performance in dynamic occupancy models
items.abstract: Finding: the right level of model complexity is a key challenge in most contexts, including ecology where data are often messy and underlying patterns complex. Dynamic occupancy models (DOMs) are increasingly used for modelling species distributions. DOMs have advantages over traditional species distribution models because their hierarchical structure allows them to explicitly model changes in occupancy over time while accounting for imperfect detection. The modelled processes (initial occupancy, colonisation, extinction, and detection) can be described as a function of covariates to account for heterogeneity in occupancy and detection dynamics. While this model structure is more complex than most alternative distribution models, in practice users of DOMs tend to fit simple linear responses to covariates with only infrequent use of non-linear responses or interactions. However, where data suffices and where ecologically justified, permitting more complex relationships between covariates and species occurrence may yield greater predictive power. Here, we assess how the complexity of covariate relationships affects the predictive performance of DOMs fit to Swiss breeding bird data. We find that models allowing quadratics and interactions tend to provide superior performance in predicting future occurrence, and that some covariates are only informative predictors when represented using non-linear relationships or interactions. Relying solely on linear relationships alone is not only inconsistent with ecological theory, but also potentially costly for predictive ability. To improve predictive power and the utility of these models for identifying important habitat and species at risk of declines, users of dynamic occupancy models should carefully consider not only their choice of candidate covariates, but also the functional forms of covariate relationships.

items.title: Oncomorphic neural agent populations for resource-limited sequential learning
items.abstract: Abstract Distributed artificial intelligence (AI) often operates under sequential task exposure, uneven compute, and decentralized coordination. Here, we present a cancer-inspired, or oncomorphic, multi-agent framework in which simulated neural agents can replicate, mutate their neural network architecture, migrate across task environments, undergo ecological turnover, and recruit learning/ecological resources from a finite shared reserve. We evaluate the framework in controlled synthetic nonlinear classification environments in which each agent trains only on its local task, allowing population ecology rather than centralized optimization to determine which neural network architectures persist. For various initial conditions, we find that stronger selection increased the endpoint local accuracy of surviving agent populations. Architecture mutation played a state-dependent role: diverse initial populations performed best at low mutation, whereas clonal large-architecture populations benefited from mutation-generated variation. Selection also increased end-of-run multi-task competence, measured by evaluating surviving agents on all environments without additional training. Recruitment and elevated baseline replication reshaped demographic support while prediction quality remained within a narrow band, consistent with redistribution of finite learning resources. Time-resolved entropy and dominance analyses revealed concentration toward successful architectures, while finite training cycles kept agents in a non-asymptotic learning regime. These results provide proof-of-concept mechanistic evidence that oncomorphic population dynamics may offer a route to decentralized adaptation in engineering applications under bounded local resources.

items.title: Seed Nutritional Traits and Bird Feeding Preferences: Laboratory Evaluation with an Exploratory Quantitative Literature Synthesis
items.abstract: Abstract Avian species impose considerable selective influences on plant ecosystems through seed consumption and endozoochorous seed dissemination; yet, the physiological and nutritional factors that dictate bird dietary preferences are not fully understood. According to the nutritional hypothesis, foraging avians are believed to weigh the metabolic dietary benefits against the costs of processing and detoxifying plant secondary compounds. items.title: Drivers of variation in nocturnal insect prey mass and quality
items.abstract: Abstract Global declines in aerial insectivores highlight the need to understand their foraging landscape. Aerial predators face unique biomechanical and aerodynamic constraints; therefore, prey profitability must be evaluated through the combined lens of nutritional value and handling costs. To address this gap, we evaluated the body mass and lipid content of nocturnal insects to determine how intrinsic (i.e. taxonomy and adult feeding strategy) and extrinsic traits (i.e. larval developmental habitat) traits of the sampled insect groups influence profitability of this group of prey. Our results demonstrate that prey quality is driven by three factors. First, taxonomy influenced nutritional profiles. Relative to their body mass, mayfly’s lipid content scaled hypo-allometrically whereas the other sampled taxa scaled isometrically. Second, intrinsic feeding strategies predicted energy stores of insects. Larval-feeders had higher body mass and lipid content than life-time-feeders. Third, developmental habitat influenced total body mass but not proportional lipid content. Terrestrial insects were heavier than aquatic-emergent insects, yet total lipid content did not differ between terrestrial and aquatic-emergent insects. While these traits define potential energetic payload for insectivores, actual profitability is strictly bounded by the handling capacity of foraging predators, particularly with regards to gape limitations. Energy-dense prey are only ecologically valuable within an optimal size range for size-selective predators. By quantifying multiple drivers of prey quality, our study provides a nuanced view of the nocturnal prey landscape, demonstrating that the nutritional ecology of aerial predators is highly context-dependent on the composition of the prey community.

items.title: mTOR and Extracellular Vesicles: Linking Chemical Stress to Ecological Communication.
items.abstract: Environmental stress, including that exerted by exposure to toxic chemicals, can shift cellular priorities from growth towards maintenance and communication. These changes in cellular resource allocation are coordinated by integrative molecular hubs such as the mechanistic Target of Rapamycin (mTOR) pathway. It regulates both the autophagy, which supports maintenance, and the release of extracellular vesicles (EVs), which mediate intercellular communication. This review discusses these interconnected processes and argues that environmental contaminants may influence not only intracellular signaling but also the molecular information exchanged among cells and potentially among organisms. EV-focused studies, performed at the intersection of chemical ecology, molecular biology, and ecotoxicology, can advance mechanistic understanding and open new opportunities for non-invasive environmental biomonitoring.

items.title: From LC-MS Metabolomic Profiling to AIEnabled Navigation of NPs Chemical Space: Recent Advances and Emerging Directions.
items.abstract: Natural products (NPs) occupy a unique region of chemical space and continue to provide privileged scaffolds for drug discovery, chemical ecology, and biotechnology. However, the exploration of NP diversity remains constrained by the complexity of biological extracts, the low annotation rate of LC-MS features, and the rediscovery of known metabolites. Recent advances in LC-HRMS/MS-based metabolomics, coupled with expanding spectral and structural databases, molecular networking, and in silico annotation methods, have considerably improved the characterization of complex metabolomes and facilitated large-scale exploration of natural chemical space. Simultaneously, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine-learning approaches are enhancing metabolite annotation, chemical classification, and prioritization, while knowledge graph technologies enable the integration of chemical, taxonomic, biological, and ecological information into interoperable, AI-ready frameworks. This mini-review highlights recent developments that support a transition from conventional metabolite annotation towards effective navigation of NP chemical space. We discuss the role of open data resources, computational metabolomics, knowledge-driven data integration, and emerging AI-assisted tools in accelerating NP discovery. We also examine how biotransformation and chemoenzymatic diversification can extend the boundaries of natural chemical space by generating nature-inspired molecules and previously inaccessible scaffolds. Together, these approaches are paving the way towards a more predictive, integrative, and data-driven paradigm for NP research and bioactive compound discovery.

items.title: Beggars can't be choosers: Competitive dominance and size-dependent resource investment jointly constrain partner associations in a multispecies mutualism.
items.abstract: Competition theory predicts that dominant species should gain preferential access to more valuable resources, whereas optimal foraging theory predicts that organisms should invest more heavily in higher-value resources. Together, these theories predict that dominant species should exhibit stronger value-dependent investment than subordinate species, consistent with the adage that 'beggars can't be choosers'. In mutualisms, where partners differ greatly in the rewards they provide, it remains unknown how competitive hierarchies influence associations with partners that vary in value. We tested whether competitive dominance and value-dependent investment jointly determine partner associations in an ant-aphid mutualism, focusing on resource quantity as a key axis of value. We measured ant responses to variation in resource quantity using experimental sugar baits and repeated censuses of wild aphid colonies spanning a range of sizes. The dominant ant preferentially recruited to larger baits and tended the largest aphid colonies, whereas subordinate ants increased recruitment with bait size only when the dominant ant was excluded. Aphid colony size also influenced behavioural investment in tending: the dominant ant showed strong increases in tending initiation, continuation and forager allocation with colony size, while subordinate ant taxa responded more weakly. Together, these results demonstrate that aphid colonies function as a graded resource whose size shapes competition among ants, leading dominant taxa to monopolize larger aphid colonies while constraining subordinate taxa to smaller ones. More broadly, these findings show that partner associations emerge from the interaction between competitive dominance and value-dependent investment, integrating classical competition and optimal foraging theories to explain partner associations in a multispecies mutualism.

items.title: Cryptic variation within and among islands in the ultraviolet reflectance of lizard throat coloration.
items.abstract: Cryptic polymorphism can bias tests of intraspecific phenotypic variation across space and time. Because many colours exist outside the range of human perception, colour variation is not always easily detected even when it plays an important role in organismal biology. In colour polymorphic lizards, recent work has demonstrated the presence of cryptic variation in ultraviolet (UV) reflectance, but the factors influencing this variation across space and time are less well known. To test among factors influencing UV reflectance variation across the landscape, we captured 771 wall lizards (Podarcis erhardii), a colour polymorphic species, across 35 islands in the Greek Cyclades and examined how UV traits vary across habitats, predator communities, and lizard densities. We discovered evidence for a cryptic, low-UV-morph phenotype nested within the known white morph phenotype, whose presence varies from absent to being fixed within several islands. Island size and geographic proximity were significant predictors of UV reflectance, but we did not find a significant correlation between either predator presence or any other island-wide environmental variables and UV-morph phenotype. We did find that on islands with both low- and high-UV-morph phenotypes, higher UV individuals are more likely to occupy greener, moister areas. We also found that lizards on islands with majority low-UV phenotype individuals are significantly larger than in mixed- and high-UV populations. Our results suggest that the presence of a cryptic, low-UV morph may have novel ecological implications for our understanding of wall lizard social dynamics, species interactions, and evolution.

items.title: Plasticity associated with adoption of social roles in clown anemonefish.
items.abstract: Central questions of animal behavior are how individual phenotypes shape and how individual phenotypes are shaped by dominance hierarchies. Using clownfish ( Amphiprion percula ) as a model system, we investigated how individuals strategically modify their phenotype during hierarchy formation. We tested the overarching hypothesis that interactions among size- and age-matched rivals will lead to the emergence of social roles (dominant, subordinate, solitary), accompanied by divergence in four aspects of individual phenotypes: growth, feeding behavior, agonistic behaviors (aggression, submission), and gene expression. To test this, we created 30 replicates of juvenile clownfish, each comprising a size-matched pair housed together, and a solitary size-matched individual housed separately. Our results show that an individual's social context shapes its growth trajectory through coordinated changes in feeding behavior, agonistic behaviors, and gene expression. Individuals emerging as dominant within pairs grew twice as much compared to those emerging as subordinates, while subordinate and solitary individuals showed comparable growth. Initially, paired individuals consumed more food per capita than solitary individuals, but this difference declined as size hierarchies became established. Agonistic behaviors also decreased over time among paired individuals as size differences emerged. Transcriptomic analyses revealed upregulation of conserved vertebrate growth pathways and ossification-related genes, and downregulation of satiety-associated genes, in dominant individuals compared to subordinates and solitaries. Here, we identify associations between changes in gene expression, growth, and feeding behavior regulation that reinforce social role differentiation during dominance hierarchy formation in clownfish. Our findings lay the foundation for a broader framework to explore the mechanisms underpinning strategic growth in social vertebrates.

items.title: Species-area relationships in honeycomb worm bioconstructions.
items.abstract: The increase of species richness with the available or sampled area is a fundamental principle in ecology, but explanatory models of this relationship have never been tested in worm reefs representing priority systems as biodiversity hotspots and habitats of conservation concern. Alternative models based on the 'random placement hypothesis' versus the occurrence of processes operating at different scales were experimentally tested in patches of the tubeworm Sabellaria alveolata. Macrofaunal assemblage structure and Hill numbers giving increasing weight to the most abundant species were compared between cores collected from the central portion of patches of three sizes ('small', 'medium', 'large') and between cores collected from the centre versus the edge of medium and large patches. Faunal richness per sampled unit was independent of patch size, consistently with passive sampling theory. Instead, diversity estimated by Hill number 1 D (exponential of Shannon entropy) progressively decreased across large, small and medium patches, while small and large patches showed higher Hill number 2 D (inverse of Simpson diversity) than medium patches, suggesting the occurrence of size-specific underlying processes. Our findings can be explained with effects of processes that would vary with the perimeter-to-area ratio of S. alveolata patches of varying size, such as wave disturbance, predation pressure and colonization patterns. This challenges the traditional view of species-area relationships, especially when focusing on small rather than biogeographic scale and multiple diversity measures, with potential implications for conservation and ecological theory. It suggests, in particular, that a mosaic of sabellariid patch sizes may be equally or even more effective than preserving or establishing large and continuous habitats for maintaining associated biodiversity and ecosystem function. It also emphasizes the importance of not assuming paradigmatically the wide validity of species-area models and incorporating within-habitat factors when attempting to apply general ecological theories to conservation and management.

items.title: Iron limitation reduces diatom carbon flow to bacteria through shifts in exometabolite consumption.
items.abstract: Iron is required for photosynthesis and thus affects carbon fixation rates in widespread aquatic regions where availability is limited. Turnover of aquatic photosynthetically derived fixed carbon is largely constrained by bacterial activity, but it is unknown how algal iron limitation alters dissolved organic matter composition and subsequent processing through the microbial loop. We examined a bacterial community dependent on carbon from the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum to investigate how iron limitation alters bacterial carbon processing. By quantifying activity at single-cell-resolution with nanoSIMS, we found that iron limitation led to a 43% reduction in carbon-fixation but an 80% reduction in carbon transfer into bacterial biomass. Ultra-high-resolution exometabolomics revealed that iron limitation led to bacterial consumption of less labile compounds including aromatics, specific lipids, and nucleobases. A population of bacteria specific to the iron-deplete condition exhibited high anabolic activity yet low incorporation of newly fixed carbon, supporting a shift to consumption of compounds with longer residence times. From metagenome assembled genomes we identified candidate taxa and gene pathways responsible for this carbon processing shift. These results provide a mechanistic link between decreased carbon flow to bacteria under iron limitation and consumption of less labile exometabolites responsible for this decreased flow. This has implications for predicting organic matter composition and turnover in iron deplete surface oceans and manipulating algal-bacterial interactions in engineered systems.

items.title: Toward a comparative endocrinology of aging: insights from insects.
items.abstract: Insulin-like signaling modulates aging and lifespan in insects. Here, we discuss a novel view of this control: insulin hormone in the adult regulates the production of the sesquiterpenoid juvenile hormone (JH) that in turn acts as the systemic regulator of aging and lifespan. Work in Drosophila establishes that insulin signaling is allatotropic - it stimulates the production and secretion of JH from the corpora allata. JH then exerts systemic effects on adult survival through its control of specific proteins, translation and proteostasis. The interdependent functions of insulin and JH allow reproduction and longevity to be coupled in many insects or decoupled in social insects with long-lived queens and in some long-lived genetic mutants of Drosophila. Features of these insulin-regulated life history syndromes are also found in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans. Recognizing the systemic role of JH in aging provides grounds to search for analogous systems in mammals that might modulate human lifespan.

items.title: Mechanisms of nitrogen-form preference in shoots and roots of invasive and native Xanthium species.
items.abstract: Background Nitrogen (N) form preference influences responses of invasive plants to soil N form changes caused by global change and the evolution of their invasiveness, and the differences in root uptake and shoot assimilation for different forms of N affect N form utilization in plants. However, the relative roles of shoots and roots in N-form preference are still unclear for invasive plants. Methods We grew the homo- and heterografted seedlings of the nitrate-preferred invasive plant Xanthium strumarium and the ammonium-preferred native plant X. sibiricum under two levels of nitrate and ammonium. Key results Under high N levels, the grafted seedlings with X. strumarium as scion, regardless of the source of the rootstock always preferred nitrate, whereas those with X. sibiricum as scion always preferred ammonium. Higher expression of nitrate reductase genes in leaves of X. strumarium relative to X. sibiricum was associated with its nitrate preference. Regardless of scion origin, the grafted seedlings with X. strumarium as rootstock always accumulated more total biomass and N than those with X. sibiricum as rootstock under both low and high N levels, which was associated with higher root surface area, volume, and NPF6.3 expression in the invasive relative to the native species. Conclusions Our results indicate that N-form preference was determined primarily by shoot identity, whereas roots contributed to the magnitude of the response, providing a novel perspective for understanding the mechanisms underlying exotic plant invasion from the viewpoint of N form utilization.

items.title: Genome shock in a migratory songbird hybrid zone.
items.abstract: The genome shock hypothesis proposes that hybridization destabilizes genome regulation, leading to increased chromatin accessibility, derepression of transposable elements (TEs), and potential reductions in hybrid fitness, contributing to speciation. While extensively studied in plants, evidence in vertebrates is limited. Here, we tested this hypothesis in a hybrid zone between two subspecies of Swainson's thrushes (Catharus ustulatus). We quantified genome-wide TE proportions, TE expression, and chromatin accessibility during both the migratory and non-migratory state using whole genome resequencing, RNA-seq, and ATAC-seq data from two migration-associated brain regions. Hybrids exhibited greater TE proportions, expression, and chromatin accessibility than parental lineages, providing the first direct evidence for genome shock in a wild avian system. TE expression and chromatin accessibility were positively correlated in all states and brain regions, but the strength of these patterns differed between states and tissues indicating that genome shock is context-dependent. Signatures of shock were localized in regulatory regions and associated with differential transcript factor binding sites linked to retinoic acid receptor signaling, a key pathway for seasonal and photoperiodic responses. Overlap between open chromatin, upregulated TEs and previously identified transgressively expressed genes in these hybrids suggest that genome shock extends beyond TE activation to directly affect gene expression. Our results motivate further investigation into genome shocks' effects on genomic incompatibilities, hybrid fitness, and speciation.

items.title: 4f-Electron-Regulated Dual-Periodic Bonding Evolution Across the Lanthanide Series.
items.abstract: Lanthanide-based catalysts have attracted increasing attention due to their unique electronic structures, yet the relationship between 4f electron evolution and catalytic behavior remains unclear. Here, using structurally uniform lanthanide single-atom catalysts as a model platform, we systematically investigate the influence of 4f electron filling on bonding evolution across the lanthanide series. We reveal a dual-periodic trend in lanthanide-support binding energies and adsorbate bonding energies, which increases from La to Eu and from Gd to Yb. This behavior originates from progressive electron redistribution between 5d and 4f orbitals, which modulates the electron population of bonding orbitals. The half-filled 4f 7 configuration induces an abrupt transition between Eu and Gd. Furthermore, similar crystal-field splitting enables robust linear relationships between binding and bonding energies across diverse coordination environments. More importantly, the persistence of these electronic characteristics across diverse coordination environments demonstrates that the dual-periodic evolution represents an intrinsic feature of lanthanide chemistry rather than a system-specific phenomenon. These findings establish a 4f-electron-regulated bonding framework for understanding lanthanide reactivity and guiding catalyst design.

items.title: Analysis of the phylogenetic position of Pseudexorchis Yamaguti, 1938 (Digenea: Opisthorchioidea) suggests new complexity in the relationships of the Cryptogonimidae.
items.abstract: Pseudexorchis Yamaguti, 1938 is a genus of opisthorchioid digeneans, which is currently classified as a member of the Heterophyidae. Only one species is recognised in this genus, Pseudexorchis major (Hasegawa, 1935), which parasitises freshwater silurid fishes as adults. The aim of this study is to evaluate the family affiliation of Pseudexorchis based on phylogenetic data. We obtained the sequences of several genetic markers from a single adult specimen of P. major ex Silurus asotus Linnaeus, 1758 from Japan, which allowed us to identify it as a member of a phylogenetic lineage previously named by Miura and Takisawa (2024) as Type B. The lineage Type B appeared as a sister to P. major Type A of Miura and Takisawa (2024). The degree of genetic differentiation between Type B and Type A, mainly based on the cox1 gene partial sequence, allows us to hypothesise the species status of these lineages. The trees based on 28S rRNA, 28S rRNA + ITS2 , and ITS1-5.8S-ITS2 datasets were most informative for phylogenetic inferences. In our analyses, Pseudexorchis was clustered with cryptogonimids Acanthostomum yahuarcaquense Cajiao-Mora and Bullard in Cajiao-Mora, Brule, Dutton, Caicedo-Portilla, and Bullard, 2025, Neocladocystis spp., Tanganyikatrema spp., and the nonugens KC489791 and KC489792 ( 28S rRNA-tree ), or only A. yahuarcaquense (28S rRNA + ITS2-tree), or Acanthostomum cf. americanum (Pérez-Vigueras, 1956) (ITS1-5.8S-ITS2-tree); the clade of these species was closer to the clade formed by opisthorchids and heterophyids than to other cryptogonimids. Thus, the presented data do not support the hypothesis that Pseudexorchis belongs to the Heterophyidae and demonstrate paraphyly of the Cryptogonimidae.

items.title: Effects of predator recovery and climate change on the long-term demography of a flagship herbivore.
items.abstract: Large herbivores play important roles in ecosystems across the globe, but limitations to study and inference have left gaps in predictive theories of their population dynamics, particularly following carnivore recoveries. Studies using spatial variation have explored the broad patterns of top-down and bottom-up forces in large herbivores. However, temporal changes in a population provide the most direct evidence for predicting future effects, and long-term studies spanning variation in top-down and bottom-up forces remain rare. We used 36 years of data on elk (Cervus canadensis) in the western United States in an integrated population model to test the effects of top-down (Puma concolor recovery) and bottom-up (drought) forces on pregnancy rates and age-based survival across a range of elk densities in the context of human harvest. We then quantified the proportion of variance in population growth attributable to those forces relative to the influences of harvest, age structure and unmodelled variation in demographic rates. Both top-down and bottom-up forces had measurable effects on elk population dynamics, with puma recovery reducing survival in the first 2 years of life and drought reducing pregnancy probability and survival at all ages. We also found negative density dependence in pregnancy, consistent with bottom-up control and positive density dependence in survival of young, consistent with predator swamping. Harvest explained the greatest proportion of variation in population growth (26%). Of the non-harvest parameters, drought severity had the largest effect, explaining as much variation (16%) as all of the unmodelled changes in demographic rates. Puma recovery explained 13% of the variation, and density dependence explained 8%. Without more long-term studies spanning sufficient ecological variation, the predictive abilities of large herbivore ecology will remain limited. With ongoing anthropogenic changes to the forces acting on large herbivores around the world, improving predictions will be invaluable to conservation.

items.title: Early-life bovine respiratory virome analysis reveals phage-driven adaptation and cross-host evolutionary signatures.
items.abstract: Past outbreaks of zoonotic viral infections highlight the importance of understanding respiratory virome ecology. As major food-producing animals with frequent human contact, cattle represent a critical host at the human-animal interface; however, the early-life establishment of their respiratory virome and its evolutionary connections to viruses from other hosts remain underexplored. Here, we longitudinally profile the upper respiratory tract (URT) virome of beef calves from birth to weaning using an optimized viral enrichment procedure and metagenomic workflow. Viral communities exhibited increased richness and turnover, reflecting ecological structuring during early life. Temperate phages dominate the URT phage community and share virulence- and mobility-associated genes with bacterial hosts, likely contributing to host adaptation and colonization persistence. Vertebrate-associated viruses emerge after the first week of life. Targeted reassembly from bovine URT viromes recovers near-complete betacoronavirus-like (CoV-D180) and adenovirus-like (AdV-D56) genomes positioned phylogenetically between bovine and human viral lineages. Competitive mapping of bovine-derived CoV-D180 and AdV-D56 to human respiratory metatranscriptomic datasets reveals genome-specific, regionally structured coverage patterns distinct from reference viruses, supporting shared sequence features in conserved genomic regions across host-associated viral lineages. Collectively, these findings reveal early-life assembly dynamics of the bovine respiratory virome and highlight cross-host signatures in a One Health framework.

items.abstract: Filamentous fungi generate chemical diversity through several evolutionary strategies, including the elaboration of conserved biosynthetic intermediates into structurally distinct secondary metabolites. Emodin and its corresponding anthrone are central intermediates in fungal aromatic polyketide metabolism, yet the enzymatic logic that remodels these precursors into more complex scaffolds remains incompletely understood. To investigate this process, we examined an infection-responsive non-reducing polyketide synthase biosynthetic gene cluster ( barc ) from the entomopathogenic fungus Metarhizium anisopliae predicted to encode an emodin-derived aromatic polyketide pathway. Heterologous reconstruction of the barc cluster in Aspergillus nidulans led to the production of the previously reported diphenyl ether barceloneic acid A (1) and the xanthene barceloneic acid C2 (2), together with two new compounds derived from 2, barceloneic acids D and E (3 and 4). Compound 3 is a cyclopentanone adduct of the xanthene 2, whereas 4 is a polyketide-indole hybrid, highlighting the chemical reactivity of the xanthene 2 scaffold. Through combinatorial heterologous expression and feeding assays, we identified a predicted glucose-methanol-choline oxidoreductase (BarcL) as the enzyme responsible for converting diphenyl ether 1 to xanthene 2. This defines a previously uncharacterised oxidative scaffold-remodelling step in barceloneic acid biosynthesis, revealing how an emodin-derived pathway can access a xanthene scaffold. Deletion of the backbone gene barcB in M. anisopliae did not significantly alter virulence towards Tenebrio molitor (mealworm) under the conditions tested, suggesting that barceloneic acids are not essential for pathogenicity in this insect model.

items.title: Spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula) nymphs demonstrate robust jumping and gripping performance following limb loss.
items.abstract: The spotted lanternfly (Lycorma delicatula) is an invasive hemipteran spreading across the USA. Eradication campaigns, such as 'See It, Squish It', rely on mechanical elimination. However, lanternflies often escape by executing hindlimb-driven leaps. Although escape rates remain unquantified, the physical nature of these eradication attempts likely results in individuals surviving with damaged/missing limbs. Lanternflies do not exhibit limb autotomy, and it remains unclear how well they tolerate injury. To evaluate the effects of limb loss on locomotor performance, we amputated a single forelimb, midlimb or hindlimb in lanternfly nymphs and measured three ecologically relevant metrics: jumping and climbing velocity and pull strength. We also tracked recovery over several days post-amputation for jumping and climbing trials. Jumping velocity and pull strength were unaffected by limb removal. In contrast, climbing velocity declined significantly across all groups, with the greatest reductions observed following forelimb and hindlimb removal. This decrease in climbing velocity was associated with changes in both stride length and stride frequency. However, because climbing velocity also declined in the control group, it remains unclear whether limb amputation alone - or the intervention itself - was responsible for these effects. No evidence of performance recovery was observed over time. These findings demonstrate the fault-tolerant nature of the lanternfly locomotor system, likely supported by mechanical redundancy and decentralized neuromuscular control. The ability to maintain essential behaviors following limb loss may represent a complementary evolutionary strategy to autotomy, centered on resilience rather than pre-programed limb sacrifice. This performance robustness likely contributes to the lanternfly's invasive success.

items.title: Propofol Modulates Fear Memory Reconsolidation by Inhibiting D2 Receptor-Expressing Neurons in the Medial Prefrontal Cortex.
items.abstract: Fear memory reconsolidation provides a temporal window for modifying established fear memories, yet the underlying cellular and neural circuit mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Using in vivo fiber photometry and chemogenetic approaches in freely moving mice, we show that propofol modulates fear memory reconsolidation by inhibiting D2 receptor-expressing neurons in the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC). These neurons exhibit heightened activity during fear memory reconsolidation and project prominently to the basolateral amygdala (BLA). Notably, local pharmacological activation of D2 receptors in the mPFC recapitulates the fear-attenuating effect of propofol when administered during the reconsolidation window. Circuit-level investigations further show that propofol suppresses the reconsolidation-associated enhancement of the mPFC D2 -BLA synaptic transmission, and chemogenetic activation of this projection counteracts the effect of propofol on fear memory reconsolidation. Moreover, selective knockdown of D2 receptors in BLA-projecting mPFC neurons diminishes the effect of propofol, supporting a critical role for D2 receptor signaling within this projection-defined circuit. Together, these findings identify the mPFC D2 -BLA circuit as a key neural substrate through which propofol modulates fear memory reconsolidation and highlight prefrontal D2 receptor signaling as a potential target for reconsolidation-based interventions aimed at maladaptive fear memories.

items.title: Only Your Mind Sets the Limits: Socio-Cognitive Pathways between Growth Mindset and Reading Achievement Across Nordic and Chinese Educational Systems.
items.abstract: Background Mindset theory has increasingly shifted from asking whether growth mindsets predict achievement to asking how, for whom, and under what conditions beliefs about intelligence become motivationally consequential. Aims This study contributes to that theoretical shift by examining mindset as a distal belief embedded within a broader social-cognitive system of achievement motivation. Sample and methods Using PISA 2018 data on 36,905 15-year-old students in Denmark, Finland, Sweden, Hong Kong, and Beijing-Shanghai-Jiangsu-Zhejiang, China, we modeled associations among mindset, socioeconomic background, mastery goals, motivation to master school tasks, reading self-concept, general self-efficacy, fear of failure, and reading achievement through a multi-group path analysis approach. Results Model results showed that a growth mindset was positively associated with reading achievement in the Nordic countries, unrelated to achievement in Hong Kong, and negatively associated with achievement in B-S-J-Z China. Indirect effects were generally small, while reading self-concept emerged as the most consistent proximal correlate of achievement. These patterns suggest that mindset is best understood not as a universal predictor of achievement but as a context-sensitive component within culturally situated socio-cognitive systems. Conclusions The study, therefore, uses cross-national evidence to refine the theoretical placement of mindset within achievement motivation, highlighting the importance of mechanisms, proximal competence beliefs, and cultural boundary conditions.

items.title: Prospective Associations Between Emotion Dysregulation, Problematic Internet Use, Internalizing Symptoms, and Life Satisfaction: A Baseline-Adjusted Two-Wave Study of Polish Adults.
items.abstract: Longitudinal evidence remains limited on whether the association between problematic Internet use (PIU) and life satisfaction persists after accounting for prior PIU, internalizing symptoms, and life satisfaction. This study examined whether baseline emotion regulation difficulties prospectively predicted PIU, depressive and generalized anxiety symptoms, and life satisfaction 6 months later. Participants were 2,122 Polish adults aged 19-98 years; 1,412 completed follow-up. All constructs were assessed at both waves. Baseline-adjusted path models used 50 multiply imputed datasets. Baseline emotion dysregulation predicted higher PIU (β = 0.155, 95 percent confidence interval [CI] [0.107, 0.204], p < 0.001) and internalizing symptoms at follow-up. Within T2, PIU was positively associated with internalizing symptoms, which were negatively associated with life satisfaction; direct PIU-life satisfaction paths were negligible (depressive symptoms: β = 0.004, 95 percent CI [-0.035, 0.042], p = 0.846; generalized anxiety symptoms: β = 0.002, 95 percent CI [-0.037, 0.041], p = 0.926). The serial indirect associations were statistically significant but very small: depressive symptoms, β = -0.004, 95 percent CI [-0.006, -0.002], p < 0.001; generalized anxiety symptoms, β = -0.004, 95 percent CI [-0.006, -0.001], p = 0.002. Reciprocal prospective sensitivity models showed small PIU-to-symptom associations but no prospective PIU-to-life-satisfaction association. Other sensitivity analyses did not materially alter the findings. The findings highlight the contribution of internalizing symptoms to the PIU-life satisfaction association after baseline adjustment, but same-wave indirect pathways do not establish temporal mediation or intervention benefits.

items.title: Disordered Eating Symptom Profiles in Low-Income, Racially Minoritized Adults.
items.abstract: Eating disorder (ED) research has traditionally assumed that symptoms cluster in the same way across populations. If this assumption is incorrect, models and assessment tools developed with advantaged samples may miss substantial symptom burden in marginalized populations. We investigated, for the first time, how ED symptoms cluster in racially minoritized, low-income adults. We used latent profile analysis to identify empirically derived ED symptom profiles in an intersectionally marginalized sample of women and men living in Detroit (N = 561; 87.5% Black; modal annual income < $10,000). We then applied BCH estimation to examine how demographic factors (age, sex, racial identity, and body mass index [BMI]) related to profile membership. The best-fitting model included seven profiles, some of which meaningfully differed from existing ED diagnostic categories and clinical heuristics. For example, two elevated symptom profiles were predominantly male, and participants in the profiles with the highest levels of restraint also had the highest BMIs. The highest levels of binge eating were observed in participants with relatively low co-occurring restraint. The most acute symptom profile was characterized by high body dissatisfaction, anxiety, depression, and restraint due to both monetary and weight/shape concerns. Disordered eating may present differently in disadvantaged populations, with decoupling of mechanisms that are more tightly linked in relatively advantaged settings (e.g., binge eating and restraint). Co-occurring restraint due to monetary and weight/shape concerns appears to be common, highlighting the importance of attending to multiple drivers of disordered eating in individuals from marginalized backgrounds.

items.title: What can machine learning discover about the nature of emotion?
items.abstract: The science of emotion increasingly relies on machine learning (ML) in the hope of making objective discoveries that resolve century-long debates. We examine research strategies in two main research traditions and show how confirmation bias can arise when theory-based hypotheses are evaluated using theory-laden sampling strategies, model specifications, and inferences. Each tradition manifests its theoretical differences in its ML methods, and, therefore, ML methods cannot settle those differences. The reciprocal relationships between starting assumptions, findings, and conclusions illustrate that ML investigations of emotion, like all scientific investigations, are never free from human experience and beliefs; however, they can be made less biased through a theory-aware research strategy to generate more justified knowledge about emotion.

items.title: Profiles of Youth With Predominantly Inattentive Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder in a Nationwide Clinical Sample in Iceland.
items.abstract: This study aimed to examine comorbidity, emotional symptoms, and cognitive profiles of youth with predominantly inattentive attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD-I) using a large nationwide clinical sample based on in-person assessments using gold-standard diagnostic procedures. Participants were 2109 children (64.7% male) aged 5-18 (M = 10.10) diagnosed with either ADHD-I (n = 636) or combined presentation (ADHD-C; n = 1473). Diagnoses of ADHD and comorbid psychiatric conditions were determined with the Schedule for Affective Disorders and Schizophrenia for School-Age Children-Present and Lifetime version (K-SADS-PL) and the Anxiety Disorders Interview Schedule for Children (ADIS-C/P). Additional measures included the Wechsler Intelligence Scale for Children (WISC-IV) and parent/teacher reports on the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire. Children with ADHD-I were, on average, 2 years older at the time of diagnosis than those with ADHD-C. Anxiety disorders, autism, depressive disorders, and tic/Tourette's disorder were equally prevalent across both the ADHD-I and ADHD-C groups. On cognitive testing, the ADHD-I group scored significantly lower on verbal comprehension (VCI), processing speed (PSI), and working memory (WMI) compared with the ADHD-C group. Findings highlight distinct challenges for youth with ADHD-I in this nationwide clinical sample. These youth are more often identified later and perform worse on certain cognitive tasks. Notably, they have a remarkably higher prevalence of comorbidities, such as anxiety disorders, than the worldwide prevalence of mental disorders in children and adolescents. The results underscore the importance of earlier screening and appropriate interventions for children presenting primarily with inattentive symptoms.

items.title: Neural, vascular, motor and autonomic habituation to high-intensity auditory stimulation: A multimodal characterization of the human defensive responses.
items.abstract: The defense reflex has been extensively characterized across sensory modalities; however, the integration of electrical, neurovascular, motor, and peripheral autonomic responses involving the central and autonomic nervous systems remains poorly understood. This study investigated defensive responses to high-intensity auditory stimulation using a multimodal approach combining electroencephalography (EEG), functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS), and peripheral physiological measures. Participants were exposed to twenty white-noise bursts (100 dB, 500 ms, instantaneous rise time) separated by silent intervals (50 ± 10 s), grouped into five blocks to assess initial responses and habituation. Hemodynamic responses revealed widespread activation of bilateral auditory and frontal regions following stimulus onset, with a progressive reduction in response amplitude and extension of active channels across blocks. Network analysis suggests progressive reorganization of functional connectivity between sensory and frontal regions across repeated stimulation. At the peripheral level, habituation was observed in phasic electrodermal activity, vascular indices, motor response, EEG-derived ocular activity, and parasympathetic cardiac modulation, primarily after the first block, whereas respiratory measures remained stable. Cardiac defense-like responses show a multi-temporal component structure, with habituation restricted to the late decelerative phase. Multivariate analyses revealed a structured yet partially independent organization of neural and autonomic responses to habituation. Together, these findings provide a comprehensive characterization of multisystem responses to intense auditory stimulation, highlighting selective habituation across central, neurovascular, motor, and autonomic systems, and offering new insights into how neurovascular and peripheral processes adapt to repeated auditory threats.

items.title: Ligand-specific effects of 5-HT2A receptor antagonists on fear extinction in C57BL/6J mice: Comparative insights from MDL 11,939 and MDL 100,907.
items.abstract: Serotonin (5-HT) 2A receptors (5-HT 2 AR) modulate corticolimbic circuits underlying fear extinction, but the behavioral consequences of 5-HT 2 AR antagonism during extinction remain poorly defined. Here, we examined the systemic effects of the 5-HT 2 A/ 2 C antagonist MDL 11,939 (Glemanserin) and the selective 5-HT 2 A antagonist MDL 100,907 (Volinanserin) on fear extinction in adult female and male C57BL/6J mice. Prior to drug administration, mice acquired comparable conditioned freezing responses during delay fear conditioning. Twenty-four hours later, acute administration of MDL 11,939 (1.0 mg/kg) or MDL 100,907 (0.01 mg/kg) increased freezing to the first conditioned stimulus (CS) presentation on Extinction Day 1 in males, indicating enhanced expression of conditioned fear. Repeated administration of MDL 11,939 significantly impaired extinction in male mice, evidenced by increased freezing across extinction trials and an increased number of trials required to reach extinction criterion. Neither acute nor repeated MDL 11,939 altered extinction in female mice. In males, MDL 100,907 produced a transient increase in freezing during extinction but did not delay extinction acquisition and had no effect in females. Because MDL 11,939 has reported affinity for 5-HT 2 C receptors, we tested potential contributions of 5-HT 2 C receptor antagonism in a separate cohort of male mice given repeated administration of the selective 5-HT 2 C antagonist SB 242084 (0.25 or 0.5 mg/kg). Neither dose affected conditioned fear expression, extinction learning, or trials required to reach extinction criterion. Together, these findings demonstrate ligand-, sex-, and dose-dependent effects of 5-HT 2 AR antagonism on fear extinction and suggest that distinct intracellular receptor signaling mechanisms may differentially regulate extinction-related behavior.
