items.title: Insights from the young people who serve on youth advisory councils in Africa: a mixed-methods study.
items.abstract: Youth Advisory Councils (YAC) are increasingly recognized as key mechanisms to promote meaningful youth engagement. Despite the rapidly growing adolescent population in Africa, existing research on youth engagement largely focuses on barriers to youth engagement in non-African contexts. This mixed-methods study expands understanding of youth engagement by examining who participates in YACs in Africa, how YAC members in Africa define meaningful youth engagement, and what factors facilitate their participation. This cross-sectional study draws on quantitative surveys (n = 154) and qualitative interviews (n = 14) with current or past YAC members living in Africa (aged 18-30 years old). Quantitative data were summarized using descriptive statistics and interviews were analyzed thematically. Findings from both sources were triangulated to identify key patterns. Participants resided across 15 countries, and the majority were current YAC members (94.2%). Despite diverse experiences within their roles on advisory councils, YAC members shared a common conceptualization of meaningful youth engagement, including co-creating and valuing youth voices. Further, YAC members voiced that co-creating and valuing youth voices is attainable through two key factors: integrating youth perspectives into organizational frameworks and providing key support. However, many participants' lived experiences as youth advisors fell short of true meaningful youth engagement. Our findings underscore the importance of youth-led engagement in Africa and organizational support to foster meaningful youth engagement, particularly in light of the continent's rapidly expanding youth demographic. Engaging and amplifying the voices of adolescents when developing policies and advocating for solutions is essential for both youth development and social and economic outcomes.

items.title: Evaluation of antibacterial activity of hydroethanolic seed extract of Descurainia sophia against multidrug-resistant Salmonella typhi isolated from typhoid patients: an integrated in silico and in vitro study.
items.abstract: Typhoid fever caused by Salmonella typhi remains a major public health problem, and multidrug-resistant (MDR) and extensively drug-resistant strains have left few oral treatment options in endemic regions such as Pakistan. Seeds of Descurainia sophia (L.) are used in Unani and folk medicine for febrile illness and contain cardenolides, glucosinolate-derived isothiocyanates and long-chain fatty acids, but their activity against MDR S. typhi and a plausible molecular target have not been examined. We therefore combined in silico and in vitro approaches to evaluate a hydroethanolic seed extract against clinical MDR S. typhi isolates. A library of 14 literature-reported seed compounds was screened by ADMET profiling (admetSAR 3.0), which selected three drug-like cardenolides (helveticoside, evomonoside and strophanthidin); these were docked against DNA gyrase A with moxifloxacin and gemifloxacin as references, and the top-ranked lead, helveticoside, was then examined in a 50 ns all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulation. The extract was characterised by GC-MS and FTIR and tested against five MDR isolates (MDR-ST1 to MDR-ST5) by disc diffusion and broth microdilution (CLSI M07). GC-MS confirmed 13 of the 14 library compounds (91.4% of total ion chromatogram area), including the three leads; erysimoside was the only compound not detected. Helveticoside (- 9.7 kcal/mol) and evomonoside (- 9.5) showed higher predicted affinities than moxifloxacin (- 7.9) and gemifloxacin (- 8.2); strophanthidin scored - 8.5. In the MD simulation, the helveticoside complex remained stable (ligand RMSD ~ 1.8 Å without dissociation; protein Cα RMSD ~ 2.2-2.5 Å after ~ 15 ns), and 12 residues, including ARG31, SER185 and GLN288, contacted the ligand in > 95% of frames, six of them also present in the docked pose. The extract inhibited all five isolates in a dose-dependent manner (mean zone of inhibition 11.5-17.15 mm at 25-100 mg/mL; 19.3 ± 0.9 mm for moxifloxacin, reported descriptively because the extract is crude), with a geometric mean MIC of 8.4 mg/mL (range 6.25-12.5) and MBC/MIC = 2 for all isolates, consistent with bactericidal activity. FTIR showed functional groups consistent with the major constituent classes.Docking and MD together generate the hypothesis that DNA gyrase A inhibition by cardenolide constituents may contribute to the antibacterial effect of the extract. The MD simulation supports the structural stability of the predicted helveticoside binding mode but does not demonstrate enzyme inhibition, and fatty acids and isothiocyanates in the extract may also contribute. Overall, the crude extract showed in vitro antibacterial activity against MDR S. typhi at high concentrations, and the study provides a testable mechanistic hypothesis that requires bioactivity-guided fractionation, pure-compound testing and target-engagement assays.

items.title: Impaired cortical inhibition in blepharospasm: evidence from reduced short-latency afferent inhibition and shortened cortical silent period.
items.abstract: Blepharospasm (BSP) is a neural network disorder with poorly understood cortical electrophysiological mechanisms. To investigate intracortical excitability and sensorimotor pathways in BSP patients and evaluate the effects of botulinum toxin A (BoNT-A) on cortical activity. Thirty BSP patients and 20 healthy controls underwent single- and paired-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) to assess indices including SAI, CSP, SICI, and ICF. Sixteen treatment-naive patients were reassessed one month post-BoNT-A injection. BSP patients showed significantly reduced SAI and shortened CSP compared to controls. Impaired SAI strongly correlated with disease severity scores (BFMDRS and GDSRS: r ranging from 0.514 to0.782, p < 0.01). SICI and ICF showed no group differences. Furthermore, BoNT-A treatment failed to reverse these central cortical abnormalities.Notably, these deficits were recorded from the clinically unaffected abductor pollicis brevis muscle and therefore represent widespread cortical trait markers rather direct evidence of dysfunction within the eyelid circuit itself. BSP is characterized by impaired cortical inhibition that is consistent with cholinergic dysfunction. BoNT-A relieves symptoms peripherally without altering fundamental central cortical excitability.The cortical deficits, recorded from an unaffected limb, indicate a generalised rather than eyelid-specific abnormality.

items.title: Construction of a machine learning model for dual-region typing of norovirus RdRp and VP1 based on genomic k-mer features.
items.abstract: Norovirus (NoV), a major global acute gastroenteritis pathogen, has high genetic diversity. Developing precise, rapid typing methods is crucial for epidemic control and vaccine development. Thus, this study develops a machine learning tool based on Norovirus genomic k-mer (length-k nucleotide fragments) features. It enables rapid, accurate dual-region typing of RdRp (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase) and VP1 (major capsid protein) without alignment or segmentation. Using k-mer frequency features with k = 11, the MurmurHash3 algorithm maps the features to a 2²⁰-dimensional space and constructs a hash feature table. A random forest model comprising 500 decision trees is then used. Each tree randomly selects 20 features during node splitting. The model is trained and evaluated using a bootstrap sampling strategy (80% training and 20% out-of-bag estimation), and prediction confidence intervals are outputted. The typing accuracy rates for the RdRp region and VP1 region reached 97.6% and 99.3%, respectively. Analysis of precision, recall, and F1-score for each genotype in the test set showed that all metrics for the 40 RdRp genotypes and 34 VP1 genotypes were ≥ 0.9. Typing accuracy across all length intervals was ≥ 0.96. This study integrates machine learning and bioinformatics to develop a novel norovirus genome analysis tool. It enables precise genotyping despite multi-region interference and reveals hidden genomic information, supporting viral classification and tracing. The feature hashing and ensemble learning strategies overcome traditional dependencies on alignment and annotation, offering a universal, efficient, scalable framework for viral genome identification.

items.title: Pteryxin disarms MRSA by suppressing the CrtN-staphyloxanthin axis and mitigates osteomyelitis-associated bone damage.
items.abstract: Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) remains a major public health concern because of its resistance to commonly used antibiotics and its association with severe infections. Staphyloxanthin (STX), a membrane-associated carotenoid pigment, contributes to MRSA virulence by protecting bacterial cells against reactive oxygen species and host immune clearance. CrtN, a dehydrosqualene desaturase, catalyzes an essential step in STX biosynthesis and represents a potential antivirulence target. In this study, an STX inhibition assay identified pteryxin (PTX), a natural coumarin derivative, as an inhibitor of STX production, with an IC50 of 4.826 µg/mL (12.49 µM). At concentrations that did not measurably affect bacterial growth, PTX reduced STX-associated pigmentation, increased susceptibility to oxidative stress and whole-blood killing and altered membrane-associated properties of USA300. Biophysical analyses, including surface plasmon resonance, thermal shift assay, cellular thermal shift assay, and intrinsic fluorescence quenching, supported an interaction between PTX and CrtN. Molecular docking predicted a possible binding mode involving Arg330 and Ser349. PTX also improved survival in a Galleria mellonella infection model and attenuated bacterial burden and bone damage in an early-treatment rat model of MRSA-associated bone infection. These findings support PTX as a potential antivirulence agent that suppresses STX biosynthesis through a CrtN-associated mechanism.

items.title: Between-hospital variation in prices for robot-assisted surgery: a multilevel analysis of Korea's 2026 non-covered price disclosure data.
items.abstract: Robot-assisted surgery is not reimbursed by Korea's National Health Insurance, and hospitals set their own prices. In April 2026, procedure-specific codes for robot-assisted surgery were introduced into the national non-covered price disclosure system, enabling procedure-level comparisons of hospital-posted prices. We analyzed posted prices retrieved in October 2026 from the Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service: 733 hospital-procedure observations from 115 hospitals across 10 procedure-specific codes, using two-level linear mixed models of log-transformed posted minimum prices. For breast surgery, which has no specific code, we classified 318 hospital-defined items from 40 hospitals. Median posted minimum prices ranged from 7.00 to 10.00 million Korean won; within procedures, the 90th-percentile price was 1.7-2.6 times the 10th-percentile price. After adjustment for procedure type and measured hospital characteristics, the between-hospital share of residual log-price variance (intraclass correlation coefficient) was 0.54 (95% CI 0.38-0.62; 0.48 after excluding one outlying hospital). University-owned hospitals posted 15.2% lower minimum prices than private hospitals; public ownership, hospital type, bed count, and location were not significantly associated with minimum price. Each additional code with a reported price was associated with a 4.2% higher posted maximum price. Among breast surgery items, 20.1% did not specify the procedure, and 22.5% of hospitals posted prices by grade alone. Because these are posted prices, they do not show what patients paid or which price tier applied. Standardized procedure codes and transparent tier definitions could improve comparability.

items.title: Key highlights of the 2026 Taiwan Hypertension Society guidelines for the management of hypertension in older adults.
items.abstract: Taiwan, in common with other high-income East Asian societies, is experiencing rapid demographic aging. Hypertension is present in the majority of older adults and remains the leading modifiable determinant of cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in this population. Yet managing blood pressure (BP) in older adults differs qualitatively from managing it in younger patients: arterial stiffening, salt sensitivity, orthostatic BP dysregulation, atrial fibrillation, frailty, cognitive vulnerability, and multimorbidity collectively alter the benefit-harm balance in ways that conventional guidelines-designed predominantly around middle-aged trial populations-do not adequately capture. To address this gap, the Taiwan Hypertension Society (THS) published the 2026 Guidelines for the Management of Hypertension in Older Adults, endorsed by the Taiwan Society of Cardiology (TSOC), the Taiwan Association of Gerontology and Geriatrics (TAGG), and the Taiwan Society of Family Medicine (TSFM). The guideline comprises 63 actionable recommendations developed through PICO-formulated clinical questions, systematic evidence appraisal, and the GRADE approach, with structured expert consensus for areas of limited evidence. Key updates include a measurement-first framework centered on validated oscillometric devices and the 7-2-2 home BP monitoring (HBPM) protocol; age- and comorbidity-stratified systolic BP (SBP) targets with frailty-sensitive safeguards; structured lifestyle prescriptions packaged as the SP-ABCDE mnemonic; individualized pharmacological management with explicit deprescribing considerations; and dedicated sections on orthostatic hypotension, atrial fibrillation, cognitive impairment, and resistant hypertension. This article summarizes the major highlights and clinical implications of the 2026 THS Hypertension guideline for older adults. Key components of the 2026 Taiwan Hypertension Society (THS) Guidelines for the Management of Hypertension in Older Adults. The upper panels summarize the diagnostic and lifestyle foundations-including the 7-2-2 home blood pressure monitoring (HBPM) protocol and the SP-ABCDE lifestyle prescription-together with the age- and risk-stratified systolic blood pressure (SBP) targets. For the intensive-versus-standard target comparison, an SBP target of <130 mmHg is a Strong recommendation for general older adults aged 65-79 years but a Conditional recommendation for those aged ≥80 years; a more intensive target of <120 mmHg may be considered (Conditional recommendation) in high-risk older adults with two or more additional cardiovascular risk factors. The lower panels summarize precision targets and frailty safeguards-including individualized targets and deprescribing considerations in frail older adults-and emphasize accurate BP measurement as a patient-safety strategy, including screening for orthostatic hypotension to prevent falls and syncope. HBPM home blood pressure monitoring, OH orthostatic hypotension SBP systolic blood pressure.

items.title: Real-world associations of antipsychotic use with clinical outcomes in schizophrenia: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
items.abstract: To systematically synthesize evidence on the association between antipsychotic medication use and diverse outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia, we searched PubMed, Embase, PsycINFO, and Web of Science from inception to May 1, 2026. Eligible studies were observational studies reporting associations between antipsychotic use and clinical outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia. Two reviewers independently extracted data and assessed study quality. Data was synthesized using multilevel random-effects models. Outcomes were categorized into mortality (including all-cause and cause-specific), somatic disorders, and other clinical outcomes. Sixty-eight studies comprising 1,424,455 individuals were included. Among individuals with schizophrenia, antipsychotic use was associated with lower all-cause mortality (pooled estimate, 0.64; 95% CI, 0.54-0.77) and lower relapse risk (pooled estimate, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.12-0.99) compared with nonuse. In contrast, compared with nonuse, antipsychotic use was associated with higher risks of cancer (1.41; 95% CI, 1.17-1.69), fractures (1.35; 95% CI, 1.17-1.56), and lung infections (1.25; 95% CI, 1.04-1.51), whereas evidence for other outcomes was non-significant. Overall, the evidence base was limited, with several pooled estimates derived from a small number of studies. Subgroup analyses suggested variation by region and study design. Antipsychotic use was associated with lower all-cause mortality and relapse risk, alongside increased risks for some adverse outcomes such as fractures and lung infections. These findings should be interpreted cautiously, as residual confounding and bias may influence the observed associations and preclude causal interpretation. Further studies using rigorous designs are needed to clarify outcome-specific associations.

items.title: Five-Year Clinical Outcomes of Surgically Treated Different Types of Tibial Pilon Fractures.
items.abstract: Background Intra-articular distal tibial pilon fractures are most commonly caused by high-energy trauma and are often associated with severe soft-tissue injuries. The literature on medium-to-long-term clinical outcomes is limited. The purpose of this follow-up study was to evaluate the 5-year clinical outcomes and patient satisfaction among patients with different types of tibial pilon fractures. Methods One hundred twenty-six consecutive patients with operatively treated tibial pilon fractures were identified between 2012 and 2016 from a level 1 trauma center. A total of 105 patients (mean age 43 years, 30 females, 100% White, 100% European) were eligible for follow-up and were contacted 5 years after the initial trauma. Outcomes were assessed using a questionnaire, Foot and Ankle Outcome Score (FAOS), American Orthopaedic Foot and Ankle Society (AOFAS) score, functional tests, and posttraumatic osteoarthritis (OA) Kellgren-Lawrence (K-L) grade. For outcome analysis, patients were categorized into the following 3 groups according to AO-OTA fracture classification: type 43B2-B3 (Group 1), type 43C1-C2 (Group 2), and type 43C3 (Group 3) tibial pilon fractures. Results No statistically significant differences between study groups were observed in FAOS (mean 74, standard deviation [SD] 16.9) and AOFAS (mean 82, SD 12.7) scores. Posttraumatic OA (K-L grade 3-4) was diagnosed in 35% in Group 1, 8% in Group 2, and 48% in Group 3. Ten patients (8%) underwent ankle arthrodesis. The incidence of deep surgical-site infections increased with severity of fracture type (no patients in Group 1, 21% in Group 2, and 23% in Group 3). Two patients (1.6%) required below-the-knee amputation. Approximately 90% of the healthcare resources were needed within the first 2 years after injury; patients in Group 3 required the most surgeries and had the longest hospitalization. Conclusions Surgically treated pilon fractures seem to result in good mid-term clinical outcomes, even for severe C3 fractures. However, type C3 fractures had more complications and required more surgical interventions, including ankle arthrodeses, longer hospitalization, and additional other healthcare resources than the less severe fractures. Level of evidence Therapeutic Level III. See Instructions for Authors for a complete description of levels of evidence.

items.title: Honeycomb-Surfels: Compact Hexagonal Primitives for Efficient Scene Rendering and Reconstruction
items.abstract: Novel view synthesis and 3D reconstruction have advanced rapidly with radiance fields and splatting, yet their memory and computational demands limit their use in resource-constrained settings. We introduce Hexels: novel planar hexagonal surface elements with a first-order spatial color field for efficient 3D scene and 2D image representation. Hexels exploit locally planar regions with smoothly varying appearance using fewer, larger primitives. Their hexagonal support provides an area- and boundary-efficient domain, while the local color field captures appearance variation within each primitive. Across 34 scenes, Hexels improve PSNR over memory-matched 2DGS by 4.53-7.38 dB across datasets while requiring lower training VRAM. We further ablate Hexels by showing that per primitive, Hexels outperform 2DGS by upto 4.74 dB while using lower training VRAM and having 2.31 times faster FPS. Even in unconstrained settings, Hexels offers complementary quality-memory trade-offs. For efficient 3D surface reconstruction, Hexels reduce error by 28.9% compared with memory-matched 2DGS across 15 DTU scans. On 6 Tanks and Temples surface scenes, Hexels achieves the highest mean F1 among compared methods (34.38%, versus 31.72% for 2DGS). We further also show that Hexels, as a general primitive, improves 2D image representation over Image-GS. Hexels push the Pareto frontier on the quality-efficiency trade-off of surface-aligned primitives.

items.title: ThinkWorld: World Imagination Reinforces Chain-of-Dynamics Reasoning
items.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.

items.title: Attention as Lattice Gauge Theory: Relations Interact Only Through Wilson Loops
items.abstract: Relations compose through the entity they share - Alice is Bob's mother and Bob is Carol's father, so Alice is Carol's grandmother - and the order matters, since a father's mother is not a mother's father; verifying a composed relation means closing the loop. We show that if each entity's coordinate frame may be rotated independently (per-entity frame freedom), three things follow. In the pure-gauge sector, relations that share no cycle cannot interact at all. The only gauge-invariant score of a triangle is a class function of its holonomy $H = T_{ij} T_{jk} T_{ki}$ - a Wilson loop. And the only equivariant update of an edge is $U = Ψ(H)\, T_{ij}$ with $Ψ$ conjugation-equivariant. Edge attention by Wilson loops is therefore not one design among many but the unique form the symmetry permits. Three communities hold pieces of this form: the commuting-operator embeddings of knowledge graphs are its abelian (commuting) sector; AlphaFold's triangle update and the Edge Transformer have its shape - an edge updated through the third vertex - without its constraints; and lattice QCD builds it equivariantly on lattices. We instantiate the equivariant sub-family on general relational graphs as holonomy attention. With no training and composition alone, it infers unobserved $S_4$ relations on sparse graphs at 0.88 with a fifth of the edges corrupted, at or slightly below specialist synchronization algorithms, where every commutative architecture is capped at 0.083; its holonomy score flags corrupted triangles at AUC 0.99 where commuting scores are capped at 0.76 by a second selection rule, and it separates clusters without labels.

items.title: KPPax: preprocess differentiable kinetic ODE for machine learning in atmospheric chemistry
items.abstract: Atmospheric chemical mechanisms are commonly distributed in the language of the Kinetic PreProcessor (KPP), which generates efficient Fortran or C code but does not fit into the differentiable programming frameworks in which machine-learning models are developed. We present KPPax, a kinetic preprocessor that generates differentiable, just-in-time compiled, and vectorisable chemistry code in JAX from mechanisms written in the KPP language. KPPax evaluates the rate law with sparse operations in log space, which keeps it differentiable, and integrates the stiff system with the implicit solvers and the forward- and reverse-mode adjoints of the \texttt{diffrax} library, so that exact sensitivities are obtained without hand-derived adjoint code. We demonstrate two applications with the POLLU benchmark mechanism. In the first, the Fisher information matrix computed from an automatically differentiated Jacobian predicts, before any fit, which of the 25 rate coefficients a flow-tube-like design can identify, and noisy synthetic estimation confirms the predicted uncertainties of the nine identifiable rate coefficients to within about 30\% while revealing clusters of fast reactions of which only ratios are constrained. In the second, a neural-network correction of an emission inventory is trained offline on per-scenario 4D-Var retrievals and then fine-tuned online through the chemical model, which reduces the error of the biogenic correction by a factor of 2.4--5 and recovers information on low-temperature emissions that the individual retrievals lose. KPPax makes KPP mechanisms directly usable for parameter estimation and hybrid physics--machine-learning modelling.

items.title: Can LLMs Uncover Hidden Physical Laws through Free Exploration?
items.abstract: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.

items.title: MuonGS: Pretraining LLMs with Relaxed Weight-Norm Control
items.abstract: Weight decay and explicit weight-norm constraints improve optimizer performance in language model pretraining, yet a unified understanding of why such control helps and how much is needed remains incomplete. We analyze norm control in Muon over the entire training trajectory using the \emph{accumulated effective learning rate}, $C_T=\sum_{t<T}η_t/\|W_t\|_F$, where $η_t$ is the nominal learning rate and $η_t/\|W_t\|_F$ is the effective learning rate relative to the weight norm. For bounded update directions, accumulation over any training interval bounds relative weight displacement. We show that vanilla Muon can accumulate only logarithmically, potentially limiting exploration and helping explain its slower empirical progress, whereas MuonW and MuonH guarantee at least linear accumulation under the stated conditions. Going beyond bounded-norm control, we show that sufficiently slow norm growth guarantees faster accumulation than the logarithmic worst case, opening up less restrictive optimizer designs. Based on this insight, we propose MuonGS, which uses Gram--Schmidt (GS) projection to remove the radial component of each Muon update without fixing the weight norm. With bounded update directions and a constant nominal learning rate, we prove that the weight norm grows at most proportionally to $\sqrt{t}$ after $t$ steps. Consequently, MuonGS guarantees $C_T=Ω(\sqrt{T})$, with accumulation sustained even in later training. Further, for smooth scale-invariant objectives we establish its $O(T^{-1/2})$ stationarity guarantee. In pretraining experiments with 160M- and 400M-parameter dense models as well as a 135M active- and 1B total- parameter MoE model, MuonGS achieves lower validation perplexity than MuonH at long training horizons. In particular, for the dense model it achieves an estimated token-equivalent speedup up to about $15\%$ at matched validation loss to MuonH.

items.title: What Improves During Pretraining? Tracking Knowledge Acquisition with Point-in-Time Models
items.abstract: Language models pretrained on web corpora collected over multiple years learn both general and domain-specific knowledge. How these different kinds of knowledge are learned as pretraining progresses remains unclear. Recent point-in-time models trained on web snapshots from different years provide a way to probe how knowledge prevalence varies over time. Using these models, we propose a temporal variability score (TVS), defined as the coefficient of variation of an item's negative log-likelihood across models. A higher score suggests that the knowledge may be less consistently represented across years of web text. We evaluate six benchmarks covering diverse topics using six models from multiple open-source model families. We find that low- and high-TVS items are learned similarly early in training, but high-TVS items improve faster later on. At the end of the pretraining run, high-TVS items outperform low-TVS items in 34 of 36 model-benchmark settings, with an average advantage of 7.3 points of chance-normalized accuracy. This pattern is most robust on knowledge-intensive tasks, even when comparing items of similar difficulty. Our findings reveal differences in how knowledge is learned over the course of pretraining, with temporal variability providing a diagnostic of these learning dynamics beyond aggregate benchmark scores.

items.title: Rare, Relevant, and Still Wrong: How Memory Fails LLM Group Decisions
items.abstract: When an LLM group's discussion is compressed into a short memory for a final decision maker, what should the memory keep? Two natural heuristics keep the rarest claims or the claims relevant to the decision criteria. On hidden-profile tasks both look attractive, because how widely a fact is held is confounded with whether it helps. We introduce CrossProfile, a diagnostic benchmark of 60 templates with automatically verified answer keys, in which the ownership of supporting, decoy, and irrelevant facts is crossed while their text is held fixed (480 tasks). Across Qwen2.5-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, and two DeepSeek models, both heuristics fail in predictable places. Selecting by relevance readmits decoys, because decoys are on topic: even a perfect relevance filter loses 23 to 31 points to rarest-first selection in the classic hidden-profile configuration. Rarest-first selection is no better than random selection on average and wins only where the rare facts happen to be the useful ones. In both cases accuracy follows the balance of evidence the memory keeps, not the policy that kept it. The decision model adds a third failure, a form of social proof: it gives extra weight to facts attributed to many agents. Removing the attribution tags, or reassigning them at random with line order fixed, raises accuracy in the classic configuration by 13 to 24 points. In natural discussions the evidence is lost before any memory acts: the complete transcript yields lower accuracy than no notes at all.

items.title: VideoLVR: Latent Visual Reasoning over Grounded Video Evidence
items.abstract: Chain-of-thought reasoning has substantially advanced video understanding in multimodal large language models (MLLMs). However, language-based reasoning traces do not provide a reliable mechanism for models to revisit relevant visual evidence, leading to visual forgetting and impairing their ability to reason over video content. Existing approaches maintain visual grounding during reasoning in two main ways: they either refer to evidence using textual coordinates, which specify symbolic locations rather than the visual content itself, or reinsert cropped regions or frames into the multimodal context, preserving visual details at the cost of substantial context expansion. To address these limitations, we introduce VideoLVR, which constructs latent visual evidence from local regions at relevant video moments, thereby providing visual support for intermediate reasoning steps. To supervise latent visual evidence generation, we introduce a visual token prediction objective that formulates visual token reconstruction as prediction over a vocabulary derived from the input video, thereby unifying visual evidence reconstruction and text generation within the same token prediction framework. This shared prediction framework enables MLLMs to reason over interleaved text tokens and latent visual states while integrating evidence from different moments. We further extend VideoLVR to reinforcement learning by treating sampled visual tokens as actions alongside text tokens and jointly optimizing the policy using final-answer rewards. By efficiently revisiting task-relevant visual information during reasoning, VideoLVR improves video understanding without substantially expanding the multimodal context. Experiments on multiple video benchmarks demonstrate its effectiveness, especially on tasks requiring fine-grained visual evidence.

items.title: Beyond Answer Changes: Matched Same-Class Controls for Local Audio Evidence
items.abstract: For audio-language models, an answer change after a local sound-event edit can reflect a response to the event's class, sensitivity to waveform rewriting, or both. We compare matched same-class and different-class replacements of a queried event. Both use the same interval, level estimate, donor fitting, and crossfade, while the same-class replacement preserves the correct answer. Across 600 synthetic soundscapes and three models from two architecture families, different-class replacements produce 49.7 to 60.9 percentage points more answer changes than same-class replacements. Same-class accuracy remains within 5.2 percentage points of original accuracy. Among trials with correct original and same-class answers, soundscape-weighted selective accuracy for the inserted class is 73.7 to 81.9%, averaging eligible trials within each soundscape and then weighting eligible soundscapes equally. This protocol tests how model answers respond to local changes in event class.

items.title: MoI-Bench: A Benchmark for Image Generation and Editing on Mobile Devices
items.abstract: Developing on-device image models requires considering practical user needs, task types and device resource constraints. However, existing benchmarks provide limited guidance on identifying capability gaps between on-device models and server-side models. We introduce MoI-Bench, a benchmark grounded in mobile user needs, comprising 64 subtasks and 1150 samples. It defines 16 operations, such as removal and replacement, and eight visual target categories covering content such as portraits and text. These form two orthogonal axes whose applicable combinations define specific tasks, such as removing facial makeup. To better guide model improvement, we further propose MoI-Eval, which introduces task-specific criteria covering instruction following, visual quality and detail preservation. We further construct sample-level evaluation questions and aggregate their scores into overall quality and capability profiles along the operation, target and criteria axes. We evaluate representative on-device and server-side models and measure mobile deployment costs. Results show that this decoupled Operation x Target design provides finer-grained guidance for improving compact models. For example, it highlights the need to prioritize specific capability gaps (e.g., text-replacement) over broad application-level goals (e.g., improving text editing). Unlike conventional benchmarks that rank models using a single score, we introduce a two-dimensional Quality-Deployability capability map to assess models for practical mobile use. The map shows that current on-device models can achieve efficient generation or editing but expanding their task coverage deserves greater attention than further improving deployment efficiency. Further progress requires improving editing quality, particularly identity preservation and text rendering, while broadening task coverage.

items.title: GAS-PFN: Graph-Aware Spatiotemporal Prior-Data Fitted Networks for Zero-Shot Traffic Forecasting
items.abstract: Traffic forecasting requires modeling complex temporal dynamics and the spatial dependencies imposed by road topology. Supervised graph-based models achieve strong performance, but are often trained for a particular dataset and sensor graph, making deployment to new or evolving networks costly. Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) offer a zero-shot alternative by learning in-context inference from synthetic task priors, which provide an explicit mechanism for encoding domain-specific assumptions. Existing forecasting PFNs, however, do not explicitly represent the graph-structured dependencies governing traffic dynamics. To combine graph-aware traffic modeling with zero-shot adaptation, we introduce the Graph-Aware Spatiotemporal Prior-Data Fitted Network (GAS-PFN). GAS-PFN incorporates sampled road topology into its synthetic task prior through random-walk diffusion, teaching the model to learn graph-coupled dynamics during pretraining. Its co-designed inference architecture uses two mask-conditioned passes through a shared Transformer backbone to separately model sensor-specific temporal dynamics and spatiotemporal interactions among neighboring sensors before integrating their representations for prediction. This design enables GAS-PFN to use target-network structure and context without parameter updates. Across six benchmarks at the 90-minute horizon, GAS-PFN reduces MSE by 34.0% on average relative to TimePFN, its closest PFN-based predecessor. It also reduces MSE by 27.7% on average relative to four recent industry-developed general-purpose zero-shot forecasters. In this comparison, all models receive 90 minutes of contiguous recent history, and any additional context is drawn from each dataset's chronological training split. These results indicate that aligning PFN priors and inference architectures with graph structure improves in-context learning for zero-shot traffic forecasting.

items.title: Understanding the limits of latent world models
items.abstract: World models are widely proposed as core components for enabling agents to reason over long temporal and spatial horizons. Yet current evaluations often emphasize task performance while providing limited insight into whether learned world models acquire predictive latent dynamics that reflect the underlying structure of the environment. Here we introduce the concept of faithful latent world models as an equivariance condition between the environment's transition map and the learned latent dynamics. We propose latent rollout consistency (LRC) as a metric to evaluate action-conditioned latent prediction. Strikingly, we find that across the studied state of the art latent world models, none solves the task by actually faithfully modeling the dynamics of the environment.

items.title: REGER: Modeling inter-item Relations with Semantic IDs for Generative Recommendation
items.abstract: Personalized recommendation depends on learning semantic and collaborative relations among items from online content and user interactions. Generative recommendation (GR) offers a promising paradigm by autoregressively generating discrete semantic IDs (SIDs) of items. However, randomly initialized SID token embeddings and GR models trained from scratch do not directly inherit the semantic relations inherent in items, while inter-item collaborative relations are learned largely implicitly through token-level attention and next-token supervision. To address this limitation, we propose REGER, a unified framework that explicitly incorporates inter-item relations into semantic pretraining, history encoding, and SID generation. We pretrain the GR model through generative semantic retrieval, enabling it to inherit inter-item semantic similarity by learning to generate semantic neighbors' SIDs. We combine global attention with local attention aligned with SID boundaries to capture historical context and directed transitions between adjacent items. We further develop a theoretical framework for hierarchical preference decomposition over the SID prefix tree, proving an exact factorization of collaborative preference distributions and a weighted decomposition of item-level KL divergence into prefix-conditional KL divergences. Building on this analysis, we distill a discriminative teacher's full conditional distributions over all legal next tokens at ground-truth prefixes along the target SID path, jointly optimizing this objective with cross-entropy. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over existing GR baselines and support the effectiveness of the proposed preference distillation.

items.title: TeamGym: A Gym for Team Decision-Making by AI Agents with Distributed Information
items.abstract: Many real-world decisions require teams to integrate information distributed across participants. Yet AI agents are still primarily trained and benchmarked in isolation. We introduce TeamGym, an environment for evaluating and training language model-based agents on team decision-making problems constructed from real-world legal, finance, medical, and software engineering corpora. TeamGym introduces a method to identify a minimal set of facts, each element of which is necessary and all of which are collectively sufficient for a correct final decision, which we call pivotal information. This enables TeamGym to both control the distribution of pivotal information and track how well agents identify and integrate pivotal information when making team decisions. Examining 8 language models on 12 source corpora, we find that current AI agents often fail to effectively share information: Distributing pivotal information across participants lowers success rate by 22.9 percentage points on average relative to giving the same information to a single model (a communication gap). We also document that participants do not effectively retrieve decision-relevant information on their own: A team's success rate is lowered by a further 19.9 points when participants must identify and extract pivotal information from source material rather than receiving it directly (a retrieval gap). To help remedy these deficits, we use TeamGym to train policies through reinforcement learning on team decision loss. Across two policy-training experiments, we find that training improves final-decision quality and induces emergent coordination in participation, speaker selection, and communication, even though the reward evaluates only the final decision.

items.title: Gym-Anything-RT: Scaling Real-Time Environments for Vision-Language Agents
items.abstract: AI agents have made substantial progress in domains where they have a non-trivial amount of time to deliberate between actions, such as mathematics, software engineering, and performing tasks on desktop applications. It is less clear how such models fare in settings that demand real-time interaction, such as playing a video game or operating a physical device. In these settings, the environment state may evolve as the agent is reasoning, or even as the underlying model is performing a forward pass. To gain insight into the real-time interaction capabilities of vision-language agents, we introduce Gym-Anything-RT. Our key idea is to construct visual minigames that demand a portfolio of capabilities required for interactive real-time settings. Gym-Anything-RT uses an agentic pipeline to automatically generate such environments based on a taxonomy of six capabilities required for real-time interaction, including the ability to perceive the environment and act under an evolving environment state. A key feature of Gym-Anything-RT is that it allows for controlled comparison of real-time interaction capabilities: we can run the same minigame in real time, or pause or slow down the environment to relax the requirement for real-time actions. We use Gym-Anything-RT to construct 100 real-time minigames and evaluate AI agents on them. We find large capability gaps in real-time interaction. For example, GPT-6 Astra (xHigh) achieves a pass rate of only 9.0% on the real-time minigames, which rises to 75.0% when the environment is paused. We also identify intriguing behaviors by the most powerful frontier agents: for instance, when given the ability to write code, these agents write code that bypasses the need to perceive and act in real time. We publicly release Gym-Anything-RT and the generated minigames to spur further research on AI agents in real-time interactive settings.

items.title: When uncertainty quantification fails: structural vulnerabilities and corrections for selective prediction under clinical class imbalance
items.abstract: Background. Selective prediction systems improve the safety of clinical artificial intelligence by deferring ambiguous cases to human experts while automating high-confidence decisions. However, this safety mechanism relies entirely on the premise that uncertainty scores accurately reflect clinical ambiguity. In prognostic tasks characterized by severe class imbalance, where the clinical outcome of interest is a minority, this assumption breaks down. Standard uncertainty measures cease to capture clinically aligned ambiguity; instead, they become a proxy for class membership, systematically penalizing minority patients regardless of their individual predictive clarity. Results. Across 56 synthetic conditions and three neurodegenerative cohorts spanning severe class imbalance to near-balanced conditions (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson's Disease, Alzheimer's Disease), our framework consistently maintained bounded, balanced risk across trajectories. In contrast, global metrics either collapsed minority Sensitivity or protected the minority at the expense of majority patients. Applying CCR with standard entropy fails to protect the minority because it breaks within-class monotonicity when tau=0.5. Combining CCR with threshold-aware metrics restores strict monotonicity, correctly identifies ambiguous patients, and safely mitigates minority exclusion. Conclusions. Under clinical class imbalance, standard uncertainty quantification measures dataset sparsity rather than clinical ambiguity, creating a systemic illusion of safety. This bias is a correctable structural flaw. Clinical pipelines deploying selective prediction under imbalance should adopt threshold-aligned uncertainty measures and class-stratified evaluation. This reduces class-specific risk imbalance, supporting safer selective prediction under the evaluated conditions without silently excluding the most vulnerable patients.

items.title: Kinematic Constraint-Referenced Evaluation for Articulated Object Manipulation
items.abstract: Manipulation policies are evaluated predominantly by binary task success, which cannot tell whether the commanded gesture is the one the object's kinematics admit. We introduce Constraint-Referenced Strategy (CRS), which projects the commanded end-effector twist onto the object's joint axis, separating progress along the joint from off-constraint waste. CRS requires a joint model and a joint-following scripted controller derived from it, but no recorded demonstration or learned judge. On 74 simulated articulated objects, success registers three transfer failures as lower rates but attributes none, while the two CRS channels give each a distinct signature. A door-trained behavior-cloning policy opens drawers in 59 of 110 episodes, and in these passes it commands about $40\times$ the off-axis rotation of a drawer-trained policy's passes ($1.27$ vs.\ $0.032$~rad/s). Relative to a scripted controller scored with the same axis, CRS verdicts are unchanged under joint-axis errors up to $30^\circ$; absolute thresholds tolerate about $8^\circ$.

items.title: When, Where, and What to Correct: Human-Guided Adaptive Residual Correction for Robot Policies
items.abstract: Imitation policies that reliably execute most of a manipulation trajectory can still fail in localized regions requiring last-mile precision. Updating the full policy or exploring residual actions everywhere treats this local failure as a global learning problem. We introduce Adaptive Residual Correction (ARC), a lightweight post-training module that uses reinforcement learning (RL) to learn a residual correction on top of a frozen policy while using sparse human corrections to structure autonomous exploration. Rather than treating human corrections as imitation targets, ARC uses pre-intervention states to determine 'when' residual control should become active and correction geometry to determine 'where' in residual action space autonomous refinement should explore; task reward determines 'what' residual is ultimately executed. Across three precision-manipulation tasks on a real robot, ARC improves average task success from 33.3% to 75.0%. The human corrections define task-dependent 2-3 dimensional subspaces of the seven-joint residual space that retain 96.0-97.7% of squared correction magnitude. Together, these results show that sparse human corrections can localize and constrain autonomous post-training without requiring the observed correction itself to serve as the final action target.

items.title: GroundControl: Satellite-Conditioned Multi-View Diffusion for Reconstruction-Free Novel View Synthesis
items.abstract: Multi-view or video diffusion models have recently emerged as state-of-the-art approaches for novel-view synthesis from sparse image collections. While they can produce high quality images, they tend to hallucinate unrealistic spatial layouts when synthesizing views outside the input views (scene extrapolation). We propose to address this challenge for outdoor scenes by using satellite images as an additional information source to condition the multi-view generative model. We introduce a new satellite-conditioned multi-view diffusion model that combines conditioning from a satellite image and street-level input images when generating novel-views. Our cross-attention based conditioning allows us to retain pretrained multi-view diffusion priors to generate seamless, realistic, novel views from a handful of source views, while also adhering to the scene layout as seen from satellite images. Our model does not use 3D scene reconstruction, and only relies on posed street and satellite views. Our experiments on outdoor datasets show that our model is better than both satellite-conditioned or street-view conditioned baselines on novel-view synthesis, especially on challenging cases where target views have very little overlap with source views. items.title: Which Hand Was Late? Diagnosis for Robot Failure Recovery in Bimanual Tool Use
items.abstract: Failure diagnosers for robot manipulation are increasingly vision--language models (VLMs), trained and evaluated on single-arm failures produced by perturbing a successful demonstration. Bimanual tool use adds failures of other kinds: a tool that slips out of its socket while still held, two correct gestures made at different times, and attempts that fail for two reasons at once. On a simulated bimanual tool-use task whose failure causes are read from the recorded trace, we measure what each sensing channel lets a diagnoser tell. The tool's slip is read on the tool hand; which hand was late is read on both arms, while a sensor on one hand reads its own hand's delay and at most part of the other's; and whether a late attempt was also pushed too weakly is not identifiable from passive sensing when the tool hand is late. Within two attempts, a repair policy that escalates when the cause is not identifiable repairs as many failures as one told the true cause. A VLM's internal state carries the late hand almost perfectly, along a direction no closer to the one its answer reads than a random one; whether the answer reports it depends on the wording of the question.

items.title: The Structure Gap: When More Data Cannot Replace Structured Reasoning
items.abstract: A persistent belief in modern AI is that sufficiently large learners trained on sufficiently much data can make explicit domain knowledge optional. This paper examines a limitation of that belief. We define structure-encoded problems: tasks whose input-output map is determined, or sharply constrained, by known structure such as a solver, symmetry group, graph, physical law, measurement operator, grammar, combinatorial search space, or optimization objective. For such tasks, the central question is not expressivity--a dense neural network may contain the desired map--but finite-data identification, extrapolation, and certification. We introduce the structure gap: the finite-resource gap between a method that receives the governing structure and a learner that receives only examples. The strongest useful form of the claim is asymptotic rather than absolute: structure-agnostic learning may approach a structured solver as coverage grows, but every finite dataset can leave residual uncertainty that the structure resolves by construction. We prove this exactly for a Gaussian inverse problem: the known-operator Wiener solver attains Bayes risk, while the dense empirical learner in the correct linear class has persistent expected excess risk. We also prove a cell-coverage lower bound and an unobserved-orbit non-identifiability result. Controlled experiments in known-operator inversion, sparse recovery, and graph reachability with size extrapolation instantiate the mechanisms. When validated structure is available, it can constrain the hypothesis space before learning begins, leaving learning to address components the structure does not specify.

items.title: Orthogonal and Parametrized Multi-Attribute Steering of LLMs
items.abstract: Activation steering offers an effective and efficient way to modify an LLM's behavior at inference time. However, it remains unclear how to apply steering such that the signal is consistently strong and the steering strength has a universally interpretable meaning. We address this first by identifying the most steerable interval for each steering vector and rescaling the steering range accordingly. Building on this, we introduce a more interpretable method for steering, called parameterized steering which instead of pushing activations in a direction, it sets them at the desired trait strength. Next, with multi-trait steering, we find that naively combining vectors causes them to interfere with one another. In response, we develop a method to orthogonalize the vectors; it decouples these traits, allowing a model to exhibit one behavior without inducing the others, thus enabling multiple traits to be steered simultaneously.

items.title: Strategyproof Deep Reinforcement Learning for Online Resource Allocation
items.abstract: Online resource allocation faces two coupled challenges: (1) allocating scarce resources efficiently under uncertain future demand, and (2) ensuring that agents report task valuations and requirements truthfully (strategyproofness). Reinforcement Learning (RL) adapts allocation decisions through experience but does not necessarily ensure strategyproofness. Existing strategyproof RL uses a linear allocation rule, which limits the resource interactions it can represent. Neural mechanism design methods offer greater expressiveness, but provide only approximate incentive guarantees. Against this background, we introduce the first strategyproof deep RL mechanism for online resource allocation. It integrates three novel components: (i) a monotonic neural network that learns nonlinear interactions by construction (higher reported value cannot reduce acceptance, while a longer reported duration or larger resource requirement cannot increase it); (ii) a generalised critical payment: the lowest accepted value, with all other inputs fixed; and (iii) training by either RL or imitation of an existing rule. Together, monotonicity and the critical payment ensure strategyproofness and individual rationality, while the neural rule provides flexibility and imitation improves training efficiency. Empirically, on a four-resource stream with two partner pairs that a linear difference cannot represent, the neural rule achieves 97.8% of an offline welfare upper bound, compared with 93.8% for a linear learner and 89.0% for first-come, first-served, closing 65% and 80% of the remaining optimality gap, respectively. Moreover, imitation reaches 97.5% in only 261 seconds, about 89 times faster than RL.

items.title: From Interaction to Capability: Task Advancement as State and Supervision for GUI Agents
items.abstract: GUI memory should preserve the results of past actions and learn reusable operations. This is difficult in long-horizon workflows, where agents must use information across applications and useful operations are interleaved with failed attempts. We introduce Task Advancement Memory (TAM), which defines task advancement as verified task progress, and supports ongoing task execution and learns reusable operations. During execution, Task Advancement State represents how verified task progress changes the remaining goals, allowing the agent to build on earlier achievements across applications. After each task, advancement supervision identifies and abstracts the interactions that produced a verified local result. The learned operations preserve the relation between required inputs, expected outcomes, and verification conditions. This retains locally successful operations from both successful and failed tasks. On MobileWorld GUI-only tasks, Advancement State alone raises success from 12.0% to 28.2%. Full TAM achieves a 17.6% relative gain in task success over the strongest evaluated baseline and reduces lifecycle tokens per solved task by 38.7%. On SPA-Bench, TAM achieves state-of-the-art task success in the single-app English Level 3 setting.

items.title: Follow the Gradient: Tracing Safety Degradation Back to Training Data
items.abstract: Fine-tuning Large Language Models (LLMs) on instruction data can quietly erode their safety, even when no training example looks harmful. Because this safety-degrading data looks benign, standard content filters struggle to catch it. We tackle this problem by developing SimpleLoRIF, a scalable gradient embedding method that identifies fine-tuning examples whose gradients align with unsafe behavior. By simplifying a low-rank attribution method and restricting backpropagation to the final four transformer blocks, SimpleLoRIF can embed datasets on the order of a million examples, boosting gradient attribution from a small-scale analysis tool into a practical filter for full post-training datasets. We first validate it on emergent misalignment, where we find that gradients can connect insecure-code training data to the broadly harmful behaviors that appear after fine-tuning, with AUC as high as 0.865 in the gradient space of misaligned models. We then use SimpleLoRIF to build SafeTulu, a version of Tulu 3 with the 20% of examples most gradient-aligned with unsafe responses removed. Training on SafeTulu reduces GCG attack success rate by up to 22% across Qwen, Llama, and Olmo, outperforming both LLM-as-a-judge and prior gradient-based filtering, while largely preserving or even improving capability. Finally, we analyzed the removed data and identify possibly under-studied sources of safety degradation, such as tool-execution failures and narrative arithmetic. We release SafeTulu along with a Hugging Face Space that lets researchers build their own customized versions of SafeTulu to fine-tune on, such as by changing the removal fraction or filtering only certain subsets.

items.title: HGPRGDel: GPR-Aware Learning and Ranking for Growth-Coupled Gene Deletion Design
items.abstract: Designing microbial strains for growth-coupled production, in which cellular growth is linked to the synthesis of a target compound through genetic interventions, is a fundamental goal in metabolic engineering. Constraint-based methods can identify growth-coupled deletion strategies, but design for each target typically requires a separate search across a large number of possible gene-deletion combinations. This motivates a reusable approach that learns from previously evaluated strain designs to prioritize candidate interventions before downstream constraint-based evaluation. We present a reproducible protocol for growth-coupled gene deletion design that learns and ranks gene-deletion priorities for each target metabolite. Using computationally curated deletion strategies as learning resources, the protocol generates continuous deletion-priority rankings, constructs candidate strategies at adjustable search-space budgets, and evaluates these candidates through constraint-based metabolic analysis. Its learning component, HGPRGDel, explicitly represents gene-protein-reaction (GPR) logic, capturing how multiple genes can jointly support a reaction or alternative genes can maintain its activity, while integrating molecular and reaction-level information. Across e_coli_core, iMM904, and iML1515, the protocol achieves the highest macro-F1 and AUC among the evaluated learning configurations. HGPRGDel's rankings recovered an average of 90% of the reference deletion genes from MetNetComp by examining fewer genes than the evaluated baseline methods. By separating learned intervention prioritization from downstream constraint-based assessment, the protocol provides a reproducible framework for reusing strain-design knowledge while controlling the size of the candidate space and retaining mechanistic evaluation of growth-coupled production.

items.title: How Reliable Is Individualized Functional-Network Attribution in Resting-State fMRI Cognitive Prediction in ADNI?
items.abstract: Individualized attribution estimates which functional networks drive a model prediction for a given subject and is often proposed as an interpretable resting-state fMRI (rs-fMRI) biomarker, but its test-retest reliability is rarely quantified. We evaluate per-subject network-ablation attribution for a frozen resting-state functional connectivity (FC) predictor (Schaefer-200 FC predicting MMSE/ADAS-Cog13) trained on N=875 subjects from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), using, and (iii) a subject-level permutation null. Split-half reliability is near-ceiling (Spearman p=0.948/0.950) but drops on scan-rescan (p=0.609/0.616). Under the mismatched-subject null, correlations remain substantial (p~0.46-0.47), indicating strong population-shared structure, yet matched pairs exceed this null (z~6.6-6.9, p<=10-4). Thus, in ADNI, individualized network attribution contains a modest but non-zero person-specific component atop a strong population-shared pattern. We recommend reporting scan-rescan reliability together with a permutation-null control, rather than within-session proxies alone, to avoid overstating individual specificity.

items.title: PerceptRL: Making Visual Perception Rewardable in MLLMs from Answers to Interactions
items.abstract: Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.

items.title: Autonomous fixed-wing interception using reinforcement learning
items.abstract: Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.

items.title: Who Shaped What? Untangling Human and AI Creative Contributions Through Spatial Provenance in Image Editing
items.abstract: Images co-edited with AI are often labeled to disclose AI use. However, creators feel these labels do not sufficiently describe their contributions to the editing process. Editing histories preserve requests, suggestions, and revisions, but how do creators use these logs to judge contribution? We investigated this with Roop, a mixed-initiative design probe that links image regions to editing histories (spatial provenance) and summarizes interactions in a heat map. Twenty participants edited images, annotated human and AI contributions, then reviewed the spatial provenance heat map. Participants credited themselves for directing changes while crediting AI for determining visual details. They judged contribution partly by whether their interactions achieved their intentions. Reviewing provenance helped participants remember interactions without always changing whom they credited. These findings motivate provenance systems that preserve enough context for creators to explain how interactions shaped their work, alongside the record of what happened.

items.title: Concordat: Typed Sessions for LLM Agents
items.abstract: Agents built on large language models are increasingly allowed to take consequential actions: cancelling bookings, issuing refunds, changing accounts. The rules that govern those actions, such as "obtain the customer's explicit confirmation before changing anything", are usually stated in the prompt and followed only as reliably as the model chooses to follow them. We present Concordat, a Python library that treats an agent as an object whose interface is a finite-state protocol, in the spirit of typestate and session types, and enforces that protocol on the model at run time. On every turn the model is offered only the tools that are legal in the current protocol state, calls outside that set are rejected before they have side effects, decisions reserved for humans can only be requested, and token and tool-call budgets are charged and split linearly across handoffs. Protocols are checked when they are defined, and a subclass of an agent is rejected if it could bypass its parent's protocol, a behavioural form of Liskov substitution. We evaluate a Concordat agent against the standard agent of tau-bench on its 50 airline tasks, adding simulated customers who pressure the agent to skip confirmation. The standard agent made changes without the required "yes" in 13 of 50 tasks with gpt-4.1 and in 29 of 128 task-runs with Claude Haiku 5.5; the Concordat agent made none, with no significant difference in task success. tau-bench's own reward did not detect most of these violations. Concordat is open source.

items.title: M4Bench: Evaluating Procedural Specification for Clinical EHR Derivation Agents
items.abstract: Clinical research over electronic health records depends on derived variables whose definitions sit outside the schema, in item codes, time windows, missingness rules, and output-grain choices that change cohorts and downstream conclusions. We introduce M4Bench, 28 clinical derivation tasks across 15 task families on MIMIC-IV and eICU, to test whether AI coding agents can reproduce such derivations and how clinician-reviewed agent skills change their results. Its controls decompose the value of skills into specification completeness, delivery format, and schema familiarity. In a Docker-isolated Codex campaign (GPT 5.4 Mini and GPT 5.5), skills raise reward by 0.136 over the no-skill baseline, with 26 of 28 tasks improving. Specification completeness accounts for most of this gain: on an eight-task control subset, an operational spec alone raises reward by 0.162, and skills add only 0.024 on top, indistinguishable from zero. On a ten-task subset, decoy skills score like no skill and raw reference SQL nearly matches targeted skills, arguing against generic context or the skill format as the explanation. Schema obfuscation and restructuring preserve 86% and 70% of the skill gain (GPT 5.4 Mini, 26 MIMIC-IV tasks), a descriptive robustness check rather than a bound on memorization. A descriptive Claude Code replication on all 28 tasks (Opus 4.7 and Sonnet 4.6, 560 runs) is directionally consistent (+0.120, 21 of 28 tasks improving). These gains are partial agreement with the reference, not completed tasks: only 25 of 280 with-skill and 13 of 280 no-skill Codex runs pass every strict check, and skills barely change which rows agents return (key F1 +0.003). Skills are released as a versioned, clinician-reviewable markdown delivery format, with a family-level reference-validity audit. M4Bench releases tasks, skills, evaluation code, and sanitized per-run evidence as an open-source benchmark.

items.title: Test-Time Communication in Trading Agent Swarms
items.abstract: Communication between agents has mostly been studied on tasks with a shared objective and fast, clear feedback. Trading has neither: each agent manages its own account, with decisions being scored by markets late and noisily. A trading swarm is thus a population of independent decision-makers rather than a team, for which convergence is a risk and not the goal. We ran 200 agents from four model families in groups of ten under five communication regimes, from isolation to message boards and shared notes, over seven US trading days (1 to 9 October 2026), logging everything each agent read before every decision. In two of the four families, communicating groups came to hold far more of the same stocks than the isolated group. A group's return was largely the return on what its members held in common. Seeing a post from a groupmate made an agent 7 percentage points more likely to reuse an eight-word phrase from it. Agents that started too close together to see each other's posts shared such a phrase in 14% of cases, the rate that common inputs produce. Seeing the post did not detectably change that morning's trades. Case studies traced the adoption of positions and decision rules over subsequent days, and communicating groups sold in step more often than isolated ones. Because isolated groups also converged on the same stocks, sometimes completely, assessments of herding need to measure excess convergence relative to a no-peer baseline.

items.title: PolyGandr: Steering Generative Models via Spatial Navigation through Latent Space
items.abstract: Generative models support content creation across text, images, videos, and design disciplines, yet their interfaces rely primarily on natural language. While effective for specifying high-level intent, language can be inefficient and imprecise for fine-grained control, iterative refinement, and open-ended exploration. We present PolyGandr, a visual interface for exploring relationships between latent representations and generated outputs, complementing natural-language model steering. PolyGandr formulates generative control as high-dimensional navigation, enabling users to define starting points, steering directions, and step sizes through a unified map-and-mixing-palette interface. Combining global exploration with local refinement supports both broad design-space navigation and fine-grained output manipulation without repeatedly translating visual intent into prompts. We evaluate PolyGandr across three use cases: StyleGAN2 face generation, Stable Diffusion chair design, and rotational kirigami engineering. A formative study indicates that PolyGandr complements existing workflows by supporting real-time editing while simultaneously providing an overview and means to explore the broader design space.

items.title: Representing the Unseen: Rethinking Visual Imagination for Spatial Reasoning
items.abstract: Visual world models increasingly support spatial reasoning by generating RGB views of unobserved states. However, RGB has become the default interface largely because it is well suited for visual generation, rather than necessarily being the most effective representation for downstream reasoning. Different spatial questions may benefit from different representations of the same imagined state: top-down geometry can facilitate global distance comparisons, while panoramic views provide broader context for reasoning about open space. To isolate the role of representation in spatial imagination, we introduce ImagiRep, a simulator-grounded benchmark of 922 questions spanning seven question types across two settings, Viewpoint Imagination and Cross-view Integration, providing oracle RGB and six alternative representations (e.g., depth, panoramic views, and top-down geometry) of the same unobserved state. This controlled comparison reveals that even accurate imagined RGB does not guarantee accurate spatial reasoning, and different questions benefit from different representations. Similar trends hold for representations derived from world-model-estimated states. Notably, estimated RGB alone can mislead spatial reasoning, while alternative representations retain complementary benefits. Building on these findings, we introduce GEARS, a lightweight test-time strategy for adaptive representation selection, outperforming existing spatial imagination methods and showing that reasoning about unseen states requires more than generating RGB views.

items.title: FeatureArc: Benchmarking Coding Agents on Evolving Features
items.abstract: A software feature usually evolves over time: developers extend its first version as new use cases and requirements arrive, and each extension builds on code written earlier. Most feature benchmarks evaluate a single request on a fixed codebase. Feature evolution requires evaluating successive extensions on an agent's own earlier code and checking whether the feature remains correct. We introduce FeatureArc to evaluate coding agents on evolving features, together with a pipeline that constructs its tasks from repository histories. The benchmark combines dependencies between successive stages of the same feature, explicit requirements and interface contracts, and executable checks across four programming languages. The pipeline validates fail-to-pass (F2P) tests for new behavior and pass-to-pass (P2P) tests for existing behavior on the reference code before and after each stage. We evaluated 10 coding agents on 73 manually reviewed tasks of 2 to 10 stages. Each agent works in one persistent session and workspace without external test feedback or rollback. The evaluation reveals a gap between first-stage and whole-feature success: pooled success falls from 62.7% at the first stage to 28.5% when the whole feature is tested on the final code. Trajectory analysis identifies inherited defects as a common failure mechanism, present in 72.9% of failed later stages. These earlier errors often remain undetected: in stages following a failure, agents leave the earlier error unnoticed about 95% of the time, and their self-tests rarely revisit earlier stages. Evolving a feature autonomously, without human checks between stages, therefore remains a substantial challenge for current coding agents. At Tencent, the pipeline extends internal evaluations to this setting and guides the development of Hunyuan, Tencent's family of large language models.
