items.title: Bayes-Adaptive MDPs for Rollout Allocation to Enhance GRPO Training
items.abstract: Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has demonstrated strong performance in LLM post-training. However, it allocates a uniform rollout budget to every training question, ignoring variations in question difficulty. As a result, highly difficult questions may receive too few rollouts to generate informative positive reward signals, limiting their contribution to training, while moderately difficult questions often receive more rollouts than necessary. In this work, we formulate the problem of difficulty-aware rollout budget allocation to maximize training utility under the same total rollout budget as standard GRPO. We propose AdaRoll-GRPO, which reformulates rollout allocation as a sequential decision-making problem and leverages a Bayes-adaptive Markov decision process (MDP) to learn an adaptive allocation policy. The learned policy is computed offline and applied during GRPO training without introducing additional online optimization overhead. Extensive experiments on multiple reasoning datasets and LLM architectures demonstrate that AdaRoll-GRPO consistently improves GRPO training performance under a fixed rollout budget, highlighting the effectiveness of adaptive rollout allocation for GRPO in LLM post-training.

items.title: Time-Dynamic Semantic-Activity Entanglement: Quantifying Communication-Based Synchrony in Collaborative VR
items.abstract: Collaborative virtual reality (VR) produces rich multimodal traces of team behavior, yet practical methods for characterizing time-varying team communication remain limited. We present time-dynamic semantic-activity entanglement (TSAE), inspired by the entanglement concept introduced by Gloor et al. (2022), to describe communication-based team synchronization within discrete time windows. TSAE is modeled by combining relative speaking activity with contextual semantic alignment for participant pairs, which is aggregated into participant-level trajectories and summarized through the Gini coefficient to understand the distribution of team-level communication synchrony. This approach is employed with German-language transcripts from fifteen collaborative VR gameplay sessions. Transcript utterances are represented using a long-context embedding model with a late-chunking strategy and analyzed within fixed game-time windows. A representative session illustrates shifting dyadic alignment and low-to-moderate participant contributions, with sporadic periods of high entanglement. Across fifteen game sessions, the metrics indicate complementary insights, offering a qualitative contrast to the core-periphery pattern reported in the foundational work. Hence, these descriptive findings support the study of communication as a dynamic process and provide a mathematically grounded approach to analyze its evolving distribution in shared interactive VR spaces.

items.title: Beyond the Readout: A Latent Numerical Frame Shared Across Modality and Operation
items.abstract: When a multimodal model computes 17+35 from text or 91-39 from a rendered image, it produces the same answer, 52. Does it use one internal concept of number for both, or separate machinery for each path? Similarity metrics such as RSA or CKA cannot settle this question. They give the same score to identical and to rotated directions, and two representations can look alike only because both prepare the same output digits. We therefore use causal interventions. For four conditions (text or image, addition or subtraction), we learn a small subspace of Gemma4-12B-it's residual stream in which swapping coordinates swaps the model's answer. The subspaces answer three questions. First, do the conditions write numbers along the same directions? They do not. Reusing a subspace from text in an image on the same operation recovers only 53.2% of its causal effect. A single rotation and rescaling maps one subspace onto the other and raises recovery to 91.4%, so the conditions share one geometry expressed in different coordinates. Second, does this shared geometry only reflect the digit the model is about to print? To test this, we split each subspace into 9 directions that the output layer reads to choose the next digit and 13 directions that it cannot see. The 13 hidden directions still carry the number, yet changing them barely alters the digit being written. Third, what are these hidden directions for? A model must emit a multi-digit answer one digit at a time, so it can compute the full result early and keep it in reserve. When two numbers share their first digit, swapping the number in the hidden directions leaves the digit being written intact and redirects the next digit in 77.6% of cases. The model thus forms an abstract numerical concept upstream and unfolds it across time: multimodal representations share meaning through relational geometry across distinct coordinate frames.

items.title: Constraining the Commit Boundary: A DIO/ODI-Informed Authorization Guardrail for Agentic Entity Resolution
items.abstract: Agentic Entity Resolution (ER) systems iteratively plan actions, retrieve evidence, revise hypotheses, and propose graph mutations. An erroneous identity hypothesis may condition later retrieval and produce apparent confirmation. This paper proposes a Digital Identity Optimization (DIO) and Ontology of Digital Identity (ODI)-informed authorization boundary between evidence available for agent reasoning and evidence eligible to authorize persistent identity-changing mutations. A domain-governed constraint-binding function maps selected reconstruction-failure distinctions to explicit identity-preserving constraints. An abstract two-phase supervisor permits a commit only when claim-specific authorization-eligible evidence supports every required proposition, relevant conflicts are resolved, the operation remains within its authorized scope, and relevant state and policy versions remain valid. Admission as UNVERIFIED does not confer authorization eligibility. Separate claim-specific promotion governs evidentiary use; insufficient support or unresolved material conflict leads to deferral. The contribution is a specification connecting diagnostic-to-constraint mapping, evidence promotion, proposition coverage, conflict handling, scope binding, and commit-time version integrity. A proposed evaluation protocol is designed to assess the mapping's incremental value beyond generic authorization and conventional identifier rules. This is a conceptual architecture without implementation or empirical validation, not a theorem of semantic correctness. Its property depends on domain-policy adequacy, evidence promotion, and enforcement. It does not prevent erroneous hypotheses or hypothesis-conditioned retrieval; dependency-aware evidence flow remains future research.

items.title: Clearing the FoG: Training KG Agents to Retrieve the Evidence Behind Their Answers
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can answer many factual questions correctly, but a correct answer is not necessarily a supported one. For an LLM agent, a knowledge graph (KG) plays two roles: as a source of answers, it supplies facts that the model lacks; as a source of evidence, it supplies the supporting triples that make an answer traceable and auditable. However, existing KG agents treat the KG only as a source of answers: their training data carries answers but not evidence, and their training rewards check the answer but not the retrieved evidence, so agents often answer correctly without retrieving the supporting triples. We propose FoG, a framework that trains KG agents to retrieve the evidence behind their answers. FoG consists of evidence-grounded synthesis, a KG interaction agent, and an evidence-coverage process reward (ECPR): the synthesis recursively hides explicit entities behind verifiable sub-questions, so that every question carries its supporting triples by construction; the agent records the triples returned by the KG; and ECPR credits each supporting triple to the turn that first retrieves it. Experiments on three KGQA benchmarks demonstrate that FoG enables 3B--4B open-source agents to outperform substantially larger baselines in answer accuracy and evidence coverage, with zero-shot cross-KG transfer.

items.title: Learning Quality-Controllable Robot Policies with Iterative Hindsight Relabeling
items.abstract: Robot policy evaluation often relies on a binary success signal for task completion. In real-world deployment, however, desired execution behaviors are also defined by quality attributes such as execution speed and motion smoothness, which need to be dynamically controlled according to task requirements. To address this, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), a robot policy that enables inference-time control over both individual quality attributes and their combinations. To extend the controllable quality range beyond initial demonstrations, we further propose an iterative hindsight relabeling loop: QCP collects online rollouts under target quality labels, adds successful trajectories to the dataset, relabels the accumulated trajectories in hindsight according to their measured quality, and fine-tunes the policy. Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval demonstrate that QCP consistently improves both task execution quality and success rates across iterations, producing successful rollouts that exceed the quality of the initial demonstrations. Finally, we validate QCP on real-world manipulation tasks, where controlling speed increases throughput in conveyor operations and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses, demonstrating that quality-controllable policies yield practical gains in physical deployment.

items.title: JEPA-Inspired Latent Field Prediction for Sparse-Pilot MIMO-OFDM Channel Reconstruction
items.abstract: Accurate acquisition of full channel state information (CSI) is essential for multiple-input multiple-output orthogonal frequency-division multiplexing (MIMO-OFDM) wireless systems, while dense pilot-based estimation incurs substantial overhead. Directly minimizing the prediction error over raw CSI coefficients is fragile in realistic propagation environments, since small-scale fading, mobility, local scattering, and small spatial perturbations can induce large phase-sensitive variations. Nevertheless, wireless channels contain strong spatial, temporal, and frequency-domain correlations that can be more predictably represented in a latent propagation-field domain. Motivated by this observation, we propose a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA)-inspired field world model, defined as a latent predictive model of the wireless propagation field, for sparse-pilot channel reconstruction. The model maps CSI observations into latent time-frequency tokens, predicts masked or future latent field states from historical multi-band context, and fuses the predicted latent prior with sparse noisy current pilots to reconstruct the full MIMO-OFDM channel. Ray-tracing experiments show that the proposed method improves normalized mean square error (NMSE) over pilot-only and direct reconstruction baselines, supporting latent field prediction as an effective prior for sparse-pilot channel acquisition.

items.title: Every route counts, but some count more: a max-plus view of the C. elegans brain
items.abstract: Brains do not simply add up every signal they receive: they select which routes dominate. Yet connectomes are usually analyzed with tools that sum over all paths and place neural states in Euclidean spaces, blurring the feedback circuits that may sustain internal states. Here we treat neural signaling as routing instead of diffusion and describe it with max-plus algebra, in which signals accumulate along a path and the strongest route prevails. We propose a model in which the functional connectome of Caenorhabditis elegans emerges from the time-varying combination of electrical, synaptic, monoaminergic, neuropeptidergic and hormonal layers, and analyze five networks within this framework. Each collapses onto a handful of dominant feedback loops, which recover well-characterized circuits and point to new candidates for experimental study. Unlike linear spectra, these structures keep the biological meaning of the data, and their order-based description suggests that brain states live in lattices rather than Euclidean spaces.

items.title: Sufficiency Theorem and Closed-Form Posterior for a Windowed Change Point Detection Task
items.abstract: To function effectively in a changing world, agents must detect changes and act on them in a timely fashion. We study this in the context of a change point detection task in which clicks arrive from a Poisson process whose rate changes at an unknown time. An agent must declare the change within a detection window of fixed width or the trial ends in a miss. Here we prove a window sufficiency theorem, which states that the posterior probability of a change depends only on the clicks within the most recent window, regardless of the prior on the change time. This result follows from combining survival conditioning, which rules out change times whose windows have already expired, with cancellations driven by independent increments of a known baseline process. Window sufficiency generalizes to an unknown post-change process, as long as the baseline process is known. For an exponential prior on the change time, we further derive the posterior in closed form as a function of the elapsed times since each click in the most recent window, the known rates, and the window width. These results suggest that discarding old evidence can be optimal rather than a limitation when decisions face a deadline.

items.title: Local learning is all you need: brain-aligned predictive coding networks
items.abstract: Predictive Coding (PC) is an influential account of how brain representations emerge through hierarchical, local, self-supervised prediction-based learning, without requiring globally propagated error signals. Despite extensive evidence supporting PC, a striking paradox persists: computational models built on these biologically grounded principles have consistently failed to match state-of-the-art Deep Neural Networks in performance and brain-alignment. Here, we show that this paradox can be overcome. We introduce Predictive Brain Networks (PBNs), a hierarchical recurrent framework that implements local PC-based learning and achieves representational alignment with the human ventral visual stream matching or exceeding established vision models. Importantly, PBN top-down predictions encode unique, brain-aligned information not captured during bottom-up feature extraction, with this contribution increasing in locally trained variants. Further, PBNs substantially outperform existing PC-inspired networks on downstream classification tasks, reproduce key signatures of PC (with higher-level predictions shaping lower-level visual responses as observed in the primate cortex), and support uncertainty estimation. PBNs therefore close a longstanding gap in computational neuroscience by combining two properties that have been largely separated: the brain-inspired learning mechanisms of predictive coding and the representational power of modern deep networks. They provide a scalable framework for studying biologically grounded learning without sacrificing the capacity to produce rich neural representations.

items.title: Exploring Neural Dynamics with Time Delays: A Numerical and Bifurcation Analysis Approach
items.abstract: The Wilson-Cowan model is a classic example of a ``neural mass model'' - a simplified yet powerful way to describe the activity of large networks of neurons. It is particularly interesting because, even in its relatively simple form, it can produce a surprising variety of behaviours, from steady rhythms to complex oscillations. A key factor influencing these dynamics is the presence of time delays, reflecting the time it takes for signals to travel between neurons. This article offers an accessible introduction to the Wilson-Cowan model, focusing on how these time delays affect its behaviour. We explore the core concepts behind the model, survey the existing literature, and introduce some numerical techniques specifically designed for analysing such delay differential equations. We also provide a practical, hands-on tutorial on using the DDE-BIFTOOL software package, demonstrating its application to the Wilson-Cowan model. Downloadable code allows the reader to reproduce our results and to explore the model's dynamics further, including MATLAB code for all computations, using DDE-BIFTOOL for the continuation, and Python versions of simulation codes.

items.title: Neuronal Identity as an Organizational Basis for Analyzing Neural Population Dynamics
items.abstract: Individual neurons exhibit diverse molecular, morphological, and electrophysiological properties that shape their distinct roles in neural circuits. While these multimodal features are largely shared across individuals, they remain an underutilized source of information in analyzing neural population dynamics. We posit that these shared biological profiles provide a common reference for relating neural dynamics across subjects and recording sessions. Our framework leverages this structure by routing neurons into latent groups based on their biological profiles and analyzing population dynamics through group-level representations. Because these assignments are anchored in biological properties that are consistent across subjects, the learned organization supports transfer to unseen animals without retraining or neuron-wise correspondence. We evaluate our framework on whole-brain calcium imaging in larval zebrafish and large-scale electrophysiology in the mouse visual cortex. Across both species and recording modalities, the framework delivers state-of-the-art performance in both neural decoding and manifold analysis: it achieves superior decoding of behavior and stimulus labels while better preserving the temporal consistency and local geometric structure of latent trajectories on unseen data. Our experiments demonstrate that not only does providing biological features improve baseline performance, but our proposed framework achieves even stronger results by using these properties to explicitly structure the population rather than treating them as auxiliary inputs. Together, these results suggest that organizing neural populations by their multimodal biological features offers a promising framework for generalizing population dynamics across subjects and recording sessions.

items.title: The geometry of cognition: from neural populations to neurotechnology
items.abstract: Cognition is implemented by distributed neural populations whose collective activity evolves through structured, low-dimensional state spaces. In this review, we survey the analytical and conceptual tools used to study latent population dynamics in biological neural networks. We begin with single-unit coding, which remains essential for interpreting neuronal selectivity, and then review population-level approaches, including population vectors, cosine similarity, principal component analysis and its mnemonic variants, multivariable linear regression axes, demixed principal component analysis, and single-trial latent-variable models, and distinguish operationally defined population subspaces from neural manifolds with reproducible geometry or topology. We use these methods to discuss sensory coding, working memory, decision-making, temporal processing, and sensorimotor transformations. Two organizing principles are emphasized throughout. First, cognitive variables can be expressed in separable or near-orthogonal population dimensions, reducing interference between sensory, mnemonic, decision-related, and motor signals. Second, such geometric separation does not require anatomically or functionally discrete cell classes; separable population readouts can coexist with a continuum of mixed-selective single-neuron responses within a shared biological substrate. We then consider recurrent neural networks as testbeds for generating and evaluating mechanistic hypotheses about how circuits produce low-dimensional dynamics, and intracortical brain-computer interfaces as a translational domain in which population geometry becomes an operational control signal. Overall, this review argues that population dynamics now provide a common language for linking neurophysiology, computational modelling, and neurotechnology.

items.title: CogArena: Benchmarking Multimodal Agents on Interactive Behavioral Experiments
items.abstract: Claims about the cognitive capabilities of large language models are typically tested by translating behavioral paradigms into text prompts, bypassing the visual interfaces and time pressure through which human participants actually engage with experiments. At the same time, AI agents can now complete online behavioral tasks and produce human-like data, which raises concerns that online datasets in the social and behavioral sciences are increasingly open to contamination. We introduce CogArena, a benchmark of ten experimental paradigms from the social and behavioral sciences. Agents complete the experiments through a standard web browser, working with the same visual stimuli and response interfaces that online participants use. A three-level scoring procedure evaluates whether the agent completed the task, how accurately it performed, and whether its data show the behavioral signatures each paradigm reliably produces in people. Across four multimodal models, each run ten times per task, we find that finishing an experiment and reproducing its signatures are different things. Many sessions did not finish, and those that did reproduced some signatures reliably and others not at all. CogArena provides the tasks, scoring code, and a public leaderboard for new submissions.

items.title: Stationary Action Principles for Neuronal Growth
items.abstract: Neuronal growth is guided by biochemical, mechanical, and geometrical cues while being influenced by stochastic fluctuations in cytoskeletal dynamics, adhesion, and growth cone sensing. Here, we develop two complementary variational descriptions of mechanically guided axonal growth. First, for neurons growing on periodic parallel micropatterns, we use Langevin and Fokker--Planck models to derive a stochastic path action incorporating deterministic substrate guidance and random fluctuations. The probability of a growth trajectory decreases exponentially with this action, and the most probable trajectories correspond to minimum action paths for fixed boundary conditions. Second, for axons growing on substrates with spatially varying stiffness, we show that stiffness dependent traction generates mechanical guidance and axonal turning at stiffness interfaces. In the quasi-static limit, this response leads to a Fermat-like spatial action with an effective axonal refractive index determined by the traction and substrate stiffness relationship. The resulting framework predicts axonal refraction across stiffness boundaries, including an approximate Snell-like relation and a critical angle condition. Although the stochastic and Fermat-like actions have distinct physical meanings and ranges of validity, both describe how substrate mechanics constrain axonal trajectories. These results connect measurable quantities, including drift, diffusion, stiffness, traction, and growth direction, to global properties of axonal paths and provide a framework for designing biomimetic substrates for controlled neuronal growth and regeneration.

items.title: JWST/MIRI Observations of Amorphous Silicates in Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS
items.abstract: We present JWST/MIRI Low Resolution Spectroscopy (LRS) of 3I/ATLAS obtained post-perihelion at a heliocentric distance of 2.21 au. Our spectrum contains a prominent 10 micron silicate emission feature with a broad, smooth shape that is distinct from those commonly observed in Solar System comets. We model the spectrum using thermal emission from amorphous carbon, amorphous olivine, and amorphous pyroxene grains. Our models strongly favor a pyroxene-dominated, amorphous silicate composition and show a degeneracy between silicate grain size and the relative abundance of silicate and carbon dust. Across a set of representative models, the best-fitting crystalline abundance is zero, and we place an upper limit of 5.3% on the crystalline fraction of the silicates. We identify an emission feature near 6.83 microns that is consistent with aliphatic C-H-bearing material. The overwhelmingly amorphous silicate composition supports previous work that measured unusual volatile and isotopic composition in suggesting that the material incorporated into the object experienced little thermal processing and preserves information about the conditions in which this interstellar planetesimal formed.

items.title: Neighborhood Deprivation Shapes Post-Flood Population Losses in Pune and Bandung
items.abstract: Disaster research in high-income settings shows that better-resourced communities see population inflows and faster recovery, while disadvantaged communities suffer prolonged population loss. Whether this pattern holds in rapidly urbanizing cities of the Global South remains unclear. Here we show, using mobile phone data from Pune, India, and Bandung, Indonesia, how neighborhood-level changes in phone presence, a proxy for short-term population movement, relate to flooding and neighborhood deprivation. We combine satellite-derived flood maps with phone records to compare flooded and non-flooded areas over the 30 days around each flood. In both cities, less deprived neighborhoods see phone presence rise after flooding, while more deprived neighborhoods see it fall, consistent with resource-seeking interpretations documented in North American and European disaster research. The cities differed, however, in how deprivation relates to flood exposure: in Pune, more deprived flooded neighborhoods showed suggestive evidence of disproportionately larger decreases in detected device presence than similarly deprived non-flooded neighborhoods; no comparable interaction was observed in Bandung. Economic considerations are associated with post-flood device-presence changes in South and Southeast Asian cities in ways that parallel high-income contexts, though local context adds variation.

items.title: Beyond urban boundaries: Percolation reveals land-consumptive growth in India
items.abstract: Cities often extend beyond their administrative boundaries, complicating assessments of urban sustainability. Using Global Human Settlement Layer data for India's 50 largest urban agglomerations (1975--2025), we develop a percolation-based framework for urban delineation. Within district-based regions, we apply unrestricted DBSCAN to spatial coordinates of 100-m cells with positive population and built-up surface. We treat neighborhood distance as the percolation control parameter and the proportion of eligible cells in the largest connected cluster as the empirical order parameter. Sharp increases in this proportion reveal characteristic percolation transitions. Post-transition connection lengths declined (median:650m to 350m), indicating that previously disconnected settlements coalesce at progressively shorter spatial distances alongside increasing urban land consumption. Urban footprint increased from 447.6 to 1,382.7km$^2$, while population densities declined. SDG11.3.1 land-consumption-to-population-growth ratios generally exceeded unity. Zipf and allometric relationships describe cross-sectional urban structure, but land-consumptive growth shows little relationship with city size. Urban delineation thus shapes sustainability assessments.

items.title: Mapping Artistic Engagement with Quantum Technologies
items.abstract: Quantum technologies (QT) are increasingly being taken up in artistic practices, for example in the form of visual artworks or quantum computer music. However, more comprehensive empirical studies on the temporal development and the different forms of QT-related art are still lacking. Therefore, this study conducted a systematic mapping and classification of QT-related artworks. To this end, a medium-independent corpus was established, and the artworks were classified into four categories: QT-Inspired, QT-Sourced, Simulated QT, and QT-Generated. This classification was LLM-assisted and checked against human-coded reference data as well as through manual review of unclear cases. In total, 281 QT-related artworks from 2010 to August 2025 were identified. The corpus shows a substantial increase in QT-related artworks since 2019, with a considerable share attributed to only a few artists. The different forms of QT relations coexist, while an increasing use of active hardware-based and simulated processes in artistic practices can be documented, particularly since 2021. Although no clear development trajectories between these categories can be identified, the observed development coincides with advances in QT and their improved accessibility. Thus, this study provides an empirical basis for further analyzing the development of QT-related art, the possible emergence of a "quantum art scene," and the reciprocal relationships between art and quantum technologies.

items.title: Superlinear cities, finite limits: Three characteristic scales of urban agglomeration
items.abstract: Urban scaling research has established that many socioeconomic outputs increase superlinearly with city population, implying rising per-capita output. Although urban scaling models have incorporated infrastructural and dissipative costs, they have generally not identified the finite population scales implied by independently scaling benefits and diseconomies. We connect the classical urban-economic trade-off between agglomeration benefits and costs to a generalized scaling framework in which these quantities follow distinct power laws. When diseconomies scale more rapidly than benefits the model yields three ordered characteristic populations: the first (smallest) maximizes net benefit per capita; the second maximizes total net benefit; and the third (largest), at which aggregate benefits equal diseconomies. Their absolute values depend on the magnitudes of benefits and costs, but their relative separation depends only on the scaling exponents. We illustrate these relationships using published scaling estimates from several countries, and examine aggregate and extensive--intensive scaling across 102 Australian Significant Urban Areas. Aggregate employee income, rental payments and daily journey to work commuting distances for journeys scale superlinearly, although the aggregate rent--income exponent difference is statistically inconclusive. Mean rent per reporting renter household and estimated mean distance for daily commutes increase more rapidly with city population than mean employee income per earner. These findings reveal intensive differences obscured by aggregate scaling. The framework shows how superlinear agglomeration benefits can coexist with still faster-scaling diseconomies and produce finite characteristic urban scales without requiring benefits themselves to become sublinear.

items.title: Unbound grains in gaseous debris discs
items.abstract: Context. Some debris discs contain cold molecular gas. The origin of this gas is one of the key questions in our understanding of the evolution of planetary systems. The effect of gas on the smallest dust grains, which are expected to be unbound due to radiation pressure, is not well understood. The unbound grains contribute to the brightness of scattered light and thermal emission from the disc halo at short wavelengths. Aims. We explored the conditions under which gas can prevent or slow down the escape of unbound grains and increase their number density in the disc halo sufficiently to affect its brightness and reveal properties of the gas. Methods. We numerically integrated the equations of motion of dust grains released on unbound orbits in optically thin, gaseous debris discs, taking into account stellar gravity, radiation pressure, Poynting-Robertson drag, and gas drag. Results. We find that gas drag can significantly slow down the escape of unbound grains only for very high gas masses, such as those expected if the gas is remnant protoplanetary gas and not of secondary origin. We also present an analytical model for estimating the density of unbound grains in gaseous discs. Conclusions. If a difference in the abundance of unbound grains between gaseous and non-gaseous debris discs were observed, it would imply that the gas in debris discs is protoplanetary. Currently, there is no evidence of such a difference, suggesting that the gas detected in debris discs is either secondary or strongly depleted protoplanetary gas.

items.title: The impact of the sulfur allotropes and sulfur hydrides on the Venus cloud chemistry
items.abstract: Venus is home to vivid sulfur chemistry, with SO$_2$ as the major sulfur gas species and a global cloud layer between 47 and~70 km composed of H$_2$SO$_4$ and H$_2$O. The chemistry in the clouds has been extensively studied with 1D models, but none is able to reproduce the three orders of magnitude decrease of SO$_2$ inside the clouds. Sulfur allotrope chemistry could be a candidate for buffering sulfur atoms, as it can grow into long chains. Sulfur hydrides such as H$_2$S is considered as one of the main sulfur-bearing compounds, possibly linked to surface reactions or have a volcanic origin like on Earth. In this study, we use for the first time a 3D model to study the climatology of the sulfur allotrope in gas and condensed phase and hydride chemistry in the clouds with an explicit photolysis calculation and updated UV cross-section. H$_2$S is close to ppmv levels below the cloud base, the third most abundant sulfur-bearing species in this region after SO$_2$ and OCS. Below the clouds, S$_8$ gas phase is the most abundant sulfur allotrope. Above, the photolysis and condensation are preponderant, and the gas phase decreases to extremely low values. Polysulfur can therefore not be the unknown absorber at cloud-top altitudes. The condensed phase polysulfurs are present from 30 to above 100~km. S$_2$ condensed phase is the most abundant due to its low saturation mixing ratios. Polysulfur species represent a substantial sulfur reservoir in the upper cloud, equivalent to a few ppmv.

items.title: Feedback autocratic strategies in stochastic games
items.abstract: A stochastic game is an optimal control problem for multiple agents in a stochastic environment. Stochastic games contain important practical problems, related to environmental issues or traffic flows. If the number of environmental states is one, such stochastic games are called repeated games. In repeated games, several strategies which unilaterally control payoffs have been proposed, and these strategies work in a mechanism similar to feedback control. In this paper, we generalize these strategies as feedback strategies in stochastic games, and investigate their properties. In particular, we provide a necessary and sufficient condition for such feedback strategies to work as controllers of payoffs under some assumptions. We demonstrate the performance of such feedback strategies in several examples related to social dilemmas. Our findings connect the theory of payoff control in repeated games to the theory of feedback control in stochastic games.

items.title: Revisiting the Photometric Modulation Amplitudes of Kepler Planet Hosts: A Confounder-Adjusted Test of Stellar Spin-Orbit Alignment
items.abstract: T. Mazeh and coworkers pioneered a method using rotational photometric modulation as a proxy to infer stellar obliquities in Kepler transiting planetary systems, based on the expected positive correlation between spot-induced modulation amplitudes and stellar inclinations. They found that planet hosts cooler than the Sun showed larger modulation amplitudes than comparison stars, consistent with low stellar obliquities. For hotter hosts, however, they reported the opposite - a negative amplitude difference (hosts minus comparison stars) - which is difficult to interpret in terms of viewing geometry. We show that this comparison is affected by confounding variables not controlled for in the sample selection. One such confounder is apparent magnitude, whose distributions differ markedly between the two samples for hotter stars and affect the observed modulation amplitudes. We develop resampling and likelihood-based approaches that enable comparison of the amplitude distributions at fixed apparent magnitude, stellar radius, and rotation period. The previously reported negative amplitude difference for hot hosts is no longer present in either analysis. The likelihood-based analysis finds a positive amplitude difference up to $\sim 6100\,\mathrm{K}$ that becomes consistent with zero at higher temperatures, while the resampling analysis shows a similar but less pronounced trend. This result is qualitatively consistent with independent $v\sin i$ analyses suggesting low obliquities for cooler super-Earth and sub-Neptune hosts and broader obliquity distributions for hotter ones. This may also indicate a gradual change in the obliquity distribution with stellar temperature, although changes in spot distributions or selection effects could also contribute to the photometric trends in hot stars.

items.title: Detailed balance and phase transition in Nash equilibria of mean-field Ising game
items.abstract: We study a finite-state mean-field game with entropic control cost. In the large population limit, we show that its stationary Nash equilibria satisfy the detailed balance condition and their distributions take the Gibbsian form with the value function playing the role of a Hamiltonian. We apply the entropic control cost to a ferromagnetic mean-field Ising game and investigate its stationary and non-stationary Nash equilibria. We find that the stationary Nash equilibria exhibit a second-order phase transition from disordered to ordered equilibria as temperature decreases. A center-manifold reduction yields non-stationary Nash equilibrium near the critical temperature and reveals the critical slowing down in the relaxation toward the stationary Nash equilibrium.

items.title: Retention of primordial atmospheres through giant impacts
items.abstract: Rocky planets the size of Earth or larger are expected to undergo one or more giant impacts during the final stages of their formation. Some of these collisions occur after protoplanetary disk dissipation, potentially driving the loss of primordial hydrogen-rich atmospheres through elevated surface temperatures. However, whether giant impacts promote atmospheric loss or retention remains unclear because they both heat planetary interiors and increase atmospheric gravitational binding. Here we model the evolution of rocky planets after their largest post-disk giant impact, accounting self-consistently for the concurrent increase in gravitational binding energy and mantle thermal energy. Whereas the entire accreted mass contributes to the increase in gravitational binding energy, only part of the impact energy raises mantle temperature. Mantle melting consumes energy as latent heat, while the impactor's metallic core transfers little energy to the mantle and remains superheated at depth. Giant impacts therefore increase gravitational binding energy more than mantle thermal energy, shifting planets towards atmospheric retention. Larger, atmosphere-bearing planets emerge preferentially through collisional growth. By contrast, smaller planets without such impacts tend to lose their primordial atmospheres under sustained stellar irradiation. At the population level, these results suggest that sub-Neptunes have, on average, more massive rocky interiors than super-Earths.

items.title: Neuroline: an integrated modular pipeline for FAIR multimodal neurophysiology data processing
items.abstract: The adoption of FAIR principles for code and data sharing in systems neuroscience is hindered by the size and diversity of datasets, the multitude of data formats and the complexity of analysis workflows. These challenges have led to the development of various data standards and modality-specific processing and analysis tools. However, it remains difficult to integrate the diverse processed data streams originating from state-of-the-art neurophysiology experiments into a common format, which is crucial for cross-modal analyses and open, FAIR sharing of data. To address this, we developed Neuroline, a Python package for processing neurophysiology data (electrophysiology, optical imaging, and behaviour) that combines multimodal integration, modularity, and standardised output within a single pipeline. It leverages established packages and consolidates the resulting processed data into the standardised Neurodata Without Borders (NWB) format. Neuroline provides a unified interface while preserving flexibility and extensibility. Here we describe the implementation and challenges of a pipeline capable of integrating different types of neuroscientific data and packages. Finally, we address how Neuroline contributes to the sustainability and accessibility of neuroscience data and software.

items.title: Neuroscience in Conversation: Tracking Scientific Change Through an Open Seminar Archive
items.abstract: Scientific talks capture how researchers frame questions, debate ideas, and communicate emerging methods, providing a complementary record of scientific change to the published literature. We investigated whether an open neuroscience seminar archive could reveal shifting scientific attention and contain predictive information about subsequent discourse. We analysed 470 English-language transcripts from the Clinical Neuroanatomy Seminars YouTube channel, spanning 2010-2026 and approximately 2.6 million words, using longitudinal vocabulary analysis, unsupervised topic clustering, conceptual comparisons, and rolling temporal forecasting. The archive captured sustained discussion of language, white matter anatomy, connectivity, clinical neuroscience, and neurobiological mechanisms, alongside changes in their relative prominence. Network-related terminology became more prominent than localisation-related terminology, references to individual variability and computational approaches increased, and open science practices became more visible in scientific discussion. Beyond retrospective description, a regression model predicted keyword frequencies one and two years ahead with approximately 12% and 17% lower mean absolute error, respectively, than a persistence baseline. This modest gain is better explained by smoothing of year-to-year fluctuations than by genuine prediction: terms showing the strongest recent growth tended to fall back rather than continue rising. These findings suggest that spoken scientific discourse shows clear longitudinal change but offers limited evidence of information about subsequent shifts in attention. Interpretation remains grounded in the archive curated scope and changing content composition. By making nearly two decades of freely accessible neuroimaging education amenable to systematic analysis, this study connects open educational practice with the study of science itself. Open seminar archives can serve as reusable research resources, preserving the conversations through which scientific communities develop and revise their ideas.

items.title: Neurotransmitter receptor architecture links local neurochemistry to semantic memory
items.abstract: A fundamental challenge in neuroscience is understanding how the molecular and neurochemical architecture of the human cortex gives rise to sophisticated higher cognitive functions. The anterior temporal lobe (ATL) is a key hub for semantic memory, and its underlying GABAergic and glutamatergic neurochemistry supports semantic memory performance. However, the molecular receptor architecture underlying these neurochemical-cognitive relationships remains unknown. Here, we combined imaging transcriptomics and in vivo magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS) to investigate how neurotransmitter receptor organisation relates to local neurochemistry and semantic memory in the human ATL. We found that the ATL exhibited a distinct transcriptomically inferred receptor-subunit profile relative to control cortical regions (occipital cortex and vertex). Individual-specific spatial estimates of receptor-subunit gene expression were systematically associated with local GABA+ and Glx concentrations, revealing preferential coupling between GABAergic receptor genes and GABA+ and between glutamatergic receptor genes and Glx, alongside widespread cross-system associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and Glx. ATL GABA+ and Glx concentrations were positively associated with semantic memory performance, and GABAergic and glutamatergic receptor-subunit expression showed selective relationships with semantic memory accuracy. Crucially, mediation analyses revealed that GABA+ mediated associations between GABAergic receptor architecture and semantic performance, whereas Glx mediated both glutamatergic and widespread GABAergic receptor associations. Together, these findings reveal a coupled molecular-neurochemical architecture of the human ATL, linking neurotransmitter receptor organisation to regional neurochemical state and individual differences in semantic memory. Our findings provide a multiscale account of how cortical molecular organisation is associated with human higher cognitive function.

items.title: Scalable hardware and software for high-density, multi-regional electrophysiology in non-human primates
items.abstract: Understanding how distributed neural circuits generate complex behaviors requires long-duration recordings from populations of individual neurons across multiple brain regions. High-density Neuropixels probes have revolutionized rodent systems neuroscience. Extending these capabilities to non-human primates (NHPs) for chronic, multi-regional recordings requires compact, implantable microdrive hardware and reliable automated spike-sorting software. NHPs provide access to complex and flexible behaviors that are difficult to study in other model systems. Extending the Neuropixels revolution to NHPs therefore depends on integrating hardware and software for long-duration, multi-regional recordings. Here, we present a scalable hardware-software platform co-designed for high-density neural data acquisition and reliable single-unit identification in NHPs. The Multi-regional Implantable NeuroDrive (MIND) is a lightweight, implantable microdrive that provides stable recordings from multiple independently positioned Neuropixels probes and is designed to support chronic, ambulatory, head-free recordings. We paired MIND with UnitAssay, an automated post-sorting curation framework that identifies and curates characteristic spike-sorting errors with minimal computational cost. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide an integrated platform for implanted, multi-regional recordings in NHPs performing complex and naturalistic behaviors. We tested MIND and UnitAssay across parietal, prefrontal, and motor cortices in rhesus macaques performing reaching and eye-movement tasks. MIND enabled stable multi-probe recordings across cortical regions and durations. UnitAssay enabled automated curation of large-scale spike-sorting output and improved reliable single-unit identification relative to Kilosort 4 labels and standard SpikeInterface quality control. Together, MIND and UnitAssay provide a scalable solution for high-density, multi-regional, long-duration electrophysiology in NHPs.

items.title: Social relationship is associated with distinct patterns of inter-brain synchrony and directed connectivity during interpersonal coordination.
items.abstract: How social relationship and effector pairing relate to behavioral coordination and inter-brain interaction during joint timing remains unclear. Using functional near-infrared spectroscopy hyperscanning during a dyadic synchronization-continuation task, we examined 21 romantic couples and 23 stranger dyads performing hand-hand and hand-foot coordination. Romantic partners showed smaller tapping deviations than strangers during continuation, while hand-foot coordination was associated with greater tapping variability. Motor-region inter-brain synchrony (IBS) was greater in romantic partners than in strangers. True-dyad IBS exceeded the pseudo-dyad baseline in the right dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, corresponding differences were not detected in the motor cortex or left temporoparietal junction. Dynamic IBS analysis identified two recurrent configurations differing in synchrony strength and global efficiency, but state-transition frequency did not differ significantly between relationship groups. Granger-causality-based directed connectivity was stronger overall in stranger dyads, with female-to-male values exceeding those in the reverse direction. Together, these findings indicate that social relationship is associated with contrasting patterns of motor-region synchrony and directed connectivity, while effector pairing is associated with behavioral variability.

items.title: Domain-associated phenotypic patterns with MACF1 variants.
items.abstract: Purpose While heterozygous de novo missense variants in the microtubule-binding GAR domain of Microtubule-actin cross-linking factor 1 (MACF1) cause Lissencephaly 9 with Complex Brainstem Malformations (LIS9) [MIM 618325], the phenotypic impact of variants outside this domain remains unclear. Methods We assembled a cohort of 5 affected individuals from 4 unrelated families with biallelic non-GAR domain MACF1 variants who exhibit partially overlapping yet unique phenotypic traits. A sixth individual with a de novo, heterozygous frameshift variant was additionally identified. Combined with previously reported cases, we analyzed genotype and phenotype data from 22 individuals using Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO)-based unsupervised hierarchical clustering. Results Clustering revealed two distinct phenotypic signatures, suggesting domain-associated effects. Variants outside the GAR domain associate with broader neurodevelopmental phenotypes and craniofacial and skeletal involvement. Enrichment analysis (p Conclusion These results expand the phenotypic spectrum of MACF1-related disorders and provide preliminary evidence for domain-associated MACF1 variant effects. While limited by sample size and lack of functional validation, these findings should be considered hypothesis-generating and underscore the utility of HPO-based clustering for systematic phenotype comparison as additional cases emerge. Comprehensive genetic and phenotypic assessments are essential for understanding the role of MACF1 in development, informing diagnosis, and guiding future research on cytoskeletal regulation in neurodevelopment.

items.title: Rate and Shape of Functional Decline in Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Identify Clinically Distinct Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis Phenotypes.
items.abstract: Objective The ALS Functional Rating Scale-Revised decline rate compresses trajectory shape into a single number, potentially missing distinct phenotypes. We tested whether shape identifies phenotypes that rate does not distinguish, and whether post-hoc analysis recovers a hidden ultrarapid subgroup. Methods From the Piemonte and Valle d'Aosta register (2000-2022), we applied 2 models to 1,686 amyotrophic lateral sclerosis patients: a Gaussian mixture model (GMM; rate axis) and a latent-class mixed model (LCMM) with cubic splines (shape axis). Concordance, prognostic performance, calibration, and clinical utility were assessed at 24 months. External validation used the Emilia-Romagna register. Results The rate model identified 4 classes (GMM-Slow 31%, GMM-Inter-slow 46%, GMM-Inter-fast 17%, GMM-Catastrophic 6%; slopes -0.44 to -3.52 points/month); the shape model 4 (LCMM-SlowLinear 46%, LCMM-PlateauFall 23%, LCMM-LateDecline 15%, LCMM-RapidEarly 16%). Concordance was modest (kappa = 0.273). Adding shape to rate changed discrimination negligibly (C-index 0.761 vs 0.755), but separated subgroups within rate classes (within GMM-Catastrophic, 30.1 vs 12.0 months). LCMM-LateDecline combined moderate early decline with reduced respiratory reserve (median forced vital capacity 83.5%) and 22.7-month median survival. The combined model gave the greatest net benefit for the composite outcome. Of 945 patients excluded for sparse sampling, 367 were ultrarapid progressors with shorter survival than LCMM-RapidEarly; findings replicated in the Emilia-Romagna register. Interpretation Rate and shape describe partially overlapping aspects of the disease. LCMM-LateDecline, with moderate early decline yet occult respiratory compromise, is clinically challenging, and the 3-visit criterion hides over half of ultrarapid patients. Rate predicts the overall burden of progression, whereas shape predicts the timing of deterioration. ANN NEUROL 2026.

items.title: The Use of Nutritional Supplements as a Therapy for Spinal Cord Injury. A Narrative Review.
items.abstract: AimTo evaluate the therapeutic potential of nutritional supplementation as a complementary strategy to mitigate secondary injury mechanisms and promote recovery in spinal cord injury (SCI).MethodsThis narrative review synthesizes current preclinical and clinical evidence on the role of micronutrients and macronutrients in SCI management, focusing on their mechanisms of action in neuroprotection, neuroregeneration, and functional recovery.ResultsSCI is a severe neurological condition characterized by long-term motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction, largely driven by secondary injury processes such as oxidative stress, neuroinflammation, excitotoxicity, and apoptosis. Evidence indicates that micronutrients-including vitamins A, B complex, C, D, and E, as well as trace elements such as selenium, zinc, copper, and magnesium-exert neuroprotective effects by modulating inflammatory responses, reducing oxidative damage, supporting mitochondrial function, and enhancing myelination. Additionally, macronutrients such as carbohydrates, amino acids, omega-3 fatty acids, and bioactive compounds including alpha-lipoic acid, N-acetylcysteine, and acetyl-L-carnitine contribute to axonal regeneration, metabolic support, and functional recovery. Collectively, these nutrients target key pathophysiological pathways involved in secondary SCI progressionConclusionsNutritional supplementation represents a promising, safe, and accessible adjunctive strategy to enhance neuroprotection and improve outcomes in individuals with SCI. However, further research is required to optimize dosing, timing, and combinatorial approaches to maximize therapeutic efficacy.

items.title: A minimal model of a forest after neutral theory
items.abstract: Community ecology seeks the mechanisms underlying biodiversity, and simplified models can reveal them. Neutral ecology exemplifies this approach, but it doesn't distinguish species, limiting its capability for forecasting and prediction. We address this by developing a predictive, minimal model for forest dynamics. We show in a neotropical forest plot that environmental variation couples to the community as a single common effect on all species' growth rates. Life history acts on that variation, forecasting species' gains and losses a decade ahead. Finally, immigration, coupled to competition and life history, allows us to predict long-run species abundances. Simple rules thus govern the dynamics of this forest: competition, immigration, and the effect of the environment on growth. Beyond that, species are set apart by their life histories alone.

items.title: Aquifer geochemistry shapes microbial diversity and carbon and nitrogen cycling potential
items.abstract: Abstract Despite the importance of groundwater and its ecosystem functions, including nitrogen cycling, subsurface microbial biodiversity and ecology remain poorly understood globally. We investigated how aquifer geochemistry shapes microbial diversity and metabolic potential across Aotearoa New Zealand using shotgun metagenomics of 39 groundwater samples from 11 regions. We recovered 494 high- and medium-quality metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), which clustered into four groups (A, B, C1 and C2), based on hydrochemistry, and differed significantly in taxonomy and metabolic pathways. Cluster A had the highest microbial diversity and was dominated by uncultured taxa, particularly Patescibacteria . Carbon fixation pathways, predominantly the Calvin-Benson-Bassham and reductive tricarboxylic acid cycles, varied among clusters and were associated with different redox metabolisms. Aerobic respiration pathways also differed, particularly the microaerophilic cbb 3 cytochrome c oxidase. Differences were also observed in nitrogen, sulfur, carbohydrate and organic acid metabolism, with several MAGs strongly correlated with nitrate, sulfate and potassium. Our findings demonstrate that aquifer geochemistry is a major determinant of microbial community structure and metabolic potential across Aotearoa New Zealand groundwater ecosystems.

items.title: From partners to pathogens: Metabolic duality in algal-bacterial interactions.
items.abstract: Interactions between phytoplankton and bacteria are often classified as beneficial or harmful, yet interactions between the same partners can shift between these states. Here, we examine bacterial pathogenicity toward marine phytoplankton, focusing on how algal-bacterial interactions become harmful. In several Roseobacter-phytoplankton systems, bacteria repurpose metabolites produced or exchanged during the interaction by altering their concentration, signaling function, or metabolic fate, thereby contributing to host damage. We define this context-dependent repurposing as metabolic duality. We contrast this strategy with algicidal activity that does not require a demonstrated prior interaction with the algal partner or an algal-derived substrate. Examples include secreted proteases and small-molecule algicides that bacteria can produce independently of host-derived metabolites. Despite their different mechanisms, these routes often converge on oxidative stress and programmed cell death-like responses in the algal host. Bacterial identity alone does not determine the outcome. Host physiological state, microbial community composition, temperature, nutrients, and the chemical environment can all shift an interaction toward or away from pathogenicity. We therefore propose that phytoplankton pathogenicity is best viewed as an emergent property of the interactions among the bacterium, host, community, and environment. This perspective shifts the central question from which bacteria are pathogens to what makes an interaction pathogenic and provides a framework for understanding when and why algal-bacterial interactions become harmful in the ocean.

items.title: Cancers under the sea: what marine biodiversity might reveal about cancer susceptibility and resistance.
items.abstract: Cancer comprises a group of diseases characterised by the uncontrolled proliferation of abnormal somatic cells in the body. It is considered a major health challenge in humans, and its global burden is projected to increase in the coming decades. However, cancer is not unique to humans, and it is hypothesised to have appeared alongside multicellularity. Therefore, it should be discussed and studied as an inherent pathology for all multicellular organisms. Guided by this evolutionary perspective, we highlight key research avenues through which marine ecosystems could improve our understanding of cancer biology and support the development of improved prevention and therapeutic strategies. In particular, marine ecosystems (1) harbour animals with some of the most extreme life history traits, thereby highlighting how natural cancer suppression might have evolved; (2) harbour animals exposed to some of the strongest oncogenic environmental contaminations, thereby providing natural systems to investigate how pre-existing anticancer mechanisms shape cancer susceptibility, and (3) harbour the most diverse set of transmissible cancers in marine bivalves, allowing us to explore mechanisms underlying inter-individual differences in resistance and disease spread within and between populations. These systems provide unique opportunities to uncover how cancer resistance evolves across deep evolutionary timescales. They also present opportunities to investigate naturally evolved anticancer mechanisms and bioactive compounds that could inspire biomimetic approaches to cancer prevention and therapy. By integrating evolutionary biology, marine ecology, and oncology, marine systems could become a powerful frontier for discovering fundamental principles of cancer resistance and exploring their potential relevance for biomedical innovations.

items.title: Microbial approaches to cadmium stress in the soil-plant interface: current understanding and biotechnological solutions for sustainable remediation.
items.abstract: Cadmium (Cd) contamination poses a critical threat to agriculture, food security, and human health due to its high solubility, toxicity, and bioavailability. Conventional remediation methods are often expensive, inefficient, and environmentally damaging, highlighting the urgent need for sustainable, biotechnology-based alternatives. This review explores microbial remediation as a promising strategy for Cd detoxification, focusing on the mechanisms that confer microbial Cd tolerance, including cell wall modification, biofilm formation, efflux systems, intracellular chelation, and genetic adaptation. Special emphasis is placed on plant growth-promoting rhizobacteria (PGPR) and endophytes, which mitigate Cd stress in plants by enhancing nutrient uptake, producing phytohormones, modulating antioxidant activity, and regulating metal transporter gene expression. The co-application of PGPR with soil amendments such as biochar and nanoparticles is shown to further improve Cd immobilization, plant resilience, and crop yield. Advancements in omics technologies and artificial intelligence (AI) offer deeper insights into microbial Cd resistance pathways, enabling the development of tailored bioinoculants and genetically engineered strains through tools like CRISPR. By integrating traditional microbiology with modern innovations, this review outlines next-generation solutions for effective Cd remediation, positioning Cd-tolerant microbes as key tools for sustainable agriculture and environmental protection.

items.title: Current Insights Into the Genus Yamadazyma: An Overview of Taxonomy, Ecology and Biotechnological Applications.
items.abstract: Yeasts of the genus Yamadazyma have received increasing attention in the last decade due to the description of new species, their diverse ecological distribution and their biotechnological potential. The genus Yamadazyma was proposed in 1989, but was not accepted until 2005 due to its polyphyletic nature. Over the years, many new species have been described, and several Candida species have been reassigned to Yamadazyma. However, some Yamadazyma species remain unvalidated, and it is unclear whether the genus Keqinozyma is truly a distinct or should be included within Yamadazyma. Currently, the genus Yamadazyma formally includes 72 species. This genus is widely distributed across various environments worldwide, including aquatic habitats, phylloplane, insects, soil, food products, and humans. Although some species and phylogenetic groups exhibit recurring ecological and geographical patterns, such associations are not generally exclusive. Overall, the genus Yamadazyma appears to be ubiquitous. The presence of this genus across various habitats has facilitated studies on its biotechnological applications including cellobiose fermentation for second-generation bioethanol production and biosynthesis of value-added metabolites such as riboflavin. The genus Yamadazyma plays an active role in food production, contributing to product quality through enzymatic and antagonistic activities, while in agriculture it shows potential through biocontrol activity against phytopathogens. Recent descriptions of new species and the reclassification of previously classified Candida species have fragmented information on this genus. This review aims to address knowledge gaps regarding Yamadazyma by providing a comprehensive resource that unifies taxonomy, ecology, biotechnology, and pathogenesis to support further studies.

items.title: Long-term sildenafil attenuates age-associated functional and reproductive decline in male rats.
items.abstract: Aging in males is accompanied by a progressive decline in physical activity, androgen status, and reproductive function. We investigated whether long-term treatment with the phosphodiesterase type 5 inhibitor sildenafil attenuates these changes and is accompanied by remodeling of mitochondrial homeostasis in the testis. Male rats were treated with low-dose sildenafil from 12 to 18 months of age, with age-matched untreated rats serving as controls and young adult rats providing a reference for the age-associated phenotype. Aging markedly reduced voluntary locomotor activity, circulating testosterone, and sperm production, while increasing circulating corticosterone. Long-term sildenafil treatment increased locomotor activity, testosterone, and sperm number, while corticosterone tended to decrease. Sildenafil-associated body weight changes were observed in animals with access to voluntary running. Treatment was also accompanied by pronounced changes in mitochondrial homeostasis-related gene expression in Leydig cells and spermatozoa. These transcriptional responses differed between cell types, particularly for genes regulating mitochondrial dynamics and quality control. Expression of mitochondrial homeostasis-related genes was more closely associated with circulating testosterone than with corticosterone and showed distinct testosterone-associated patterns in Leydig cells and spermatozoa. Recovery toward young levels differed among parameters, being more pronounced for reproductive and endocrine measures than for locomotor activity. These findings indicate that long-term low-dose sildenafil attenuates age-associated functional and reproductive decline and promotes a partial shift toward a younger male phenotype, accompanied by cell-specific mitochondrial transcriptional remodeling.

items.title: Habitat preference in two European fireflies is reflected in their colour vision.
items.abstract: Colour vision has so far been demonstrated in only a single firefly species, the European Lampyris noctiluca. Lamprohiza splendidula is another widespread European species that often co-occurs with L. noctiluca. First, in field surveys, we quantitatively demonstrated that the former species prefers open habitats, while the latter shows a stronger preference for densely vegetated areas. Second, by measuring compound eye spectral sensitivity with electroretinography and assuming dichromatic colour vision, we used a basic psychophysical colour space model to quantify the physiological experience sensed by L. splendidula and L. noctiluca males viewing the females' bioluminescent signal with eyes adapted to spectral conditions of a densely vegetated and open areas illuminated by the late twilight sky, when the activity of these fireflies is maximal. Dark-adapted eyes of both species were mostly sensitive to the yellowish green spectral region (559-568 nm), well matching the bioluminescence's peak wavelength of the females (556 nm). Recordings on green-adapted eye preparations revealed the presence of a second, blue-sensitive photoreceptor (423-456 nm). We also found that the spectral separation between the blue- and green-sensitive receptors was greater in L. splendidula than in L. noctiluca. According to our colour vision modeling, differences in the spectral sensitivities of the two species' visual systems may help maintain colour vision performance and facilitate female detection in their respective preferred habitats.

items.title: Phytophthora cactorum: From Pathogen Biology to Disease Management.
items.abstract: Phytophthora cactorum is a versatile plant pathogen with a wide host spectrum causing substantial yield losses in various forest and agricultural systems, the most affected being apple, ginseng, and strawberry. This review synthesizes the current knowledge on the biology and epidemiology of P . cactorum and presents an extensive overview of the available management strategies, including preventive measures, cultural practices, detection tools, and chemical and biological control. Beyond compiling existing data, this review also highlights emerging conceptual shifts in our understanding of P . cactorum , particularly the transition from viewing it as a single broadly infective generalist to recognizing the presence of partially specialized lineages with host- and organ-specific adaptations. We further link advances in molecular biology, including effector repertoire characterization, with practical implications for disease management in agricultural and nursery systems. By integrating insights across disciplines, we aim to establish a strong foundation for deciphering the mechanisms underlying pathogenicity and to support the development of more effective and sustainable management strategies. items.title: “Choosing the right test begins with the right questions”: An interactive decision tree for statistical analysis
items.abstract: Selecting an appropriate statistical analysis is a central challenge in empirical research, requiring researchers to connect their question with the measurement level of variables, study design, dependence of observations, and statistical assumptions. Students and researchers may know how to run a procedure yet find it difficult to decide when that procedure is appropriate. We present the Statistical Decision Tree, a free, browser-based tool designed to make this reasoning process visible. The tool guides users through sequential questions about their analytical goal and data, retains their answers as an inspectable decision path, and recommends a compatible procedure. Users can also search directly for a procedure and view the associated path. Recommendations link to explanations of assumptions, examples from psychology and sport science, downloadable datasets, jamovi and R instructions, effect-size guidance, and reporting scaffolds. The tool covers a broad range of statistical methods, including classical hypothesis tests, regression and mixed models, factor analysis and other latent-variable methods, machine-learning approaches, and meta-analysis. The interface is available in English, German, French, Spanish, and Italian. This article describes the tool’s design rationale and development, then demonstrates its use through two worked examples: a paired-samples t-test and cluster analysis for exploratory discovery. Statistical method selection can often be organized into a constrained sequence of decisions, and the distinctive contribution of the Statistical Decision Tree is to connect those decisions with explanation, execution, and reporting.

items.title: Moralised Essentialism and Identity Closure in Moral Character Judgement
items.abstract: Accepting an excuse lowers blame, but whether it changes what observers think of the person is unsettled. An excuse admits an act was wrong but pleads reduced responsibility. Read as folk psychology, character accounts of excuse imply that an excuse making an act less revealing should soften judgement of the person. Moralised Essentialism predicts otherwise. Its central rule, identity closure, holds that once a wrong is taken to reveal who the actor is, excuses explain the act and reduce blame but leave the view of the person unchanged. The claim is that excuses stop reaching that judgement, not that they carry less weight. As excuses strengthen, observers should attribute the act more to the situation and blame less, while their judgements of who the actor is, and their forecasts of the actor’s conduct elsewhere, barely move. Retraction and reinterpretation, unlike excuses, change what the act was and should lower those judgements, which strict belief perseverance denies. A proposed experiment fixes two tests beforehand. Meaningful revision of those judgements under excuses observers credit as mitigating would reject the account. Judgements that hold or rise after accepted retraction or reinterpretation would reject closure as the explanation of their stability under excuses.

items.title: Reducing belief in conspiracy theories as they unfold using large language models
items.abstract: The emergence of conspiracy theories in the wake of major events is a significant societal challenge. Here we test whether conversational dialogues with a large language model (LLM) can reduce belief in immediately unfolding conspiracies. In experiments conducted in the days following the July 2024 assassination attempt on Donald Trump and the September 2025 assassination of Charlie Kirk, U.S. adults (Experiment 1: N = 472; Experiment 2: N = 1042) holding conspiratorial views about the crisis event engaged in a multi-turn conversation with an LLM prompted to reduce their conspiracy belief. Compared to control participants who either discussed an irrelevant topic with an LLM or viewed a static fact sheet, participants in the LLM treatment showed significantly reduced conspiracy beliefs in both experiments. We also found some suggestive evidence of downstream effects of the LLM treatment, observing reduced belief in some—but not all—analyses of different conspiratorial beliefs one to two months later. These results shed light on the psychology of emerging conspiracies and highlight the potential for scalable, cognitively-focused interventions to counteract misinformation in the immediate aftermath of high-profile societal events.

items.title: “We love our jobs!” Systems Thinking and Participatory Action Research for the future of neurodiversity and skilled employment
items.abstract: Although neurodivergent people can achieve high levels of academic and vocational training in the same professions as others, they remain un- and under-employed; this is in part due to the “wickedness” of the problem. To address the complexity we convened a group of neurodivergent lived experience and employment experts to 1) define which problems in neurodiversity and skilled employment are most urgent to address; 2) create actionable strategies with potential leverage for generating the desired employment outcomes. We used qualitative methods from the systems thinking field: Soft Systems Methodology, futures visioning and SWOT analysis, and Group Model Building (system dynamics). The workshops resulted in identifying intervention leverage between organizational psychology constructs of employee wellbeing, workplace climate, and mutually beneficial workplace relationships, in conjunction with a new disability stress construct, rather than specific skills building or remediation of disability characteristics. Reaching a future in which neurodivergent people love their jobs will take education, resources, champions from the outside and inside, universal access, paradigm shifts, infrastructure, and recognition of individual and social complexity. We recommend examining the organizational psychology literature for adaptable interventions; focusing on peer support; leveraging emerging technology to manage complexity; and supporting supervisor behavior change based on authentic understanding.

items.title: CogFlow: Open-Source Solution for the Construction of Modular Cognitive Psychology Experiments
items.abstract: Proliferating web-based experimentation platforms have substantially broadened access to cognitive psychology research infrastructure, yet no existing tool simultaneously supports continuous and trial-based paradigms, maintains institutional data-protection compliance, works across online and laboratory settings, and operates within the constraints of collaborative multi-site teams. We present CogFlow, a free, open-source, self-hostable web platform for constructing, deploying, and managing cognitive psychology experiments. CogFlow’s JSON-centric architecture uses a single declarative configuration file to specify both study design and runtime instructions for the Interpreter engine, supporting a broad task library including Random Dot Motion, Flanker, SART, Stroop and Emotional Stroop, Simon, Task Switching, PVT, MOT, N-back, Gabor patch, Continuous Image Presentation, and Security Operations Center (SOC)-style multitask environments, in both trial-based and continuous-presentation modes. A no-code graphical Builder lowers the barrier to experiment authoring while preserving full parameter-level configurability for researchers who require it; results are collected as encrypted payloads with multi-factor authentication gating and pseudonymized participant linkage, supporting compliance with GDPR, UK GDPR, and IRB data management requirements. The platform integrates natively with SONA Systems and Prolific Academic for participant recruitment, provides in-portal descriptive analysis and charting, and includes a CogFlow To Go packaging mode for offline laboratory deployment with Lab Streaming Layer (LSL) support for physiological co-registration. Software-layer runtime benchmarks confirm stable performance consistent with the broader literature on browser-based platforms. CogFlow is available at https://cogflow.app under the BSD 3-Clause license; contributor roles are tracked using the CRediT taxonomy with versioned archival via Zenodo.

items.title: The Prediction and Mediating Role of Lifetime and Daily Aggressive Sexual Fantasies: An Experience-Sampling Study.
items.abstract: Aggressive sexual fantasies (ASF) have consistently been associated with different sexual-aggression measures and mediated the effects of other risk factors on sexual aggression. Little, however, is known about the predictors of ASF and whether they should be considered as an independent risk factor for sexual aggression or rather an expression of aggression-related sexual interests. The present study, therefore, assessed lifetime ASF cross-sectionally ( N = 422; M age = 28.14; SD = 9.76) and over a 14-day experience-sampling period ( n = 230; M age = 27.38; SD = 9.08). Of the participants, 87% reported to have experienced ASF at least once in their lives; 11% reported ASF during the experience-sampling period. Psychopathy, violent pornography consumption, sexual interest in sexual sadism, and the interactions between hypersexuality and sexual-abuse experiences, Machiavellianism, and sexual interest in sadism were associated with higher lifetime ASF. Sexual interest in sadism positively predicted ASF during the experience-sampling period, but only in men. Lifetime ASF were the strongest predictor of sexual aggression and mediated the cross-sectional associations between sexual interest in sadism, hypersexuality, and violent pornography consumption and sexual aggression. These findings support the notion that ASF are an important cognitive risk factor for sexual aggression, partially independent from sexual interest, and require stronger attention by research and practice.
