items.title: Consensual Unwanted Sex and Body Dissatisfaction Among Cisgender Heterosexual Women and Queer Women/Gender Expansive Individuals.
items.abstract: People (especially women) often consent to unwanted sexual activity (especially with men). Reasons for consenting to unwanted sex include facilitating desired and avoiding undesired outcomes, and both positive and negative outcomes are common. Much of this research has focused on cisgender women's experiences consenting to unwanted sex with cisgender men and associated relationship and emotional outcomes. Building on existing work, we examined how consenting to unwanted sex was associated with body-related harms among samples of cisgender heterosexual (cis/het) women ( N = 491) and Queer women and gender expansive individuals ( N = 529). Using survey data, we examined whether self-objectification explained the relationship between consensual unwanted sex (yes/no) and body dissatisfaction, and whether sexual/gender identity moderated those relationships. We also explored reasons for consenting to unwanted sex and how those reasons were associated with self-objectification and body dissatisfaction. Results found 70% of participants had ever consented to unwanted sex, and that consenting to unwanted sex was more common among Queer women/gender expansive individuals than cis/het women. There was a significant indirect effect of consensual unwanted sex on body dissatisfaction via self-objectification for both cis/het and Queer participants. Moreover, the frequency of different reasons for consenting to unwanted sex were similar for cis/het women and Queer women and gender expansive individuals. Only avoidance reasons were associated with greater self-objectification and body dissatisfaction. Overall, consenting to unwanted sex was associated with body-related harms, and such harms were experienced by both cis/het women and Queer women/gender expansive individuals.

items.title: Prevalence of Sexual Acts and Materials Provided for Financial Compensation Among Young Adults in the United States.
items.abstract: Providing in-person (e.g., sex) and virtual (e.g., photos) sexual acts for pay or financial compensation (SAMP) is underreported due to stigma and substantial measurement issues. Prior research using a single item may have underestimated the prevalence and associated characteristics. This study sought to determine lifetime SAMP prevalence and associated characteristics of SAMP in a nationally representative sample in young adults (18-34 years old) in the United States. We administered a cross-sectional web-based survey through the National Opinion Research Council ( N = 2,935). We used the validated, behaviorally specific, 10-item SAMP index to assess prevalence and circumstances, standardized measures of health and childhood experiences, and demographics. Over one-third (36%) of participants reported providing SAMP. Of those, 22% first provided SAMP as minors and 65.5% reported coercion. Prevalence differed by gender, sexuality, race, education, employment, income, and parenthood. Participants who provided SAMP had higher odds of depression, PTSD, problematic substance use, rape victimization, childhood adversity, discrimination, and lower social support. Findings suggest that SAMP is more common than previously assumed. Significant differences among those reporting SAMP underscore the need for harm reducing public health approaches to address health disparities, systemic social issues, diverse experiences, and SAMP's spectrum of agency and victimization.

items.title: Infant Sleep Consolidation Assessed by Maternal Perception and Actigraphy.
items.abstract: Aim This study aims to (1) compare three different subjective and objective measures in assessing the proportion of infants sleeping through the night and (2) identify which sleep variables contribute to maternal appraisal of sleeping through the night. Methods Fifty-six mothers of 6-months-old infants completed the Sleep Practices Questionnaire (SPQ), assessing at what age their infant started to sleep through the night. Infants were dichotomized as sleeping through the night or not at 6 months. Total nocturnal sleep duration, longest consecutive sleep duration, and total duration of nocturnal awakenings were measured with sleep diaries and actigraphy (12 nights). The proportion of infants sleeping through the night was assessed using the SPQ, sleep diaries and actigraphy. Forward binary logistic regression was used to determine which diary or actigraphy variables contributed to maternal appraisal. Results Less than half of infants were sleeping through the night when using the SPQ (44.2%) and sleep diaries (39.5%), while this proportion increased to 90.7% with actigraphy. Sleep-diary consecutive sleep duration was the only variable contributing to maternal appraisals of sleeping through the night. Conclusion While the type of measurements yielded different proportions, sleep-diary derived longest consecutive sleep duration was highly associated with maternal appraisal.

items.title: How to Practice Open Science: A Cookbook for Clinical Psychology and Psychotherapy Research.
items.abstract: Even though Open Science practices advance the credibility and accessibility of knowledge gained through research, they are not yet as common in clinical psychology as in other subfields of psychology. This paper presents an overview of how to implement Open Science practices in clinical psychology and psychotherapy research. We will address frequently encountered challenges and present different ways to deal with sensitive topics within the specific field. We explain Open Science practices while planning a study, during data collection and preparation of a publication, and for the publication of results. Finally, we will show options for how to structure a whole research group in support of Open Science practices. With different types of actions - of varying degrees of complexity and openness - we can continually and ethically move toward more Open Science, which will strengthen clinical research and is therefore essential for people with lived experiences of psychological symptoms, patients, psychotherapists, and for investments in psychological treatments.

items.title: Mapping the Literature on Self-Efficacy Levels Among Medical Students in Higher Education: Protocol for a Scoping Review to Guide Educational Strategies.
items.abstract: Background Self-efficacy significantly influences medical students' academic performance. Rooted in Albert Bandura's social cognitive theory, self-efficacy is defined as an individual's subjective judgment of their capability to organize and execute courses of action required to attain designated types of performances. Unlike general self-esteem, self-efficacy is task- and context-specific. In undergraduate medical education, self-efficacy operates across three interdependent subdomains: (1) academic self-efficacy, encompassing cognitive confidence to master biomedical curricula; (2) clinical skills self-efficacy, reflecting perceived competence in procedural tasks and clinical reasoning; and (3) interpersonal and communication self-efficacy, denoting confidence in empathetic history taking and interprofessional collaboration. These subdomains are presented as a provisional analytical heuristic informed by Bandura's social cognitive theory and prior reviews of self-efficacy in medical education. Objective This scoping review aims to map and analyze the literature on self-efficacy among medical students, identifying factors in its construction and influence on academic performance. The review also aims to catalog the instruments used to measure self-efficacy and examine changes in self-efficacy over time and across stages of medical training. Methods Following the frameworks of Arksey and O'Malley, Levac et al, and the Joanna Briggs Institute, this review addresses the question, "What has been published about self-efficacy levels in higher education among medical students?" Comprehensive searches across major electronic databases and gray literature will include studies from January 2019 to September 2026, in English, Portuguese, or Spanish, focusing on undergraduate medical students. Searches will be conducted in the Embase, Cochrane Library, PubMed, Scopus, Virtual Health Library, Web of Science databases and in the education- and psychology-focused databases ERIC and PsycInfo using an expanded search strategy incorporating controlled vocabulary (MeSH [Medical Subject Headings], Emtree, and DeCS [Descritores em Ciências da Saúde]) and free-text synonyms. Screening will be performed using Covidence software (Veritas Health Innovation), with discrepancies resolved by a third senior reviewer. Data will be narratively synthesized through descriptive qualitative mapping and structured tabular summaries, without quantitative statistical pooling. Results This protocol was registered prospectively on the Open Science Framework before manuscript submission. This research has not received specific funding from any agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. No data have been collected as of September 2026. Each of the 4 review phases is estimated to take 2 months. Results are expected to be published approximately 9 to 12 months following the initiation of database searches. Conclusions The resulting evidence map will clarify self-efficacy constructs within medical education, delineate psychometric assessment practices, and identify curricular strategies that foster clinical and academic self-efficacy, providing actionable guidance for medical educators and curriculum planners. Trial registration Open Science Framework 10.17605/OSF.IO/RHZDX; https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/RHZDX. International registered report identifier (irrid) PRR1-10.2196/95032.

items.title: Longitudinal Relationships Between Neuroticism, Peer Attachment, and Bullying Victimization Among Chinese Left-Behind Children.
items.abstract: A substantial body of evidence indicates that neuroticism influences bullying victimization and peer attachment among left-behind children (LBC). However, how these three constructs interact at the within-person level remains underexplored. To address this gap, the present study, grounded in the transactional model, employed a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model to examine the longitudinal bidirectional relationships among neuroticism, distinct dimensions of bullying victimization, and peer attachment. A cohort of 604 LBC ( M age = 9.64, SD age = 0.71; 397 boys, 207 girls) was followed across four annual waves. At the within-person level, the results revealed that neuroticism and relational victimization, as well as neuroticism and physical victimization, exhibited bidirectional relationships, whereas neuroticism only unidirectionally and positively predicted verbal victimization. Furthermore, verbal victimization, relational victimization, and physical victimization each unidirectionally and negatively predicted peer attachment. These findings elucidate the dynamic interplay among neuroticism, distinct forms of bullying victimization, and peer attachment among LBC in middle childhood, highlighting the importance of distinguishing among victimization types and targeting bullying victimization as an important intervention focus for reducing neuroticism and promoting healthier peer relationships among LBC.

items.title: Psychedelics and psychosis: A systematic review of recent-era studies (1984-2025).
items.abstract: Purpose This systematic review evaluates the relationship between classical psychedelic drugs (D-Lysergic acid N , N -diethylamide, psilocybin, ayahuasca/ N - N -dimethyl-tryptamine, and mescaline) and the emergence of psychotic symptoms, aiming to synthesize evidence from contemporary studies (1984-2025) regarding the risk factors, prevalence, and clinical characteristics of psychosis related to psychedelic use, to provide clinicians, therapists, and policymakers with a framework for identifying and mitigating risks related to these substances. Major findings Fifty-two papers were included, comprising 1 larger-scale studies involving over 100,000 individuals and 34 case reports. Population-based data showed no consistent correlation between lifetime psychedelic use and psychosis. Controlled clinical settings showed minimal risk, with one documented case of transient delusions across all trials. Emergency and toxicological data reported higher rates of psychotic symptoms, likely reflecting the severity of cases prompting medical attention. Among case reports, 58% of individuals had a personal or family psychiatric history. First-episode psychosis, although rare, was documented in otherwise healthy individuals. Conclusions The risk of prolonged psychosis remains remarkably low in controlled clinical settings where rigorous screening and supervision are employed. Personal/family history of psychosis and unsupervised, naturalistic use appear to be risk factors for psychosis. Although causality remains difficult to establish, these findings support the need for careful risk stratification, the adoption of clear diagnostic parameters, and trained clinical oversight as psychedelic-assisted therapies advance toward broader clinical populations.

items.title: Response inhibition in children and adolescents with fragile X syndrome.
items.abstract: Limited knowledge exists on the high degree of overlap, such as in executive functioning, between fragile X syndrome (FXS) and autism. We aimed to better understand the shared response inhibition difficulties and the underlying neurocognitive mechanisms in individuals with FXS and autism. Children and adolescents with (1) FXS ( n = 29), (2) a positive autism screening (hereafter: autism group) ( n = 28), or (3) neurotypical development ( n = 25) were recruited. To assess response inhibition abilities, we used a go/no-go task and the auditory attention + response set inhibition subtask of the NEPSY-II. To compare the amount of cognitive effort that is elicited during response inhibition, we investigated the pupil response during the go/no-go task. Children and adolescents with FXS showed more difficulties with inhibiting responses compared to the autism and neurotypical groups across the different response inhibition tasks. The autism and neurotypical groups did not differ in performance on the tasks. Pupillometric analysis showed subtle, but significant differences in pupil size between the FXS and both other groups. The autism and neurotypical groups did not differ in pupil size. Children and adolescents with FXS have difficulties with inhibiting their responses compared to the neurotypical and autism group, even when a task is relatively simple. This may reflect reduced cognitive effort in FXS, as indicated by reduced pupil dilation. Future research should explore other executive functions in FXS at behavioral and physiological measurement levels, to identify neurocognitive mechanisms across domains.

items.title: Temporal Comparisons Elicit Greater Pride, Lower Shame, and Stronger Improvement Orientation Among Chinese Children.
items.abstract: Background Upward social comparisons are widely used to encourage effort, yet they often lead to negative emotions. Temporal comparisons may support self-improvement while preserving positive self-experience. This study investigates whether temporal comparisons offer these potential benefits for Chinese children. Methods Two between-subjects experiments were conducted with Chinese primary and secondary school students (aged 8-16 years) in autumn 2024. We manipulated comparison type and comparison direction through reading-writing tasks. Study 1 (N = 632, 51% girls) used writing tasks involving comparisons with better or worse peers or past selves, alongside a no-comparison control. Study 2 added 285 participants (51% girls) who imagined and wrote about better or worse future selves, sharing the social-comparison and control groups from Study 1. After the tasks, participants reported pride, shame, improvement goals, and superiority goals. Results Past-self comparisons elicited greater pride, less shame, and a higher improvement-to-superiority goal ratio than social comparisons and no comparison; Comparing with a better past self elicited greater pride and lower shame than comparing with superior others. Future-self comparisons elicited greater pride, less shame, and a higher improvement-to-superiority goal ratio than social comparisons; Comparison with a worse future self preserved greater pride than comparison with superior others. Conclusions Temporal comparisons, including both past-self and future-self comparisons, showed emotional and motivational advantages among Chinese children.

items.title: Early socioeconomic deprivation, the preschool home learning environment, and language and literacy skills in ethnically diverse school children.
items.abstract: Children with more exposure to socioeconomic deprivation have lower language and literacy. Minority ethnic children often experience more deprivation but are under-represented in the research literature. We examined socioeconomic deprivation (during pregnancy), home learning environment (2 years), and language and literacy at school entry (4-5 years) and primary school (6-7 years) in a diverse UK cohort (N = 7064). Using latent structural equation modelling, we identified a persistent negative effect of deprivation on school language and literacy. Despite higher deprivation, being read to less often and fewer learning resources during preschool, children of Pakistani ethnicity had school language and literacy largely on par with White British children and children of other ethnicities. Deprivation effects were not mediated by home learning environment; literacy in primary school was partially mediated by school-entry language and literacy. There may be additional factors within minority ethnic families that help mitigate impacts of socioeconomic deprivation, and standard home learning environment measures may not fully capture experiences of Pakistani ethnicity children.

items.title: Familial factors inflate the estimated effects of genetic liability to ADHD on behavioural outcomes
items.abstract: Background: People with ADHD have worse health, behavioural and social outcomes, widely interpreted as evidence that ADHD causes these harms, justifying early identification and treatment. But ADHD clusters in families, and conventional studies cannot separate the effect of a person's own ADHD from the family environment in which it arises. We used a family-based genetic design to distinguish the two. Methods: We used up to 22 genome-wide significant variants associated with ADHD (38,691 cases, 186,843 controls) to estimate effects of genetic liability to ADHD on 16 health and behavioural outcomes. We compared population-based estimates with family-based estimates from within-sibship analyses of up to 164,220 siblings. We tested for heterogeneity between the designs, and applied sensitivity analyses. We involved individuals with lived experience of ADHD in interpreting the findings and shaping how the clinical/public-health implications were described. Findings: Population-based analyses implied that greater genetic liability to ADHD increased smoking, alcohol use and depressive symptoms, and reduced educational attainment, age at first child and cognitive performance. In family-based analyses, these effects attenuated. For example, the effect on number of depressive symptoms fell from 0.059 SD (95% CI 0.039, 0.080) to 0.002 SD (-0.052, 0.055), and age at first child increased from -0.045 SD (-0.058, -0.033) to 0.003 SD (-0.040, 0.047), with significant differences between designs (p=0.048 and p=0.034). Findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses. Interpretation: Much of the excess health and behavioural burden attributed to ADHD may reflect the family and environmental context in which ADHD occurs, rather than an individual's own ADHD. Interventions targeting the individual might not reduce these outcomes as much as expected. Distinguishing such effects requires family-based designs. items.title: A bivalent Lassa virus mRNA vaccine protects guinea pigs from lethal infection with Lassa virus
items.abstract: Lassa virus (LASV), the causative agent of the life-threatening febrile disease, Lassa fever, remains a major public health concern in West Africa, where hundreds of thousands of infections occur annually. However, no licensed vaccine is currently available, highlighting the urgent need for effective preventive measures. We previously demonstrated that an mRNA-lipid nanoparticle (LNP) vaccine expressing LASV glycoprotein precursor (GPC; LASgpc-mRNA-LNP) conferred protection against lethal infection with a recombinant lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus expressing LASV GPC in mice. In this study, we extended our previous work with the aim of evaluating the efficacy of an mRNA-LNP vaccine expressing LASV nucleoprotein (NP; LASnp-mRNA-LNP) and a bivalent vaccine combining LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP. Using a lethal CBA/N mouse model of infection with ML29, an LASV live-attenuated vaccine candidate encoding LASV GPC and NP, we found that LASgpc-mRNA-LNP and LASnp-mRNA-LNP each conferred protection in the absence of detectable neutralizing antibody responses. We identified LASV GPC- and NP-derived CD4⁺ and CD8⁺ T-cell epitope peptides in CBA/N mice and demonstrated that vaccination induced robust antigen-specific T-cell responses. Importantly, the bivalent vaccine provided complete protection against lethal challenge with doses at which monovalent vaccines failed to protect all mice, suggesting a potential dose-sparing benefit of the bivalent formulation. Furthermore, the bivalent vaccine fully protected guinea pigs against lethal challenge with authentic LASV. Together, these findings establish LASV NP, in addition to GPC, as a protective antigen in the mRNA vaccine platform and provide a rationale for developing bivalent mRNA-LNP vaccines to improve protection against Lassa fever.

items.title: Barriers to Community-Based Health Insurance Enrollment in South West Ethiopia: A Qualitative Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background High out-of-pocket (OOP) expenditures remain a major barrier to financial protection. Community-based health insurance (CBHI) aims to reduce these financial barriers. However, low enrollment rates hinder its sustainability in Low- and Middle-income Countries (LMICs), including Ethiopia. Therefore, this study explored barriers influencing CBHI enrollment in the Southwest Region of Ethiopia. Methods An exploratory qualitative study was conducted from June 1 to 30, 2026 across six zones in the region. Using purposive sampling, study participants with CBHI scheme experiences were recruited. Data were gathered through 55 Key Informant Interviews (KII), 36 In-depth Interviews (IDI), and 18 Focus Group Discussions (FGD) involving community members, health facility leaders, and healthcare workers. MAXQDA Analytics Pro 26.3.0 was used for analysis following a six-step thematic analysis approach developed by Braun and Clarke. Results CBHI non-enrolment in the region has been driven by interconnected community and health system-level challenges. The community side was the predominant source of barriers. This includes low awareness about CBHI, poor perception, beliefs, and trust. Followed by service-delivery-related challenges, which include frequent medicine stock-outs, poor laboratory capacity, health workforce shortages, long waiting times, referral hurdles, poor quality services, limited health facility coverage, and persistent out-of-pocket costs. Financial and socioeconomic barriers like inability to afford the premium, inappropriate timing, and conflicting payment schedules were additionally identified challenges. Administrative bottlenecks, such as CBHI scheme implementation, and health system governance and leadership limitations, and area-specific security issues were further identified challenges. Conclusions Community and health service-related challenges influenced low uptake of CBHI enrolment in the region. Therefore, improving the enrollment rate requires tailored efforts that address community-level knowledge and socioeconomic limitations, improve service delivery by equipping public health facilities, improve CBHI scheme management, and strengthen health system leadership and governance.

items.title: Dietary Patterns of Preschool Children (Aged 3–6) in Public Primary Schools of Avaradrano District in Antananarivo Madagascar: A Descriptive Cross-Sectional 24-Hour Dietary Recall Study
items.abstract: Abstract Background Malnutrition remains a major public health challenge in Madagascar, affecting nearly two out of five children under five years of age. Research on child nutrition provides nationally representative data on child health, anthropometry, dietary diversity, and feeding practices. This study provides updated, quantitative assessments of total energy and nutrient intake among preschool children, with a detailed analysis of daily dietary composition. In addition, particular attention has been given to the contribution of snacks to children's daily diets. Methods Cross-sectional dietary data were collected from 253 children aged 3 to 6 years via the 24-hour dietary recall method. This approach allowed for the estimation of the types and quantities of foods consumed by participants during the 24 hours preceding the survey. The nutritional value of foods was estimated via data from the CIQUAL food composition table (French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health & Safety), which is supported by relevant literature. Data processing was conducted via R statistical software version 4.5.1 (2025-06-13, UCRT). Results The median energy intake was 1061 kcal (95% CI: 1003—1122). On average, carbohydrates provided 69% of the total energy, with protein and fat contributing 12% and 15%, respectively. The mean dietary diversity score was 4.49 ± 1.20, reflecting a high consumption of cereals and starchy foods (99.6%) and a low intake of dairy products (4.7%). Nearly all the children (98%) consumed three meals per day—breakfast, lunch, and dinner—while 2% skipped dinner. Snacking was common, with 98% of the children consuming at least one snack daily. Among those who snack, 25% did so only in the morning, whereas 4% had snacks exclusively in the afternoon. Conclusions Despite the consumption of meals and snacks, the nutritional and energy intake of the children aged 3–6 years remains below the recommended requirements for this age group, indicating a risk of nutrient deficiencies. Snacks play a significant role in children's diets and represent a valuable opportunity to increase the nutritional quality of their diet by contributing to energy intake and supplementing essential nutrient requirements.

items.title: Does fiscal policy influence industrialization in Sub-Saharan Africa? An explanation using the staggered lag autoregressive (ARDL) panel approach
items.abstract: Abstract This paper empirically studies the effect of fiscal policy on industrialization in Sub-Saharan Africa. Over the period 1994–2018, using data from the World Bank (WDI, 2021), on a sample of 24 countries using a panel ARDL (autoregressive lag) model, we obtain two main results. First, fiscal policy has a positive influence on industrialization in sub-Saharan Africa, and the same is true for financial openness, which appears to have a positive coefficient in the short run than in the long run. Secondly, on the other hand, variables such as services and agriculture deteriorate manufacturing value added. Thus, it would be necessary to focus on obtaining a return on investment in service provision, especially on investment in public sector infrastructure, which receives the largest share of the budget such as education and health.

items.title: Enhanced Defluoridation Using Aluminium-Modified Freshwater Mussel Shell Biosorbent
items.abstract: Abstract Groundwater fluoride contamination poses a significant public health challenge, necessitating affordable and sustainable defluoridation technologies. This study investigated raw and aluminium-modified freshwater mussel shell biochars, prepared by pyrolyzing Lake Victoria mussel shells at 800°C, as low-cost adsorbents for fluoride removal from water. Surface characterization and batch adsorption experiments optimized pH, adsorbent dosage, fluoride concentration, contact time, and temperature. Aluminium modification introduced Al–O/Al–OH functional groups and significantly enhanced the surface area and porosity of the mussel shell biosorbent. The Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy confirmed aluminium incorporation and fluoride binding, while X-ray Diffraction analysis indicated enhanced crystallinity in modified forms of the shells. The modified mussel biochars exhibited better removal efficiencies at higher concentrations compared to the unmodified forms. Additionally, modified mussel shell exhibited the highest adsorption capacity of 0.202 mg/g at optimal pH 7 and temperature of 25°C. The reaction mechanism followed Freundlich model (R² > 0.96), suggesting multilayer adsorption on heterogeneous surfaces. Kinetic modeling showed that adsorption best fits the pseudo-second-order model, indicating chemisorption as the dominant mechanism. The modified mussel biochars sorbent applied to real samples reduced fluorides permissible levels. This study paves way for simple, cost effective and efficient approaches to water defluoridation and environmental management.

items.title: Environmental Health Risks in School Children Due to Air Pollution Exposure: Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Abstract Exposure to outdoor and indoor PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀ represents a major global environmental health risk. School-aged children are more susceptible than adults to adverse respiratory effects resulting from particulate matter (PM) inhalation. Given the substantial time children spend in school, the air quality in schools can influence their health. Therefore, this systematic review aimed to synthesize current evidence regarding PM₂.₅ and PM₁₀ exposure in schools, evaluate associated respiratory health risks, and identify research gaps for future studies. We conducted a systematic literature review in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 guidelines and a prospectively registered PROSPERO protocol (CRD420261282406). We retrieved articles published between 2015 and 2025 from PubMed, Scopus, and Taylor & Francis using a PEO-based search strategy. We included 12 studies that met the predefined eligibility criteria for the final synthesis. The review compared findings from Environmental Health Risk Assessment (EHRA), epidemiological analyses, regression models, and Multiple Path Particle Dosimetry (MPPD) and STELLA modelling. The results showed that PM 2.5 and PM 10 concentrations in the indoor and outdoor environments of the school were assessed, PM 2.5 and PM 10 refer to particulate matter with aerodynamic diameters of ≤ 2.5 µm and ≤ 10 µm respectively. The Risk Quotient (RQ) results for the non-carcinogenic risk assessment showed that several students had RQ values greater than 1. Children are at risk of experiencing worse health effects because of their higher respiratory rate relative to body mass. A study in Bandung, Indonesia found an inverse relationship between PM 2.5 exposure and lung function (FEV1 and FVC). Modeling of respiratory diseases indicates that higher particulate matter (PM) deposition occurs in the respiratory tracts of children. High levels of PM 2.5 and PM 10 exposure in school environments across the country pose a significant health risk to students, particularly in respiratory diseases. These findings support the need to strengthen indoor and outdoor air quality management in schools through improved ventilation, reduction of traffic-related emissions, and routine air quality monitoring. Future longitudinal studies using standardized exposure and health outcome measurements are needed to strengthen the evidence base and support the development of evidence-informed public health policies.

items.title: Why Mothers Die in India: Bridging the Gap Between Healthcare Access and Maternal Mortality in a Tertiary Care Centre
items.abstract: Abstract Background Maternal mortality remains a major public health challenge in low- and middle-income countries despite improvements in institutional deliveries and emergency obstetric care. Objective To determine the direct and indirect causes of maternal mortality and assess the contribution of the Three-Delay Model among maternal deaths at a tertiary care referral centre. Methods A retrospective observational study was conducted at the Department of Obstetrics and Gynaecology, VMMC & Safdarjung Hospital, New Delhi, India, including maternal deaths occurring between January 2020 and December 2024. Maternal deaths meeting World Health Organization criteria were identified from maternal death registers, case records, referral documents, and Maternal Death Review forms. Demographic characteristics, antenatal care status, referral patterns, causes of death, and delays in care were analysed using descriptive statistics. Results A total of 650 maternal deaths were analysed. Obstetric haemorrhage, sepsis, and hypertensive disorders were the leading direct causes of death, while anaemia and medical comorbidities were the predominant indirect causes. Most deaths occurred among un-booked women. Delay-1 (delay in seeking care) was the most frequent contributor, followed by Delay-2 (delay in reaching a healthcare facility). The findings identified deficiencies in antenatal care utilization, referral pathways, transport systems, and emergency obstetric preparedness. Conclusion Maternal mortality at tertiary referral centres is largely attributable to preventable obstetric complications compounded by delays in accessing timely care. Strengthening antenatal risk identification, referral systems, transport services, emergency obstetric care, blood transfusion facilities, and intensive care support is essential to reduce preventable maternal deaths and advance national and global maternal health goals.

items.title: Multivariate Quality Framework Combining Factor Analysis, PCA, Clustering, and Robustness Validation in Saudi Arabia using Open Government Hospital Data
items.abstract: Abstract This work presents a reproducible multivariate quality analysis in Saudi Arabia with the help of official open government health datasets for assessing regional hospital performance. Indicators at region level describe hospital utilization, emergency readiness, inpatient flow, chronic disease service demand, intensive care capacity, national health system context and population exposure that are harmonized through an integrated analytical matrix. To identify dominant latent dimensions of hospital performance Principal component analysis (PCA) is used. Factor analysis is done with utilization intensity, service pressure, varimax rotation provided interpretable underlying constructs which is related to capacity and population adjusted demand. Using retained principal components to rank health regions a variance weighted Hospital Performance Index is constructed and to classify regions into distinct performance archetypes clustering analysis is applied. To examine robustness equal weighted comparison, cluster stability validation, leave one variable out analysis, alternative index definitions, cluster stability validation and cluster stability validation was used. Spearman correlation analysis, PCA, PCA weighted index construction, k-means clustering, varimax rotated factor analysis, and robustness validation were performed. The stability of PCA is supported by Bartlett’s test of sphericity where χ² = 121.49 and p = 3.36 × 10⁻¹¹. Three principal components are retained, explaining 82.7% of the total variance, with PC1/2/3 contributing 38.2%, 33.09%, and 11.40%, respectively. Robustness analyses has good agreement between PCA and equal weighted indices (Spearman ρ = 0.924, p = 3.34 × 10⁻⁷). The results demonstrates that Saudi health regions show clear multidimensional heterogeneity with difference performance shaped through interaction of critical care availability, turnover, bed utilization, length of stay, chronic disease service use and emergency bed readiness. Instead of relying on isolated indicators this proposed framework comes up with transparent evidence system for regional benchmarking through fragmented public datasets. This Study supports data driven planning aligned with Saudi healthcare transformation priorities and contributes a scalable open data methodology to health system intelligence.

items.title: A semi-quantitative framework to prioritize the zoonotic risks of invasive alien species
items.abstract: Abstract Invasive alien species (IAS) contribute to zoonotic disease emergence, yet human health impacts are rarely incorporated into IAS prioritization frameworks. This study presents a semi-quantitative tool to evaluate zoonotic risk from invasive mammals in Europe by integrating epidemiological and spatial information. The framework combines four parameters: pathogen prevalence, disease severity based on the biosafety level of associated pathogens, geographic distribution, and potential human exposure derived from spatial overlap between IAS distributions and human population density. Parameters were standardized using a five-point ordinal scale and combined into a human health impact score. The framework was applied to eight EU-regulated invasive mammal species. Six species were classified as having a Major potential impact on human health, one as Moderate, and one as Minor. No species reached the Minimal or Massive categories. Comparison with impact assessment systems revealed partial agreement, with the strongest association observed between the proposed score and the Generic Impact Scoring System (GISS) overall score. Weaker correlations with EU biodiversity impact scores and the GISS human health category suggest that existing assessments provide useful but incomplete information on zoonotic risk. At country level, variation was observed in potential human exposure to invasive mammals and public health preparedness. Some highly exposed countries showed high preparedness, whereas others combined high exposure with lower preparedness. The framework provides a quantitative and replicable tool for identifying IAS and regions where zoonotic risk may require greater attention, supporting management and public health preparedness under a One Health perspective.

items.title: Leaching Potential and Environmental Implications of Gold Ore Tailings From Ileki Ijesha, Osun State, Nigeria
items.abstract: Abstract Gold mining in Nigeria, particularly artisanal and small-scale operations, generates large volumes of tailings that pose serious environmental and public health risks due to heavy metal leaching and potential acid mine drainage (AMD). This study assessed the leaching behavior and geochemical characteristics of gold ore tailings from Ileki Ijesha, Osun State, using batch and dynamic column leaching experiments. Five representative samples were analyzed for pH and concentrations of key metals (Fe, Mn, Pb, Cd, Zn, Cr, Ca) by Atomic Absorption Spectrometry. Leachates were further evaluated through PHREEQC geochemical modeling for speciation, saturation indices, and sensitivity analysis. Results revealed elevated iron (up to 22.2 mg/L) and manganese (up to 11.2 mg/L) concentrations, with moderate lead levels (6.6–7.81 mg/L) under near-neutral pH conditions (6.06–7.73). Modeling indicated supersaturation with iron (oxy) hydroxides and a critical pH threshold (~ 5.5) for accelerated metal release. These findings highlight significant long-term AMD risks and underscore the urgent need for improved tailings management and regulatory frameworks in Nigerian gold mining regions.

items.title: The Use of Indigenous Knowledge Medicine by Traditional Health Practitioners to Treat Infertility in Mavhunda Village, Vhembe District: An Ethnomedicinal Inquiry
items.abstract: Abstract Infertility represents a complex reproductive health challenge worldwide, generating severe psychological distress, familial instability, and acute social stigmatization. In resource-constrained rural localities such as Mavhunda Village in the Vhembe District of Limpopo Province, structural barriers compel community members to seek healthcare from traditional health practitioners. This study examines the role of indigenous knowledge medicine in diagnosing and treating infertility. Framed through Ethnomedicine Theory, this qualitative single-case study employed purposive sampling to investigate experienced traditional health practitioners (n'anga and mungome) with over a decade of clinical practice. Empirical data gathered through semi-structured interviews and observational fieldwork reveal that practitioners utilize a sophisticated botanical pharmacopeia—including Muthavhatsindi ( Brackenridgea zanguebarica ), Musuma ( Diospyros mespiliformis ), Museto, and Mapfura steam therapies—alongside customary restorative rituals like U swela . The article calls for progressive public health policy reforms and formal collaborative referral networks.

items.title: Short-Term Forecasting of Monthly Syphilis Cases Using a Stability and Recency-Aware Selective Ensemble
items.abstract: Abstract Accurate short-term forecasting of syphilis cases is important for disease surveillance and public health planning. This study developed a stability and recency-aware selective ensemble (SRSE) framework using monthly syphilis cases in Jiangsu Province from 2021–2024 for model development and 2025 data for independent testing. Nine statistical forecasting models were evaluated by expanding-window rolling-origin validation. SRSE integrated recency-weighted errors, cross-origin stability, and candidate-model screening, with key hyperparameters optimized using Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Genetic Algorithm (GA), and Sparrow Search Algorithm (SSA). PSO-SRSE achieved the lowest test errors, with MAE, RMSE, MAPE, and sMAPE of 109.39, 132.35, 3.89%, and 3.87%, respectively, outperforming the unoptimized SRSE, equal-weighted ensemble, and all individual models. These findings suggest that PSO-SRSE may improve point forecasting for short monthly syphilis surveillance series.

items.title: Culturally Grounded Malaria Knowledge among Traditional Health Practitioners and Elders in Rural Limpopo South Africa
items.abstract: Abstract Community participation is central to malaria elimination, particularly in rural settings where Indigenous and biomedical health systems coexist. South African studies have documented household knowledge, attitudes and practices, but less is known about how traditional health practitioners and elders organise, communicate and apply malaria knowledge. Understanding these knowledge systems may strengthen culturally credible communication, timely referral and participation in elimination activities. This study explored culturally grounded knowledge of malaria symptoms, transmission, seasonal risk and prevention among traditional health practitioners and elders in Dan Village, Limpopo Province, and considered its implications for community engagement in malaria elimination. An exploratory qualitative design informed by Afrocentricity was used. Twenty-five participants - five diviners, five herbalists and fifteen elders aged 70 years or older - were purposively selected. Semi-structured interviews were conducted in Sepedi or Xitsonga, audio-recorded and transcribed. Thematic content analysis identified units of meaning, clustered related accounts and interpreted the resulting themes through cultural location, Nommo, Maat and Ubuntu. Participant accounts were distinguished from clinically or epidemiologically verified claims. Four themes were identified: recognition of malaria through symptom clusters; mosquito transmission within plural explanations of illness; seasonal ecological knowledge; and prevention as collective environmental responsibility. Participants linked fever, headache, chills, weakness and gastrointestinal symptoms with mosquito bites, rainfall, humidity, standing water and vegetation change. Their prevention accounts emphasised environmental management, reduced mosquito contact, community cooperation and early response to symptoms. Plant-based and spiritual practices were also reported but were not evaluated for safety or efficacy. The accounts showed areas of convergence with public-health guidance alongside claims requiring clarification or empirical assessment. Traditional practitioners and elders held context-specific knowledge that could support locally credible malaria communication, seasonal mobilisation and referral. Elimination programmes should engage trusted knowledge holders through structured, evidence-informed partnerships that preserve prompt parasitological diagnosis and recommended treatment while correcting unsafe or unverified claims.

items.title: Community Responses to Urban Heat Risk in Prayagraj Municipal Corporation, India
items.abstract: Abstract The increasing frequency and intensity of heatwaves under climate change are emerging as major public health concerns across rapidly urbanising regions of South Asia. This study examines heatwave awareness and perception, behavioural adaptation practices, and heat-related health outcomes among urban households in Prayagraj, a climatically vulnerable city in India's Indo-Gangetic Plain. The analysis is based on primary household-level data collected from 422 households through multistage cluster random sampling conducted between February and March 2026. Descriptive statistics and chi-square tests were used to examine socio-demographic variation in heat-related awareness, adaptive behaviour, and self-reported health outcomes. At the same time, Cronbach’s alpha was used to assess the internal consistency of behavioural adaptation and health outcome variables. Qualitative field narratives were additionally incorporated to contextualise lived experiences of heat exposure and adaptation constraints. The findings reveal widespread perception of increasing heatwave intensity, with 91.5% of respondents reporting rising heat exposure over their lifetime. Although adaptive practices such as increased hydration, dietary modification, and protective clothing use were widely adopted, a substantial proportion of households continued to report heat-related symptoms, including muscle weakness or cramps (49%), severe fatigue or exhaustion (42%), dizziness or fainting (31.3%), and heat stroke or high fever (27.1%). Significant socio-demographic disparities were observed across educational, occupational, and social groups, with informal workers and economically vulnerable households reporting comparatively greater heat-related health burden. The study underscores the need for inclusive and structurally grounded urban heat adaptation strategies that address occupational exposure, housing vulnerability, and broader social determinants of heat-health risk in rapidly growing Indian cities.

items.title: Incorporating public involvement in public health research: a co-designed qualitative evaluation of SPECTRUM consortium public involvement panels
items.abstract: Abstract Background : Patient and public involvement (PPI) is increasingly recognised as essential in health research, yet most evidence focuses on clinical contexts, with limited exploration of public involvement (PI) in population-level prevention research. This study aims to address this gap by exploring experiences of PI within SPECTRUM, a UK-based research consortium investigating the commercial determinants of health. Methods : A qualitative, reflexive evaluation was conducted using interviews (n=16) and small-group discussions (n=4) between April and September 2024 and analysed using reflexive thematic analysis, informed by an established framework for evaluating public involvement. Interviews and focus groups were held either online via MS Teams or in person at the University of Stirling with PI members (n=23), academic PI leads (n=6), and researchers (n=6) involved in the three SPECTRUM PI groups (focused on alcohol and food research, lived experience of using tobacco and/or nicotine, and lived experience of nicotine use and mental health service use). Results : Researchers reported that PI contributed to research relevance, accessibility, and methodological rigour, while fostering researcher motivation and skill development. PI members perceived that involvement enhanced knowledge, confidence, and sense of contribution to meaningful change. Organisational and interpersonal factors, including facilitation, funding, group dynamics, and institutional support, shaped experiences of PI. Challenges included resource constraints, inconsistent feedback to contributors, risks of tokenism, difficulties balancing diverse stakeholder perspectives, and concerns about group diversity and representativeness. Researchers, facilitators and members all believed that long-term involvement led some members to develop “lay expertise,” which participants felt presented both benefits and tensions regarding representativeness. Potential unintended harms included facilitators concern about emotional burden linked to lived experience, and members reflecting on instances when they had felt their contributions were undervalued. Conclusions : The SPECTRUM consortium demonstrated good practice by providing funding for PI across the research cycle, developing skills of panel members, and supporting researchers through well-planned facilitation. Improvements are needed in feedback processes, diversity and inclusion, and better funding and training for PI. Future research should explore how diversity is defined in nationally representative PI and how the broader impact of PI can be evaluated beyond research outcomes.

items.title: Discovering pathogens and evaluating the microbial and chemical contamination in the Machángara and the San Pedro Rivers in Quito, Ecuador: A temporal and longitudinal analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Water pollution poses major environmental and public health challenges, particularly in regions with insufficient wastewater treatment. This study evaluated seasonal changes in microbial and chemical contamination at three sampling points along the San Pedro and Machángara Rivers in Quito, Ecuador, during two rainy seasons and one dry season. Escherichia coli , total coliforms, yeasts, molds, and Candida spp. were quantified by selective culture, while selected pathogens were identified by PCR and Sanger sequencing. E. coli and total coliform levels frequently exceeded international standards. Giardia intestinalis , Cryptosporidium parvum , and Mycobacterium tuberculosis were consistently detected, whereas Helicobacter pylori , Campylobacter jejuni , C. upsaliensis , M. leprae , and several E. coli pathotypes were detected sporadically. Physico-chemical parameters showed seasonal variation, with elevated pH and chemical oxygen demand in the Machángara River and excessive nitrite concentrations in both rivers. Several metals, including Al, Fe, Cr, and Mn, exceeded Ecuadorian limits, indicating impaired water quality. Kruskal–Wallis analyses showed significant differences in most microbial and physico-chemical parameters among sampling points, particularly between upstream reference and downstream contaminated sites, whereas seasonal differences in pathogen occurrence were generally not significant. These findings provide an integrated seasonal assessment of microbial and chemical pollution in urban Andean rivers and highlight the need for improved wastewater treatment, continuous water-quality monitoring, and targeted remediation strategies.

items.title: In Vitro Study of the Antibacterial Efficacy of Commercial Alcohol-Based Hand Gels Available on the Lebanese Market
items.abstract: Abstract Background & Purpose: Hand hygiene is universally recognized as the single most essential intervention for preventing infection transmission in healthcare and community settings. During the COVID-19 pandemic and the concurrent financial crisis in Lebanon (2019–present), commercial alcohol-based hand gels proliferated rapidly across local markets. However, independent quality verification of commercial hydrogels against multi-drug resistant (MDR) clinical pathogens remains scarce. This study evaluated the in vitro antibacterial efficacy of seven commercial hand gels commercially distributed in Lebanon (HG1–HG7) against clinically relevant bacterial pathogens. Methods: Antibacterial activity was assessed using standardized agar well diffusion on Mueller-Hinton agar, measuring mean inhibition zone diameters (mm ± SD). Results: Profound variation in antibacterial performance was observed among the tested commercial products. HG1 (locally manufactured, claiming 65% ethanol) demonstrated broad-spectrum inhibitory activity against S. aureus, Salmonella spp., E. coli, and K. pneumoniae. HG2 and HG7 displayed narrow-spectrum activity limited strictly to S. aureus. Crucially, HG3, HG4, HG5, and HG6 exhibited no detectable antibacterial activity across all tested bacterial strains, despite manufacturer label claims of 70% ethanol (HG3, HG6) or denatured alcohol (HG4, HG5). Multidrug-resistant P. aeruginosa proved completely resistant to all seven commercial hand gels. Conclusion: Alarming quality failures and market inconsistencies exist among commercial hand gels distributed in Lebanon. Regulatory agencies, including the Ministry of Public Health and the Lebanese Standards Institution (LIBNOR), must establish mandatory post-market analytical oversight, requiring Gas Chromatography verification of active alcohol concentrations and standardized efficacy certification prior to commercial distribution.

items.title: Meat and Chicken Retailers in Oman Pose a Considerable Threat to Public Health
items.abstract: Abstract This study investigated bacterial contamination ( Salmonella and Campylobacter ) in meat and chicken from 20 retailers in the Muscat and Barka regions, collecting 100 samples from cutting boards, machines, knives, carcasses, and workers' hands. Molecular techniques, particularly PCR assays, confirmed the presence of Salmonella enterica and Campylobacter coli . Results showed Salmonella contamination in 46% of samples (CI = 36–56) and Campylobacter in 25% (CI = 17–34), with both pathogens found in 13% of samples. Meat retailers contributed 22% of Salmonella isolates, while 24% came from chicken. For Campylobacter , 15 positive samples came from red meat and 10 from chicken. Notably, Salmonella was primarily found on workers' hands (23.9% of positive samples), and Campylobacter mainly in carcasses (32% of positives). All 20 retailers tested positive for Salmonella , and 50% of both meat and chicken retailers were positive for Campylobacter . Serotyping revealed four Salmonella enterica serotypes: Typhimurium (50%), Weltevreden (28.6%), Enteritidis (14.3%), and Hadar (7.1%). Typhimurium and Weltevreden were found in meat retailers, while all four serotypes were present in chicken retailers, indicating greater diversity in poultry products.

items.title: Perspectives on traumatic brain injury screening among intersecting underserved populations: an exploratory study.
items.abstract: Purpose This study aimed to explore barriers and facilitators in traumatic brain injury (TBI) screening for underserved individuals and knowledge translation efforts to address challenges. Materials and methods Guided by qualitative description, we conducted four virtual focus groups: 10 people (7 female, 3 male) with lived experience of precarious housing, criminal legal involvement, and/or violence and 11 service providers (9 female, 2 male) supporting these populations with TBI. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings Barriers to TBI screening included (1) inconsistent implementation and competing priorities within organizations; (2) stigmatization and systemic challenges in service provision; and (3) a lack of a universal screening system and follow-up pathways. While potential facilitators to screening involved language, knowledge and resources, as identified in the following themes: (1) language matters: shaping conversations in TBI screening; (2) screening for all: knowledge and access; and (3) easy and engaging tools for screening. Conclusions Barriers to TBI screening persist. Systemic changes and targeted educational initiatives are needed to improve knowledge and awareness of TBI with sensitivity to potential circumstances of specific populations. Affirming conversational language in screening, along with providing tailored resources and access to follow-up support services that address social determinants of health, are essential.

items.title: Development and Pilot Evaluation of a Standardized and Accessible Rubric (OMNI) for Assessing Generative AI in Health Care Contexts: Four-Stage Mixed Methods Study.
items.abstract: Background The rapid adoption of generative AI in the community and health care necessitates reliable, human-led evaluation. Objective This study aimed to develop a standardized rubric to support health care professionals, administrators, and researchers in evaluating generative AI outputs in health contexts. Methods A rubric was developed through a 4-stage mixed methods study: literature synthesis, expert refinement, pilot application, and post-pilot feedback. The rubric was informed by 69 publications and refined through iterative feedback from a multidisciplinary expert panel (n=23). The pilot rubric was applied to 4 health care scenarios: responses to health-related Reddit questions, generation of health-related images and videos, responses to health professional continuing education questions, and automated physician-to-physician clinical documentation generation. Via these scenarios, 15 clinicians (medical practitioners, pharmacists, and medical oncologists) evaluated 250 input-output pairs using domain-level ratings and qualitative comments. The evaluated outputs included 200 AI-generated responses across the 4 health care scenarios and 50 physician-tagged replies in the health-related Reddit questions scenario. Results The final rubric, OMNI, comprised 10 evaluation domains (Accuracy, Safety, Recognizes Uncertainty, Completeness, Communicates Clearly, Empathetic, Context Aware, Referencing, Follows Instructions, and Avoids Coerciveness) assessed on 4-point Likert scales, supported by detailed instructional and example materials. Via the 4 pilot scenarios, assessors generated 9600 domain-level ratings and 4010 qualitative comments. The mean pairwise agreement for the 4-point Likert groups ranged from 30.8% to 53.4%, increasing to 59.3% to 79.6% when collapsed into broad agreement categories; Gwet's AC2 ranged from 0.49 to 0.80. OMNI differentiated strengths and weaknesses between models within scenarios, while recurrent limitations in Referencing, Recognizes Uncertainty, Completeness, Empathetic, and Accuracy were identified across scenarios. Multimodal image and video outputs had the highest occurrence of negative rating domains. Assessors reported OMNI was usable and indicated they would reuse it. Conclusions OMNI is a standardized, accessible rubric for expert-led evaluation of generative AI outputs in health contexts. Pilot application demonstrated that OMNI could differentiate AI performance across models and domains while generating structured feedback. Further work is needed to assess its applicability to purpose-built health AI tools, agentic systems, and organizational evaluation settings.

items.title: Driving Quality Improvement in Gynecology - A Quality Indicator System for China's County-Level Hospitals.
items.abstract: Background Gynecologic diseases are a significant yet often underrecognized global health burden, negatively impacting women's quality of life. In China, county-level public hospitals serve as the primary providers of care or first line of defense for managing these conditions, highlighting the urgent need for improved service quality. However, a systematic framework with specific quality indicators for gynecologic care remains underdeveloped both in China and internationally. Compared with obstetrics, progress in gynecologic care quality assessment has lagged, creating a gap between evidence and practice. The authors aimed to develop and preliminarily implement a quality indicator system to guide gynecologic care quality improvement efforts. Methods Quality indicators were identified through a comprehensive literature review and refined using a two-round modified Delphi survey (January-April 2024) involving 29 experts. Expert consensus on the importance and feasibility of each indicator was obtained. Based on this indicator system, the authors conducted the China Gynaecological Healthcare Quality Survey, a national cross-sectional survey across 31 provinces in mainland China (April-December 2024), sampling 435 hospitals of different types and levels. After data cleaning, a final sample of 178 hospitals was included for analysis. A hybrid weighting approach combining subjective expert judgment (percentage weight and multiplicative methods) with objective empirical data (entropy weight method) was applied. The TOPSIS (Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution) method was used to derive a comprehensive quality score (closeness coefficient [ C i ]) for each hospital. Results The Delphi process yielded a final framework comprising three first-level, 16 second-level, and 43 third-level indicators. Mean importance scores ranged from 7.69 to 8.97 on a nine-point scale, with variation coefficients between 0.02 and 0.20. Kendall's W coefficients increased from 0.149 to 0.220 between rounds, indicating growing consensus. The average authority coefficient across experts was 0.90, supporting the reliability of the results. The combined weights assigned to structure, process, and outcome domains were 0.455, 0.301, and 0.245, respectively. In the national survey, 178 hospitals (84 county-level and 94 provincial and municipal) were analyzed. Provincial and municipal hospitals achieved significantly higher comprehensive quality scores than county-level hospitals (median C i : 0.421 vs. 0.397; z=-5.533, P C i : 0.425, 0.407, and 0.402; χ 2 =12.214, P=0.002). No significant differences were found among hospital types (χ 2 =4.174, P=0.124). Conclusions The authors established mainland China's first validated indicator system for gynecologic care quality. National implementation across 178 hospitals demonstrates the framework's practical utility while revealing significant quality differences across hospital tiers and regions. This standardized evaluation framework provides a practical tool for targeted quality assessment and precision improvement in primary gynecologic care.

items.title: Target Trial of Semaglutide Versus Dulaglutide or Liraglutide in Patients Receiving Hemodialysis.
items.abstract: Objective To evaluate the comparative effectiveness of semaglutide versus dulaglutide or liraglutide in patients with diabetes receiving maintenance hemodialysis. Research design and methods Using 2011-2022 U.S. Renal Data System and Medicare data, we emulated a target trial evaluating semaglutide versus dulaglutide or liraglutide in patients receiving hemodialysis. Overlap weights were used to adjust for confounders. Fine-Gray models were used to assess death on dialysis and hospitalization. A generalized estimating equation was used for repeated measures of body weight. Results We identified 1,312 semaglutide and 2,601 dulaglutide or liraglutide users. After overlap weighting, the effective sample size was 3,200 patients (mean age 61; 63% White; 28% Black; 52% male; median [interquartile range] BMI 34 [29-40] kg/m2; median follow-up 1.1 [0.6-1.9] years). Semaglutide versus dulaglutide or liraglutide was associated with a mortality on dialysis subdistribution hazard ratio (sHR) of 0.82 (95% CI 0.70-0.97; 1-year cumulative incidence 11% vs. 13%) and all-cause hospitalization sHR of 0.91 (95% CI 0.83-0.99; 1-year incidence 57% vs. 62%). Body weight loss was higher with semaglutide (-4.8%, 95% CI -5.3% to -4.2%) at 1 year vs. -3.4%, 95% CI -3.9% to -3.1%). Direct comparisons of semaglutide versus dulaglutide showed similar results for mortality (sHR 0.82, 95% CI 0.69-0.97) and hospitalization (sHR 0.88, 95% CI 0.81-0.97), but semaglutide versus liraglutide showed no statistically significant benefit for mortality or hospitalization. Conclusions Among patients with diabetes receiving hemodialysis and equipoise between semaglutide and dulaglutide or liraglutide, semaglutide may be the preferred glucagon-like peptide 1 agent compared with dulaglutide.

items.title: Safety of Sodium-Glucose Cotransporter 2 Inhibitors in Older Adults With Type 2 Diabetes: A Cohort Study.
items.abstract: Objective Sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors (SGLT2is) have demonstrated cardiorenal benefits in individuals with type 2 diabetes, but safety data in older adults remain limited. We evaluated the real-world safety of SGLT2is compared with dipeptidyl peptidase 4 inhibitors (DPP-4is) among individuals aged ≥75 years with type 2 diabetes. Research design and methods We conducted a population-based, active-comparator, new-user cohort study using administrative health databases from British Columbia, Canada. We included individuals aged ≥75 years with type 2 diabetes initiating SGLT2is or DPP-4is between 1 January 2021 and 31 December 2023. Primary outcomes were infection, diabetic ketoacidosis, acute kidney injury, fall, fracture, and all-cause hospitalization. Cox regression with propensity score-based standardized mortality ratio weighting was used to estimate hazard ratios (HRs). Results The study included 4,997 SGLT2i initiators (median age, 79 years; 37% women) and 1,289 DPP-4i initiators (median age, 82 years; 50% women). Compared with DPP-4i initiation, SGLT2i initiation was associated with lower risks of acute kidney injury (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.60-0.95) and all-cause hospitalization (HR 0.87, 95% CI 0.77-0.98), with no difference in risk of infection. No differences were observed in risk of diabetic ketoacidosis, falls, or fractures, although CIs were compatible with both benefit and harm. Conclusions In individuals aged ≥75 years with type 2 diabetes, SGLT2i initiation was not associated with increased risk of harm compared with DPP-4i initiation, although estimates were imprecise for some outcomes. These findings may support consideration of SGLT2is as a treatment option in this population.

items.title: Sleeper agents: asymptomatic Acinetobacter colonization and underlying mechanisms.
items.abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii and other Acinetobacter species are a growing public health concern because they commonly cause healthcare-associated infections. Acinetobacter spp. are often multi-drug resistant, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. Therefore, understanding the reservoirs for Acinetobacter spp. in healthcare settings is particularly important to infection control. Acinetobacter spp. are known to asymptomatically colonize the human gut, skin, and respiratory flora, and recent work has found the prevalence of Acinetobacter colonization is high in patients in healthcare environments, such as hospitals and long-term care facilities. Patients colonized by A. baumannii are at increased risk of developing clinical infections, including by the same strains. Additionally, multiple studies report transmission of A. baumannii strains to other patients in the same healthcare setting. Recent mechanistic studies on A. baumannii gut colonization have found that the microbiota, host immunity, and diet contribute to colonization resistance in animal models. Here, we review the epidemiologic evidence for asymptomatic colonization as a clinically important reservoir for A. baumannii and examine the nascent study of the molecular mechanisms of Acinetobacter colonization. We discuss future prospects for understanding Acinetobacter colonization that may help develop strategies to support colonization resistance and prevent infections.

items.title: The impact of sequential analysis on drug decision-making in Canada.
items.abstract: Aim: In Canada (excluding Québec), public drug coverage generally relies on health technology assessment and reimbursement recommendations produced by Canada's Drug Agency - L'Agence des medicaments du Canada (CDA-AMC). At CDA-AMC, when multiple comparators are included in the pharmacoeconomic analysis, the corresponding results are reported using a sequential analysis. The aim of this review was to understand how the sequential analysis approach impacts the price reductions recommended in CDA-AMC drug reimbursement reviews. Materials & methods: A search was conducted of CDA-AMC reimbursement review reports published from January 2022 to December 2023 that included a cost-utility analysis with sequential analysis performed by the Sponsor and the economic re-analysis by CDA-AMC. An analysis of included reimbursement reviews was conducted to determine if the comparators chosen through the sequential analysis and selected for the price reduction in the final reimbursement recommendation were also the comparators most commonly used in current clinical practice. Additional analyses further examining reported market shares and list prices were conducted among reimbursement recommendations where the selected comparator was not the most commonly used comparator. An assessment examining the impact of comparator selection based on the sequential analysis on cost-effectiveness conclusions in CDA-AMC reimbursement reviews was also conducted. Results are presented by type of drug review (i.e., oncology vs nononcology products). Results: A total of 150 CDA-AMC reimbursement reviews published from January 2022 to December 2023 were identified and screened for eligibility. Of these, 37 reimbursement reviews - comprising a total of 60 recommendations (13 oncology and 47 nononcology products) based on sequential analyses - were included in the analysis. Among the included reimbursement recommendations, CDA-AMC chose a comparator that was not the most commonly used in clinical practice in 25 (42%) recommendations when determining the price reduction of the new medication (in accordance with CDA-AMC guidelines that permit selection of any comparator regardless of clinical utilization). Among these 25 reimbursement recommendations, the selected comparator represented Conclusion: Comparator selection is a vital aspect of health technology assessment. At CDA-AMC, comparator selection is driven by the sequential analysis approach, playing an important role in their economic assessment and reimbursement recommendation. Despite the relatively small number of sequential analyses examined, this review found that CDA-AMC recommendations based on a sequential analysis frequently refer to a comparator that is not widely used in real-world clinical practice, which can impede subsequent health technology assessment decisions that need to consider clinically prevalent comparators. This is notable as pairwise analyses conducted for this review demonstrated that selecting the treatments most often used in clinical practice as the comparator, rather than the CDA-AMC comparator, likely yields lower price reductions for new treatments that are more costly and more effective. These findings reinforce the importance of transparent and clinically informed comparator selection and points to the need for CDA-AMC to commit to providing economic assessments of all clinically relevant comparators to ensure payers have a complete and balanced picture of the evidence.

items.title: The Aspergillus fumigatus septation components Bud4 and Rho4 are essential for virulence.
items.abstract: Aspergillus fumigatus is the primary etiologic agent of pulmonary mold infections, the most severe of which is invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA). As the currently approved antifungal drugs are threatened by growing resistance rates and host toxicity, novel therapeutic options are urgently needed. Our recent work suggests that septation inhibition may be one such strategy, as aseptate strains of A. fumigatus are hypersusceptible to the echinocandin antifungal drugs and display significantly reduced virulence in animal models of IPA. In the current study, we expand upon our understanding of the anillin-like protein, Bud4, and Rho GTPase, Rho4, which regulate septation in Aspergillus nidulans and A. fumigatus , respectively. Whereas AnBud4 is not essential for septation in A. nidulans , deletion of the A. fumigatus ortholog (∆ bud4 ) resulted in complete loss of septation. A similar phenotype was also observed in ∆ rho4 , consistent with previous studies. Supporting a critical role for hyphal septation in the establishment of invasive aspergillosis, we find that ∆ bud4 and ∆ rho4 display avirulence in a mouse model of IPA characterized by a loss of tissue-invasive growth. Furthermore, both deletion mutations were able to convert anti-A spergillus echinocandin activity from static to cidal. Through titratable bud4 expression using a doxycycline-repressible promoter system, we also find that even partial repression of septation significantly increases echinocandin susceptibility. Taken together, these studies support a therapeutic strategy which could incorporate a septation inhibitor in combination with echinocandins to reduce tissue-invasive growth and improve antifungal susceptibility.

items.title: Next-Generation Bed Nets to Control Malaria in Côte d'Ivoire.
items.abstract: Background Next-generation long-lasting insecticidal nets (LLINs) treated with more than one insecticide have been insufficiently evaluated in West Africa. Methods In this cluster randomized clinical trial, 33 clusters of villages (1-3 villages per cluster) in Côte d'Ivoire were randomly assigned (11 clusters per group) to use pyrethroid-only (py-only; MAGNet) (control), piperonyl butoxide-pyrethroid (PBO-py; Veeralin), or chlorfenapyr-pyrethroid (CFP-py; Interceptor G2) LLINs. One net was distributed for every two people, followed by door-to-door visits to assist with hanging the nets and to promote their use. The primary outcome was the incidence of malaria cases among children aged 6 months to 9 years over the year following net distribution. Incidence rate ratios compared cases per child-year between clusters randomly assigned to use PBO-py versus py-only nets and CFP-py versus py-only nets. Results A total of 25,660 LLINs were distributed to 11,283 households (py-only, n=3797; PBO-py, n=3559; and CFP-py, n=3927). The primary outcome analyses included 549, 551, and 549 children in the py-only, PBO-py, and CFP-py groups, respectively. Mean malaria incidence over 12 months was 1.11 cases per child-year in the py-only group (control), 0.84 in the PBO-py group, and 0.65 in the CFP-py group. The incidence rate ratios were as follows: PBO-py versus py-only nets, 0.72 (95% confidence interval [CI], 0.52 to 0.99; P=0.045); and CFP-py versus py-only nets, 0.57 (95% CI, 0.43 to 0.75; P Conclusions Malaria incidence over 12 months was significantly reduced among children aged 6 months to 9 years residing in clusters of villages in Côte d'Ivoire that were randomly assigned to use CFP-py versus py-only LLINs and PBO-py versus py-only LLINs. (Funded by The Global Fund to Fight AIDS, Tuberculosis and Malaria; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT05796193.).

items.title: Colorectal Cancer among U.S. Adults, 2000-2023.
items.abstract: AbstractUsing data from the National Cancer Institute's Surveillance, Epidemiology, and End Results (SEER) Program, we examined colorectal cancer incidence rates in the United States between 2000 and 2023. SEER 21 covers 45.8% of the U.S. population. The age-adjusted incidence rate was 55.2 per 100,000 (95% CI, 54.8 to 55.6) in 2000, 36.7 per 100,000 (95% CI, 36.4 to 37.0) in 2022, and 38.3 per 100,000 (95% CI, 38.0 to 38.6) in 2023. The apparent increase in 2023 was the first since the inception of SEER 21 and warrants additional surveillance and investigation.

items.title: Factors associated with receipt of prescription medication for menopause-related symptoms.
items.abstract: Objective To evaluate the association of patient- and clinician-level factors and receipt of prescription medication for menopause-related symptoms in a large academic health care system. Methods We conducted a retrospective cohort study of women aged 40-55 years seeking care for menopause-related symptoms in any outpatient encounter with family medicine, internal medicine, endocrinology, and OB/Gyn from 2016 to 2023. Prescriptions associated with menopause-related ICD-10 diagnoses were extracted. Bivariate and multivariable logistic regression were used to evaluate the association of patient- and clinician-level characteristics and receipt of prescription treatment. Results We identified 5,491 women with an outpatient encounter with an associated ICD-10 code for menopause-related symptoms. Relative to White women, Black women were less likely to receive any prescription treatment for menopause-related symptoms (OR: 0.79, 95% CI: 0.67-0.95), including systemic estrogen (OR: 0.64, 95% CI: 0.47-0.87); however, were more likely to receive SSRIs (OR: 1.49, 95% CI: 1.04-2.14). Relative to patients seeking care within OB/Gyn settings, patients were less likely to be prescribed any treatment by internal medicine (OR: 0.45, 95% CI: 0.36-0.56), family medicine (OR: 0.52, 95% CI: 0.14-0.40), and endocrinology clinicians (OR: 0.23, 95% CI: 0.14-0.40). Conclusion Our study demonstrates differential prescribing patterns for menopause-related symptoms with respect to race, insurance status, and clinician specialty. Our results underscore the need for equitable care for women experiencing menopause symptoms.
