items.title: Assessing the construct validity of cross-national harmonized cognitive assessments using age.
items.abstract: Harmonized cognitive measures are key to cross-national comparisons of dementia risk. However, validating such measures cross-nationally is challenging due to differences in cognitive measures and a lack of a reference standard. Age, a characteristic strongly associated with cognition and widely measured, can serve as a benchmark for evaluating how well harmonized cognitive measures are broadly compatible with a common construct. We used cross-nationally harmonized measures from three studies in the US and five studies in England, Chile, Mexico, India, and South Africa ( N = 27,317). Study-specific estimates of the association between general cognitive scores and age ranged from -0.040 to -0.075 SD units/year of age. The coefficient of variation was 24.1%, indicating moderate relative variability. Results support the hypothesis that cross-nationally harmonized scores, derived from partially overlapping test batteries, measure a broadly similar construct across countries. Future studies should further evaluate criterion, construct, and content validity of cognitive testing in cross-national populations.

items.title: Peer-led examination simulation reshapes psychophysiological and emotional state profiles during problem-based medical learning.
items.abstract: Repeated problem-based learning (PBL) sessions are intended to sustain active, collaborative, and self-directed learning, yet evidence is mixed as to whether familiar PBL routines consistently maintain an appropriate level of learner activation over time. This repeated-measures study examined whether embedding a peer-led examination simulation into regular PBL reshapes psychophysiological and achievement-emotional state profiles. Forty-two medical students were assessed during resting reference, regular PBL, and PBL with peer-led examination simulation. Heart rate variability (HRV) was quantified using RMSSD, SDNN, pNN50, and LF/HF, alongside anxiety, perceived stress, achievement emotions, motivation, self-rated performance, and post-session appraisal. Both PBL formats reduced HRV relative to rest, indicating autonomic activation during regular PBL itself. Compared with regular PBL, examination simulation produced additional HRV withdrawal, higher anxiety and perceived stress, and lower boredom. Baseline-adjusted mixed models supported effects for RMSSD and SDNN; pNN50 did not survive false-discovery-rate correction, and LF/HF showed no robust effect. Enjoyment, motivation, and self-rated performance did not differ significantly. Students reported greater perceived benefit from and stronger preference for the simulation format. Peer-led examination simulation thus shifted PBL toward a more salient, assessment-like psychophysiological and emotional state profile.

items.title: Management of shift work disorder: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline.
items.abstract: Introduction This guideline establishes recommendations for the treatment of SWD. Methods The American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) commissioned a task force of experts in sleep and circadian medicine to develop recommendations and assign strengths based on a systematic review of the literature and an assessment of the evidence using the GRADE process. The task force summarized the relevant literature and the quality of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, and resource use considerations supporting the recommendations. The AASM Board of Directors approved the final recommendations. Recommendations The following recommendations are intended as a guide for clinicians in choosing specific treatment(s) for symptoms of excessive sleepiness and/or insomnia, and for circadian adaptation in adults with SWD. Each recommendation statement is assigned a strength (e.g., "Strong" or "Conditional"). For SWD, there were only "conditional" recommendations for or against (i.e., "We suggest…") and those requiring the clinician to use clinical knowledge and experience and consider the individual patient's values and preferences to determine the best course of action. Interventions in recommendation statements were compared to no treatment. Adults with SWD with symptoms of excessive sleepiness associated with work schedule: 1. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of armodafinil or modafinil taken 30 to 60 minutes prior to the night shift over no armodafinil or modafinil (Conditional recommendation, moderate certainty of evidence). 2. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of bright light over no bright light during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Remark Individuals with SWD who exhibit insomnia and daytime function impairments may also benefit from using bright light during their night shift. 3. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of caffeine taken prior to and/or during the night shift over no caffeine (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Remark Caffeine intake close to bedtime can disrupt sleep onset and quality, which may exacerbate symptoms of SWD. 4. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the use of a clockwise rotating shift schedule over a counterclockwise rotating shift schedule (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 5. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests taking a nap over no nap prior to the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Remark Sleep inertia occurring soon after the nap may temporarily increase sleepiness, decrease cognitive performance, and increase accident risk. Allowing adequate time for resolution of sleep inertia prior to driving or performing other safety-sensitive behaviors may be needed to reduce these risks. 6. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests either not eating or eating a snack rather than eating a full meal during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 7. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the combination of caffeine and bright light over the combination of no caffeine and no bright light (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Remark Caffeine intake close to bedtime can disrupt sleep onset and quality, which may exacerbate symptoms of SWD. 8. In adults with SWD with excessive sleepiness, the AASM suggests the combination of taking a nap and caffeine over the combination of no nap and no caffeine prior to the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Adults with SWD with sleep disturbance/insomnia: 9. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia the AASM suggests the use of CBT-I over no CBT-I (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 10. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia following the night shift, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). 11. In adults with SWD with sleep disturbance/insomnia, when transitioning from daytime to nighttime sleep, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin for night sleep following shift work (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 12. In adults with SWD who desire to take a nap prior to the first night shift, the AASM suggests the use of melatonin over no melatonin prior to the nap (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Remark Melatonin may temporarily increase sleepiness, decrease cognitive performance, and increase accident risk. Allowing adequate time for resolution of sleepiness prior to driving, returning to work or performing other safety-sensitive behaviors may be needed to reduce these risks. 13. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests the use of ramelteon or other melatonin receptor agonists over no melatonin receptor agonist (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 14. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests the use of suvorexant or other dual orexin receptor antagonists over no dual orexin receptor antagonists (Conditional recommendation, low certainty of evidence). 15. In adults with SWD with daytime sleep disturbance/insomnia, the AASM suggests against the use of triazolam and other benzodiazepines (conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation: 16. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the use of bright light over no bright light during the night shift (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty). Remark For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. 17. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the combination of bright light at night and fixed daytime sleep timing over the combination of no bright light and no fixed sleep timing (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Remark For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. 18. In adults with SWD seeking circadian adaptation to the night shift, the AASM suggests the combination of bright light at night, fixed daytime sleep timing, and reduced-light-transmittance glasses in the morning over the combination of no bright light, no fixed sleep timing, and no reduced-light-transmittance glasses (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Remark 1 : For individuals who work rotating or frequently changing shifts, circadian adaptation is not a realistic goal of treatment and therefore they would not be expected to benefit from this intervention. The evidence supporting this recommendation came from studies in which individuals reached partial circadian adaptation to the night shift. Remark 2: Attention to driving safety is important when wearing reduced-light-transmittance glasses. Other considerations for adults with SWD: 19. In adults with SWD who are working either an 8-hour or 12-hour night shift, the AASM does not suggest working one shift duration over the other (Conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Remark This recommendation does not consider other shift durations, rotation, or the number of consecutive shifts. This guideline did not look at shift durations exceeding 12 hours. The total number of hours worked per week ranged from 36 to 52.

items.title: Management of shift work disorder: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine systematic review, meta-analysis, and GRADE assessment.
items.abstract: Introduction The purpose of this systematic review is to provide supporting evidence for a clinical practice guideline on the treatment of adults with shift work disorder (SWD). Methods The American Academy of Sleep Medicine commissioned a task force of six experts in sleep and circadian medicine. A systematic review was conducted to identify randomized controlled trials, observational studies, and treatment trials in which treatments for the symptoms of excessive sleepiness and/or sleep disturbance/insomnia in adults with SWD, and for circadian adaptation to shift work schedules was tested. Evidence from controlled laboratory trials of simulated shift work and of field-based trials of shift workers with and without a diagnosis of SWD was included. Statistical analyses were performed to determine the significance of critical and important outcomes and clinically meaningful thresholds were set to determine the clinical relevance of treatments on the outcomes examined, where possible. Finally, the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development, and Evaluation (GRADE) process was used to assess the evidence for making recommendations. Results The literature search resulted in 3,045 articles; 118 studies provided data suitable for statistical analyses. The task force provided a detailed summary of the evidence along with the quality of evidence, the balance of benefits and harms, patient values and preferences, and resource use considerations.

items.title: The SUPA mechanisms of crime opportunity evolution.
items.abstract: The nature of crime is changing, and so are the opportunities that enable it. Fifty years since the seminal work on crime as opportunity, we suggest that there is a need to consider ways to measure how and why opportunities have evolved. Specifically, we propose four mechanisms of crime opportunity evolution, inspired by biological speciation theory and adapted here to account for the cultural transmission of criminal behaviour, with evolution measured through changes in modus operandi. These are the SUPA mechanisms: Space-Driven (allopatric), Utility-Motivated (sympatric), Pressure-Driven (peripatric), and Attraction-Led (parapatric). We connect these mechanisms of evolution to crime opportunity theory and situational crime prevention. Space-driven opportunities arise through distinct geographic contexts; utility-motivated as a result of success (through choice or chance) within the same opportunity context (often made possible by new tools or technologies); pressure-driven evolution through the blocking of prior crime context-mechanism combinations; and, attraction-led evolution through a voluntary change in context. We illustrate each mechanism with historical examples, discuss how we might best prepare for each type, and consider how the SUPA mechanisms might apply to horizon scanning and future crime prevention practice.

items.title: Influence of Mating Systems, Contemporary Niches, and Historical Demography on the Genetic Patterns of Flagship Plants From the Amazonian Cangas.
items.abstract: Genetic diversity is shaped by multiple factors, including life-history traits, contemporary range distributions, niche constraints, and historical demography. The interplay of these drivers remains largely unexplored, particularly at scales proven to be relevant to conservation management of tropical biodiversity hotspots. Here, we investigate the relative contribution of each of these factors in shaping the current patterns of genetic diversity of 13 plant species occurring in Carajás, Southeastern Amazon, Brazil. We further test whether species associated with iron-rich substrates in Carajás, known as cangas, share a common demographic history despite their differences in life-history traits, distributions, and niches. We found that inbreeding levels are likely determined by mating systems, while both observed and expected heterozygosity were negatively associated with niche marginality. Surprisingly, distribution range and niche breadth had no effects on genetic parameters, likely due to the absence of correlations with ecological specialization. Demographic reconstructions revealed a lack of synchronous population histories across co-distributed cangas plants, which likely reflects variation in the diversified life-history traits affecting the timing of their responses to past climatic changes. Our results offer valuable insights into future demographic trends of cangas -associated species, refining predictions on the fate of species in the face of anthropogenic pressures such as habitat loss and climate change. Our data further contribute to subsidizing analyses to determine priority areas and species for conservation.

items.title: Synergistic effects of fibrolytic enzymes and lactic acid bacteria on cassava leaf silage quality and microbial community.
items.abstract: Cassava leaves are a valuable protein-rich feed resource, but their high fiber content and poor fermentation characteristics can reduce silage quality. To address these challenges, this study evaluated the synergistic effects of fiber-degrading enzymes and lactic acid bacteria (LAB) on the fermentation profiles, nutritional quality, and microbial community of cassava leaf silage. Silage was prepared using five treatments: CK (2% glucose), T1 (Lactobacillus plantarum + 2% glucose), T2 (glucanase + L. plantarum + 2% glucose), T3 (cellulase + L. plantarum + 2% glucose), and T4 (glucanase + cellulase + L. plantarum + 2% glucose), and ensiled for 0, 21, and 42 days. The findings demonstrated that additive treatments (T1-T4) rapidly decreased silage pH and increased lactic acid compared to the CK (P 93%, P = 0.036), compared to only 13.1% in CK, which contained higher proportions of Pediococcus and Weissella species. Collectively, the synergistic application of fibrolytic enzymes and LAB improves cassava leaf silage quality by accelerating acidification, reducing fiber fractions, and establishing a highly favorable L. plantarum-dominated microbial community.

items.title: Arboreal signals in the skeletal proportions of the Gorilla foot.
items.abstract: Postcranial skeletal proportions in living apes have been linked to patterns of arboreal behaviors within and between populations, offering a comparative baseline for interpreting arboreal behavior in fossil hominoids. We quantified metatarsal and proximal phalangeal lengths across all five pedal rays in Gorilla, comparing western lowland gorillas (Gorilla gorilla gorilla), low- and high-elevation Grauer's gorillas (Gorilla beringei graueri), and two ecologically distinct mountain gorilla (Gorilla beringei beringei) populations: those of Bwindi Impenetrable National Park, Uganda, and the Virunga Massif (Volcanoes National Park, Rwanda). The Bwindi sample, assembled from individuals recovered by the Mountain Gorilla Skeletal Project between 2017 and 2025, represents the first substantial pedal dataset for this population. After separately scaling element lengths by estimated body mass and hindlimb length, Bwindi gorillas' third and fourth metatarsal lengths fell consistently between those of the more arboreal western lowland and highly terrestrial Virunga gorillas, while proximal phalangeal and hallux lengths varied little across populations. Additionally, Virunga gorillas showed longer second metatarsals compared to other populations, a feature we link to their strongly terrestrial locomotor habits. In comparing relative manual and pedal element lengths from the same individuals, metacarpals were relatively longer than metatarsals across all populations in rays 2-5, with this pattern reversed in the hallux; among these, only the second ray showed a significant interpopulation difference, with western lowland gorillas exhibiting relatively longer metacarpals than all other groups. Though interpopulation differences in the lengths of pedal elements were generally weaker than those found in the manual elements of the same individuals, these findings suggest that habitat-associated variation in foot morphology can be detected between populations of gorilla subspecies, underscoring the value of fine-grained, population-level skeletal comparisons for refining locomotor inference in the hominoid and hominin fossil record.

items.title: Career-Choice Regret Among Medical Students in the United Kingdom: An Exploratory Mixed-Methods Study of Occupational and Organizational Perceptions.
items.abstract: Background Career-choice regret has been reported among medical students internationally, but less is known about how career-choice responses coexist with perceptions of medicine as a profession and the National Health Service (NHS) as a potential employer among United Kingdom (UK) medical students. This study explored career-choice responses and occupational and organizational perceptions among UK medical students. Methods An exploratory cross-sectional mixed-methods online survey was completed by 31 medical students from 22 UK universities who were recruited through convenience and snowball sampling. The primary outcome was participants' response to whether they would choose medicine again. Occupational and organizational perceptions were assessed using two newly developed, unvalidated 10-item composite perception measures. Participants also rated the importance of and expected satisfaction with career characteristics. Quantitative data were analyzed descriptively, and free-text responses from 18 participants were analyzed thematically. Results Of 31 participants, 14 (45.2%) reported that they would choose medicine again, 10 (32.3%) were unsure, and 7 (22.6%) reported that they would not. Mean occupational and organizational composite scores were 25.23 (SD 6.34) and 38.97 (SD 8.20), respectively. Item-level responses suggested positive views of medicine as a profession alongside negative perceptions of several aspects of NHS employment. The largest gaps were between the importance attached to career characteristics and expected satisfaction related to work location, access to specialty training, work-life balance, and the work environment. Twenty-seven participants (87.1%) considered regret and dissatisfaction among medical students to be a common problem. Free-text responses highlighted concerns about medical education and postgraduate training, work-life balance, future career prospects, financial and working conditions, and feeling undervalued by the NHS. Other responses conveyed continued enthusiasm for medicine despite concerns about the organizational context. Conclusions In this small, self-selected sample, positive perceptions of medicine as a profession coexisted with negative perceptions of the NHS as an organization, while fewer than half of participants reported that they would choose medicine again. These exploratory findings describe career-choice responses and occupational and organizational perceptions but do not establish a causal relationship between organizational dissatisfaction and stated willingness to choose medicine again or predict future career decisions. Larger studies using more diverse samples, validated measures, and longitudinal follow-up are needed to investigate how these perceptions relate to career choices over time.

items.title: Multitask Interactions in Recurrent Dynamics across 100 Cognitive Tasks
items.abstract: The brain continually learns tasks with very different computational demands. Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) have been used as dynamical surrogates for studying task solutions, with recent work extending this approach to joint training on multitask batteries. However, it remains unclear how tasks interact as these batteries grow in scale and heterogeneity: under what conditions do they transfer or interfere with one another, and how do these effects relate to task complexity and model structure? We study this question by simultaneously training hierarchical Almost-Linear RNNs (AL-RNNs) on 100 tasks spanning a wide range of cognitive demands. AL-RNNs allow us to vary the amount of nonlinearity in the recurrence, while hierarchical task features provide a low-dimensional interface for task-specific adaptation within shared dynamics. On this task battery, performance improves with both nonlinear capacity and task-feature dimensionality, with the joint hierarchical model outperforming both individually trained models and a single unstructured joint model. Many tasks are individually solvable with linear dynamics, yet cannot be solved together by a shared linear model. Through hierarchical task features, task-specific linear region usage, and task geometry, the trained model provides several related but distinct measures of task similarity that capture how computations are separated and combined within the shared backbone. Across a series of experiments, we relate these representations to individual task complexity, joint solvability, pairwise transfer learning, and leave-one-out adaptation. Together, our experiments characterize task interactions in multitask recurrent learning while demonstrating both the potential and the challenges of reusable dynamical backbones for cognitive computation.

items.title: Sensorimotor behaviour from an untrained brain-and-nerve-cord connectome
items.abstract: Connectomes now map the neurons and synapses of an adult fly's brain and nerve cord, but how much of behaviour follows from the wiring is unknown. Here we turn one such connectome into a spiking network of 172,433 neurons with a published brain model's untuned parameters, and run it alone and inside a simulated body. Two fixed rules join them: odours and looming objects drive sensory neurons, and motor neurons move the legs. Alone, the network passes a signal to the motor neurons it is known to drive when the pathway supplies about 2% or more of their input. In the body, the fly navigates around obstacles to 95% of the odour sources. A rewiring that keeps each neuron's connection counts and signs reaches 18%, and the fly's leg commands replayed with the senses off reach almost none, so navigation needs the measured wiring and sensory feedback. Dopamine-gated weakening of the mushroom body's output synapses turns approach to an odour into avoidance, which requires the pairing and is odour-specific once one olfactory synapse class is scaled. An untrained connectome thus supports a behaviour and its learned reversal, and the pathways it cannot drive mark what the diagram leaves out.

items.title: Efficiency--Complexity Tradeoff and Constrained Percolation
items.abstract: We study the efficiency--complexity tradeoff for resource-limited agents through directed first-passage percolation. Nonnegative i.i.d. edge weights represent physical energy expenditure, while the logarithmic size of a constrained path family measures representational complexity. For translation-invariant families, a path-joining property yields deterministic large-distance costs in rational directions and joint convexity in constraint parameter and direction, under suitable moment and feasibility assumptions. Our main result concerns the limiting cost parameterized by path-family entropy. Using techniques from analytic combinatorics in several variables (ACSV), we establish its almost-sure existence and joint continuity in entropy and direction for nested families satisfying additional generating-function conditions, on the corresponding entropy range. Path-count asymptotics supply the change of parameter linking this cost to the constraint-parameterized cost. Two planar examples constrain the number of turns or the number of East-runs of length at least two.

items.title: Interplay Between Network Heterogeneity and Activation Thresholds in Global Cascades
items.abstract: The onset of global cascades in complex networks depends on both the distribution of activation thresholds and the underlying network topology. Here we investigate how these two sources of heterogeneity interact within the Watts threshold model, using beta-distributed activation thresholds and beta-binomial degree distributions to systematically vary their respective properties. Analyzing the onset of cascades from infinitesimal seeds, we identify two distinct boundaries governing the large-connectivity behavior of vulnerable branching. The first separates regimes in which increasing connectivity enhances or suppresses propagation, depending on the abundance of individuals with low activation thresholds. The second distinguishes two mechanisms of suppression: one controlled by the scarcity of low-threshold individuals and the other by the diminishing abundance of low-degree nodes as connectivity increases. At the boundary between these mechanisms, their competing contributions produce a logarithmic correction to the asymptotic scaling. Our results demonstrate how the interplay between network structure and individual activation thresholds determines the conditions for extensive propagation.

items.title: The Fate of Ice Sheets on Near-Synchronously Rotating Land Planets
items.abstract: Rocky exoplanets orbiting M dwarf stars are often assumed to be synchronously rotating, such that water-trapping in ice sheets on the permanent nightside may pose a threat to habitability. However, in compact M dwarf systems, gravitational interactions between planets may cause the substellar point to librate or circulate on millennial timescales and sporadically change direction or speed. Here, we use a 3D global climate model to quantify, for the first time, the water-trapping capabilities of these "near"-synchronously rotating exoplanets, with TRAPPIST-1e as our test case. Across a range of synodic day lengths, we find that there is a permanent polar ice reservoir and an increasingly large build-up of lower-latitude transient nightside ice for longer days. A persistent ice-free region develops on the dayside where surface conditions can sustain liquid water. However, this steady-state ice distribution may never be realized since the accumulation timescale may be slower than changes in the spin regime. Additionally, we revise the nightside ice build-up on a synchronously rotating exoplanet using a coupled atmosphere+ice numerical model that accounts for atmospheric lapse rate and isostatic adjustment feedbacks. We find that accounting for this ice-elevation feedback reduces the predicted ice accumulation by a factor of ~3. Taken together, our study suggests that water-trapping in ice sheets is less severe than previously thought for land planets orbiting M dwarf stars.

items.title: On the Evolution of Circumstellar Disks Modified by the Presence of a Binary
items.abstract: Stars form within circumstellar disks, and some binary stars develop circumbinary disks surrounding the pair. Observations suggest that disks that form around binary star systems are less common than those around single stars. One possible explanation is that binary stars may disrupt or shorten the lifespan of their surrounding disks relative to those around single stars. To investigate this, we used the DISCO hydrodynamics code to compute the lifetimes of circumstellar disks with and without a binary. Our results indicate that binary systems can reduce the lifetime of a circumbinary disk by a modest factor of two to three compared to disks around single stars. This effect is present when the binary separation is at least one-tenth of the disk radius. While our findings show that binaries can shorten circumbinary disk lifetimes, this alone might not be enough to fully account for the scarcity of these disks.

items.title: Cutting Corners or Saving Lives? The Evolutionary Stability of Ethics in Pharma Medicine
items.abstract: The pharmaceutical industry operates at the intersection of financial incentives, state oversight, and public scrutiny. We model corporate compliance with a three-population replicator system of ethical firms, active regulators, and active public scrutiny, whose payoffs are motivated by a prisoner's dilemma of first-mover advantage, an inspection game between firms and the FDA, and a volunteer's dilemma in early-stage research. The eight payoff constants are fitted by bounded L-BFGS-B optimization to composite indices for 2010--2024, and a fully sourced dataset of fifteen heavily penalized firms links the model's strategy types to R&D intensity and penalties. The calibrated system has no interior fixed point: an exact identity shows that public scrutiny decays at a rate set by the difference between the regulators' and the public's cost-to-benefit ratios. Without public scrutiny the firm--regulator dynamics are conformally Hamiltonian, so the two populations cycle neutrally around a center, and Lyapunov exponents give no evidence of chaos. Bureaucratic friction $k$, which enters compliance costs as $k^3$, organizes two thresholds: above $k^*\approx0.75$ regulators saturate and compliance rests on public scrutiny, and above $k^{**}\approx0.81$ compliance collapses. The empirical friction index crosses both between 2016 and 2020, as the compliance index falls from $0.85$ to $0.60$. Relative to revenue, penalties are highest for the firms with the lowest R&D intensity. Ethical compliance is therefore an oscillating rather than a permanent state, persisting only while friction stays below the combined incentive of subsidies, fines, and public penalties.

items.title: Spatial variability of CH4-to-CO conversion pathways in irradiated gas giant atmospheres: implications for chemical relaxation and 1D quench schemes
items.abstract: Close-in gas giant atmospheres are in chemical disequilibrium. Solving 3D kinetics to capture one source of this disequilibrium, transport-induced quenching, is computationally demanding, so simplifications are used. General circulation models (GCMs) relax abundances on the timescale of a single conversion pathway. 1D models place a quench level and hold abundances vertically uniform above it. We test both simplifications on CH4 against aerosol-free, solar-composition GCM simulations with thermochemical kinetics for HAT-P-11b, HD 189733b, HD 209458b and WASP-17b. We find ten CH4-to-CO conversion pathways, varying with depth, longitude and planet. A single pathway controls CH4 quenching on the three cooler planets; on WASP-17b two compete. The CH4 quench level is 3D: where the atmosphere is hotter, or a faster pathway takes over, the conversion timescale shortens, the quench level rises and the quench-level abundance falls. On WASP-17b the pathway switch lifts the quench level over the substellar tropics, deepening equatorial CH4 depletion. A 1D quench treatment with the Zahnle & Marley timescale typically locates the quench level within a factor of two in pressure for CH4 and about four for CO on every planet. It fails above the quench level, where every quench scheme holds abundances vertically uniform. The minor carbon carrier, CH4 or CO depending on the planet, is wrong by up to two orders of magnitude, on HD 189733b in opposite directions at different latitudes. Quenching sets an abundance at the quench level but does not fix it thereafter; even without photochemistry, transport and conversion keep that abundance spatially structured.

items.title: Machine Learning Prediction of Transport Properties in Amorphous Polymer Electrolytes Using Chemically Informed Structural Descriptors
items.abstract: Abstract Amorphous polymer electrolytes are promising candidates for next-generation lithium batteries. They offer improved safety and mechanical stability compared to conventional liquid electrolytes. However, predicting their transport performance remains challenging. Ionic conductivity and diffusivity depend on complex, coupled interactions between polymer structure, chemistry, and ion dynamics. This work leverages machine learning to predict four key transport properties in amorphous polymer electrolytes using a molecular dynamics data set of more than 6,000 polymer electrolyte systems. These are ionic conductivity, bis(trifluoromethanesulfonyl)imide (TFSI) diffusivity, lithium-ion diffusivity, and polymer diffusivity. To enhance predictive capability and preserve mechanistic interpretability, we engineered chemically and structurally meaningful features from Simplified Molecular-Input Line-Entry System (SMILES) representations. Selected features include elemental composition, functional group densities, polarity descriptors, and polymer flexibility metrics. Three modeling frameworks were trained and evaluated under 5-fold cross-validation, including random forest, gradient boosting, and neural networks. The neural network achieved the highest predictive performance across all four targets and exceeded prior benchmarks on three of them. It also exhibited substantially greater robustness to data partitioning than the tree-based baselines. Feature importance analysis was performed using both impurity-based rankings and Shapley additive explanations. Polymer backbone flexibility, polarity, and ionic environment were found to dominate transport behavior. Directional attribution further identified primary and secondary amines and carboxylate groups as specific negative contributors to lithium-ion mobility. The results of this work demonstrate that chemically informed structural descriptors can effectively predict electrolyte performance while yielding mechanistic insight. This enables accelerated screening and design of high-efficiency polymer electrolytes for future energy storage applications.

items.title: The Collaborative Strategy for Civic Character Education in Indonesia: Education System, BPIP, and Society
items.abstract: Indonesia needs a strong civic character amidst the challenges of globalization and digitalization. Patterns and strategies are urgently needed to strengthen civic character, especially in education and government, so that internalizing civic character values can significantly impact national growth. The library research method examines various papers, such as books, journal articles, and reports, which are analyzed critically and in depth, using data inclusion techniques based on the SPIDER (Sample, Phenomenon of Interest, Design, Evaluation, Research Type) approach to ensure a rigorous and comprehensive review. Furthermore, interactive data analysis techniques are used, namely reducing, presenting, and concluding the data. The findings show a lack of institutionalized collaboration between education and other institutions in producing a generation with a national character aligned with Pancasila values. Another finding shows the importance of harmonizing the policies of the Agency for Fostering Pancasila Ideology, Republic of Indonesia (BPIP) as a laboratory of Pancasila values, formal education, and society (non-formal) in accommodating learning resources, ideological discourse, and national symposiums. Collaborative governance is needed, where BPIP provides ideological direction and schools, universities, families, and communities apply these principles into contextual, participatory, and digitally responsive learning experiences.

items.title: Substrate chemistry in cancer bioelectronics: phenotype-dependent cell-electrode coupling and motility
items.abstract: Electrode coatings are routinely applied to promote cell attachment in bioelectronics, yet their influence on what the electrode reports is less examined. This is particularly relevant for cell types whose electrical signatures are yet to be fully understood and where coating selection is largely inherited from neuroscience. Here, we compare three breast epithelial phenotypes of increasing invasiveness on interdigitated gold microelectrodes carrying six surface chemistries: uncoated gold, poly-L-lysine (PLL), fibronectin, laminin, and PLL under-layered with each protein (PLL+F, PLL+L). Continuous impedance recording at 1 kHz and 41.5 kHz over the first 17 h, spatial impedance mapping at 24 h, 50 h migration assays and single-cell trajectory analysis were used to evaluate cell-electrode coupling and relate it to motility in the two extremes of the spectrum. Each cell line produced its electrical and migratory signature, and the effect of coating depended on phenotype. Initial coupling and motility were found to be inversely related in the invasive line and unrelated in the non-tumorigenic one. We conclude that the electrode coating is an experimental variable that interacts with phenotype and carries its own electrical signature, and the choice of coating must be driven, beyond physiological relevance, by the requirement for adherent vs. motile cells.

items.title: Neurospirituality Reappraised: Brain Mechanisms of Transcendent Experience and Beyond
items.abstract: Background:Subjective experiences featuring altered self-awareness, temporal perception, or spatial boundaries—termed Non-Ordinary Experiences (NOEs)—occur across clinical neurology, psychiatry, and psychedelic medicine, including in insular ecstatic seizures, meditation, breathwork, hypnosis, and psychedelic therapy. Objective: To synthesize neurobiological and clinical literature on NOEs for neurologists by presenting three heuristic frameworks: 1.A six-dimension phenomenological taxonomy; 2.A tri-level descriptive taxonomy (computational "software", neuromodulatory-autonomic "firmware", and network "hardware"); 3.The Trigger–Dynamic Psyche–4E Appraisal–Outcome Model, which maps how acute neurodynamic shifts resolve into adaptive growth or clinical distress without reducing existential meaning to neural activity. Methods: Narrative synthesis of systematic reviews, coordinate-based meta-analyses, and key theoretical frameworks sourced via PubMed/MEDLINE. Results: Conflating spirituality, religion, and NOEs causes construct contamination in neuroimaging, compounded by unvalidated single-item measures and non-independent cohorts. An fMRI meta-analysis of meditation (34 studies, N=700) reveals aggregate recruitment of the right rolandic operculum, left insula, supplementary motor area, and hippocampus, arguing against a singular "spiritual center". First-person reports are mapped using a six-dimension schema (experiential content, temporal dynamics, spatial dynamics, volitional dynamics/agency, ownership/embodiment, cognitive stance). Mechanistically, states are organized across three bidirectionally coupled levels: computational inference ("software"), neuromodulatory-autonomic state-setting ("firmware"), and large-scale networks ("hardware"). Five entry routes (meditation, psychedelics, breathwork, hypnosis, focal neurological events) are hypothesized to share shifts in Bayesian precision weighting and network decoupling within the master Trigger–Dynamic Psyche–4E Appraisal–Outcome Model. Crucially, long-term outcomes (integration vs. distress) are not dictated by acute brain states alone, but are mediated by contextual filtering through the 4E Appraisal Prism (embodied, embedded, enacted, extended dimensions). Conclusions: Neurospirituality bridges network neuroscience, clinical neurology, and person-centered care. Clarifying biological substrates does not resolve existential validity. Clinicians must maintain a strict distinction between biological mechanisms, subjective experiences, and personal meanings (the Epistemological Invariant) to avoid pathologizing adaptive states or romanticizing neurological disease. Key terms: Spirituality; Neuroimaging; Meditation; Hallucinogens; Epilepsy.

items.title: Algorithmic Circuit Psychiatry: A Roadmap for Precision Treatment of Serious Mental Illness
items.abstract: Treating serious mental illness is a formidable challenge, in part because current diagnostic categories may not capture the biological processes determining treatment response. Progress in genetics, systems neuroscience and neuroimaging has produced important mechanistic insights, yet these advances have not yielded a practical framework for precision psychiatry. We propose Algorithmic Circuit Psychiatry (ACP) as a roadmap for precision treatment of serious mental illness, where stratification is realized at the level of algorithms: computational processes identified via clinically relevant tasks and mappable onto neural substrates. Using psychotic spectrum disorders as a primary case study, we argue that algorithmic description may connect circuit mechanisms to clinical symptoms more effectively than isolated neural measures. We review evidence showing how frontal thalamocortical interactions support reasoning under uncertainty, how disruption of the relevant networks produces schizophrenia-relevant behavioral signatures, and how corresponding behavioral and neural readouts may serve as algorithmic circuit biomarkers. We then outline how these biomarkers, combined with pharmacological perturbation, support trial design logic that can yield mechanistic insights regardless of whether a trial achieves its primary endpoint.

items.title: CortexLens: Systematically Decoding Interpretable Visual Patterns from Human Visual Cortex
items.abstract: Understanding how the human brain encodes visual information remains a fundamental challenge in cognitive neuroscience. Sparse dictionary learning (SDL) has recently been applied to fMRI to discover visual features represented in the visual cortex. Existing approaches, however, depend on a vision-language model to identify the feature at discovery, and report limited discovery of the low-level visual features processed in early retinotopic visual regions that play an essential role in human visual cognition. We propose an automatic framework that systematically discovers visual features encoded in the human visual cortex, encompassing both high-level and low-level visual features. The framework decomposes fMRI responses across the full visual hierarchy with Matryoshka sparse autoencoders applied per region of interest, interprets the resulting fMRI activity patterns with a vision-language model, and introduces a set of feature channels to recover the low-level visual features that language-based interpretation fails to capture. On the Natural Scenes Dataset (NSD) and on the Brain Encoder Generated Dataset (BEGD), a separate set of synthesized responses from a transformer brain encoder, the low-level stream recovers thousands of interpretable low-level visual features from early retinotopic visual regions, where prior language-based pipelines report limited discovery. The high-level stream recovers interpretable semantic visual features on both datasets and generalizes to BOLD5000. Our analysis further reveals a systematic confound in language-based interpretation: fMRI activity patterns whose true representation is a low-level visual feature can be misidentified as a semantic visual feature when that feature co-varies with a salient semantic visual feature.

items.title: Urban Aesthetics: Beauty and Interestingness of the City
items.abstract: This paper develops an empirically informed aesthetics of the city by introducing interestingness as acomplementary category to beauty. While beauty has long defined architectural value throughharmony and rightness, urban life also requires experiences of dissonance, openness, and surprise.Contrasting Scruton’s notion of architectural beauty with Mumford’s conception of the city as secularand dramatic, I side with Mumford’s more open understanding of urban life.Conceptually, I propose a middle way that neither centers exclusively on beauty nor simply endorsesa pluralist aesthetics of the city, as is common in contemporary philosophy of the city. To capture thepsychology of urban life, I focus on aesthetic emotions that help explain the experiences of beauty,interestingness, and belonging. Methodologically, I likewise argue for a middle way that combinesphilosophical reflection with empirical research on the psychology and neuroscience of the builtenvironment. Taken together, the paper outlines an urban-theoretical framework that understandsurban public space, in particular, as an aesthetic interface linking perception, affect, and cognition toforms of civic participation. Beauty provides coherence; interestingness sustains vitality. Together,they define the aesthetic and psychological livability of the city.KeywordsAesthetic emotions; Affordances; Beauty; Empirical aesthetics; Interestingness; Neurourbanism,Urban Aesthetics

items.title: Role of Ventral Tegmental Area Dopamine Neurons in Emergence from Dexmedetomidine, Fentanyl, and Ketamine Anesthesia in Rats.
items.abstract: Background Dopamine neurons in the ventral tegmental area (VTA), a midbrain structure, have been widely implicated in promoting emergence from general anesthesia. However, most studies have focused on anesthetics that primarily target γ-aminobutyric acid type A receptors. Whether these neurons also facilitate emergence from mechanistically diverse drug-induced unconscious states is not known. This study examined the specific contribution of VTA dopamine neurons in restoring arousal after sevoflurane-, dexmedetomidine-, fentanyl-, and ketamine-induced unconsciousness. Methods Adult Sprague Dawley rats received viral constructs driving selective expression in tyrosine hydroxylase-positive VTA neurons of either channelrhodopsin or the control protein, yellow fluorescent protein. Accurate targeting in VTA TH:ChR was confirmed by assessing righting in response to photostimulation during continuous sevoflurane inhalation (1.4 to 2.0%). In a randomized block design, the rats were exposed to dexmedetomidine (15 µg/kg IV bolus), fentanyl (50 µg/kg IV bolus), or ketamine (50 mg/kg IV infusion). After loss of the righting reflex, behavioral arousal and frontal electroencephalography activity were recorded with or without photostimulation. The proportion of animals righting during the light-on and light-off conditions was assessed in a mixed-effects Cox regression model, and spectral power differences were quantified with effect size estimates. Results Optogenetic stimulation of VTA dopamine neurons during continuous sevoflurane inhalation restored righting in VTA TH:ChR rats, with a median latency of 4.7 min (95% CI, 2.6 to 6.4) after the onset of photostimulation. VTA TH:ChR rats were significantly more likely to right during photostimulation after dexmedetomidine (hazard ratio, 27.7; 95% CI, 2.7 to 287.1; P = 0.0053), and responders showed attenuated spectral power in low frequencies (less than 12 Hz) in VTA TH:ChR . Optogenetic stimulation did not affect behavioral nor neurophysiologic measures of arousal after fentanyl. Finally, optogenetic stimulation in VTA TH:ChR rats modestly delayed emergence from ketamine sedation without altering electroencephalography spectral power. Conclusions These data suggest that the role of dopamine VTA neurons in anesthetic emergence is agent specific and likely shaped by distinct and sometimes opposing neural pathways.

items.title: Nationwide citizen science reveals core and rare osmotolerant yeast communities in Swedish honey
items.abstract: Honey represents an extreme microbial habitat, comprising >80% sugar, low pH, oxidative stress, and antimicrobial compounds. Despite these conditions, specialized yeast species persist in nectar and honey microbial communities, where their metabolic activity may contribute to honey maturation and chemistry. To characterize the diversity and functional traits of honey-associated yeasts, we conducted a nationwide citizen science survey with the help of Swedish beekeepers, yielding ~2,400 isolates from 119 honey samples across 103 locations. Sequencing of ITS and LSU barcode regions of cultured isolates identified 85 species across 26 genera, dominated by Entelexis, Starmerella, Zygosaccharomyces, Rhodotorula, Aureobasidium, and Metschnikowia. While a small number of core taxa were consistently detected across geographic and environmental gradients, most species were rare and locally restricted, indicating a highly uneven community structure. Phenotypic assays of representative strains, typically one per isolated species, revealed broad osmotolerance, with several Entelexis, Starmerella and Zygosaccharomyces strains capable of growth at up to 80% glucose. Sugar utilization experiments showed widespread fructophilic metabolism, particularly under high-sugar conditions, and this trait was enriched among the most frequently recovered taxa. Selected isolates also fermented diluted honey, altering both its volatile profile and chemical composition. Together, these results demonstrate that honey hosts a taxonomically diverse but functionally specialized yeast community shaped by strong osmotic selection. This study establishes the largest culture-based collection of honey-associated yeasts to date, underscores the value of citizen science for large-scale microbial ecology, and identifies honey as an important reservoir of osmotolerant and fructophilic yeasts with ecological and biotechnological relevance.

items.title: A note on the history, morphology, and distribution ecology of the boreal felt lichen, Erioderma pedicellatum (Hue) in the northern hemisphere.
items.abstract: The complex history of discovery, population declines, extinctions, and rediscoveries of the boreal felt lichen in the northern hemisphere is examined here for the first time in 124 years following its detection in Canada. We also present evidence of the presence of two distinct morphological forms of the boreal felt lichen. The southern form is in Atlantic Canada and is characterized by a darker, hairless exciple, shorter spores, and a pruina. The northern form occurs in Norway, Alaska, Kamchatka, Quebec, Labrador and northwestern Newfoundland. Although the morphology of the northern form seems identical across North America, Europe, and Asia, the community ecology for patterns for the lichen in Quebec and Labrador deviate from the other subpopulations. New genomic analyses will be required to untangle the population structure of the boreal felt lichen. Since the last IUCN assessment, the number of mature individuals has increased 42-fold, and its geographic distribution has expanded to include western north America, Asia, and the boreal mainland of Canada. This significant increase in population, combined with extensive un-surveyed suitable habitat, and the metapopulation dynamics of this lichen, will make future assessments challenging and will require more field research.

items.title: SORTEE five years on: taking stock of the Society for Open, Reliable, and Transparent Ecology and Evolutionary biology
items.abstract: In five years, the Society for Open, Reliable, and Transparent Ecology and Evolutionary Biology (SORTEE) has grown from a small network of like-minded researchers into a grassroots, international community. Founded in late 2020, SORTEE works to make ecology and evolutionary biology more open, reliable, and transparent at a time when prevailing incentives in academia often reward novelty and quantity over rigour. The society is run largely by early-career researchers and sustained by volunteers and small donations. Around this community, SORTEE has built a portfolio of services and infrastructure: EcoEvoRxiv, a community-governed preprint and postprint server; an annual virtual conference; monthly Code Clubs; a regular workshop and webinar series; and collaborative meta-research projects. The society also produced the first standardised guidelines for data and code quality control in ecology and evolutionary biology, now used by data editors at multiple journals. Over the next five years, SORTEE aims to build on this momentum to promote evidence-based change in how research is funded, conducted, evaluated, and taught, with a particular focus on education, regional outreach, advocacy, and meta-research to inform science policy. SORTEE offers a model for how volunteer-led communities can help drive cultural change in research.

items.title: Asynchronous fruit ripening alters biochemical traits of Terminalia catappa, shaping fruit bat selection and seed dispersal dynamics
items.abstract: Fruit phenology and biochemical traits are crucial in shaping plant frugivore interactions and seed dispersal outcomes. In plants dispersed by bats, asynchronous fruit ripening may serve as an adaptive strategy to regulate fruit availability and enhance reproductive success. We examined the ontogenetic changes in nutrients, minerals, and secondary metabolites in T. catappa and their impact on fruit selection and seed dispersal by three sympatric fruit bats (Pteropus giganteus, Cynopterus sphinx and Rousettus leschenaultia). Across 10 trees (900 fruits analyzed), nutrient and mineral concentrations significantly increased with ripening (ANOVA, p < 0.05), while deterrent secondary metabolites, such as tannins, declined sharply (r = -0.97, p < 0.001). Bat visitation peaked during periods of ripe fruit availability, with distinct interspecific differences in foraging behaviour. Larger bats (P. giganteus) exhibited shorter handling times (10.33 ± 0.15 min) and dispersed seeds up to 500 to 1000 m, whereas smaller bats required longer handling times (23.95 ± 1.73 min) and dispersed seeds up to 50 to 500 m. Seed dispersal surveys conducted consistently at 06:00 h revealed spatially structured dispersal kernels that reflected species specific movement ecology. Behavioral responses were strongly linked to fruit chemistry, with bats preferentially selecting nutrient rich, low defense fruits. We demonstrated that asynchronous ripening enhances the fitness of T. catappa by maintaining a continuous but limited supply of attractive fruits, promoting competitive removal, and reducing density dependent mortality. This trait mediated mechanism connects fruit biochemistry, frugivore sensory ecology, and multiscale seed dispersal dynamics in tropical ecosystems

items.title: Key Informants’ Perspectives on Rural Water Sustainability Governance in the Shoalhaven Region of Australia
items.abstract: Abstract Rural landscapes are central to ecology and agriculture, yet they remain under-recognised in water policy. This study examined rural water sustainability in the Shoalhaven region, New South Wales, Australia. The overall aims were to explore how key informants conceptualise water sustainability; to examine their perceptions of the current state of water sustainability conditions and governance; and to identify priority reforms for strengthening rural water governance in alignment with Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) targets. Fifteen semi-structured key informant interviews were conducted with government representatives, water utilities, community groups, industry representatives, and academic researchers. The data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis across 19 thematic domains. Informants articulated water sustainability through seven distinct conceptual lenses, reflecting a spectrum from ecological non-deterioration to practical resource sufficiency. Notably, no participant gave an unqualified assessment that current actions were sufficient, highlighting widespread concern about the adequacy of current governance arrangements. Three main governance problems were identified specific to rural areas. First, a crisis-management funding model in which episodic disaster funds substitute for sustained preventive investment. Second, a perceived rural prioritisation deficit, whereby informants considered rural water sustainability to receive less sustained governance attention and investment than urban water systems, despite the catchment's contribution to metropolitan water security. Third, a landscape-specific governance gap in which intersecting agricultural, estuarine, and metropolitan pressures demand coordinated catchment-scale management that no existing institution is configured to deliver. Six interdependent governance reforms are proposed, grounded in practitioner knowledge and directed at structural rather than program-level changes. The findings offer transferable insights for rural water sustainability governance in other coastal catchments facing intersecting agricultural, ecological, and metropolitan water demands.

items.title: Dorsal Crypsis and Chemical Defense Jointly Shape Brain Size in Toads.
items.abstract: The cognitive benefits of having a large brain must outweigh its substantial energetic demands for such an organ to evolve. The cognitive buffer hypothesis proposes that large brains facilitate survival in complex environments via flexible behaviors. Because active predator evasion is likely more cognitively demanding than a cryptic lifestyle, we reasoned that the evolution of crypsis could relax selection on brain size. To test this hypothesis, we examined the effect of dorsal crypsis, ventral crypsis, and granular glands on relative total brain evolution in eight toad species. As predicted, total relative brain size was negatively associated with dorsal crypsis across species, but was not related to either the volume or the count of granular glands. Additionally, because certain brain regions may be specifically involved in predator evasion, we assessed relationships between five major brain region sizes and both dorsal crypsis and granular gland traits. Only the olfactory nerves and telencephalon showed negative associations with dorsal crypsis, whereas optic tectum volume correlated positively with granular gland volume. These regions support complex evasion strategies. Our findings indicate that increased dorsal crypsis relaxes selection on cognitively demanding evasion, leading to smaller brains. Thus, crypsis evolution is a previously underexplored factor in vertebrate brain anatomy evolution.

items.title: Decoding the winning mindset: elite athletes’ beliefs about winning
items.abstract: Although notions of a ‘winning mindset’ are repeatedly put forth in self-help books, podcasts, and sport psychology publications, there appears to be little to no compelling evidence that such a mindset exists. The aim of the current study was to investigate the beliefs elite athletes hold about the nature of winning and to examine whether these beliefs may suggest a winning mindset. Using a theory-informed qualitative design, semi-structured interviews were conducted with nine athletes who had represented New Zealand across seven sports. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis with a hybrid inductive–deductive approach. Results suggest that athletes conceptualise winning in two markedly different ways. Winning-is-Proving comprises beliefs that winning means beating others and not losing, whereas Winning-is-Improving comprises beliefs that winning means self-betterment and realising one’s potential. These beliefs were associated with coherent patterns of goals, expectations, and attributions, providing support for their interpretation as a mindset about winning. To our knowledge, these results provide the first preliminary evidence for the existence of a winning mindset and, in doing so, lay the groundwork for research currently underway to develop and validate winning mindset as a novel psychological construct. Implications for mindset theory and sport psychology, as well as for coaches and support staff working with elite athletes, are considered.

items.title: Don't just do something, sit there! Decisiveness as a product of mindfulness and acceptance traits
items.abstract: Decisiveness, the capacity to commit to difficult choices, has traditionally been studied through cognitive and motivational frameworks, leaving the role of one's relationship to inner experience open. Two studies examine dispositional mindfulness, acceptance, and regret sensitivity as predictors of decisiveness. In Study 1 (n = 64), all three significantly predicted decisiveness. In Study 2 (n = 49), regret sensitivity and mindfulness remained significant, though acceptance's association attenuated, coinciding with a stronger acceptance-mindfulness correlation. Across both studies, regret sensitivity was the strongest and most consistent predictor (β = -.31 in Study 1 and -.50 in Study 2), suggesting that an unwillingness to accept the irreversibility of past choices may undermine confident commitment to future ones. Mindfulness and acceptance predicted decisiveness independently of their association with regret. These findings extend decision avoidance research beyond cognitive and affective accounts, positioning decisiveness as an expression of practical wisdom within a broader psychology of character.

items.title: Do people believe diet impacts physical and mental health? Development and validation of the Diet-Health Belief Scale (DHBS)
items.abstract: Diet can impact on physical and mental health, but to what extent do people believe this? Health psychology theory proposes that beliefs about the impact diet has on health likely shape behaviour. Yet, diet-health beliefs have not been systematically studied and methodology used in existing research is limited. This two-part study aimed to explore UK adults’ beliefs about the impact diet has on short-term and long-term physical and mental health conditions, and to conduct initial development and validation of a scale to measure diet-health beliefs. An initial 20-item scale was completed by a general population sample of 399 UK adults online. Results show that participants had inconsistent beliefs about the impact diet has on long-term and short-term physical health outcomes. Participants tended not to believe that diet impacts mental health. Next, exploratory and confirmatory factor analysis of survey responses indicated a 15-item two factor (physical health, mental health) scale provided the most statistically appropriate measure of diet-health beliefs. The scale was found to be reliable at both full (ωₜ = 0.93) and subscale level (factor 1: physical health, ωₜ = 0.90, factor 2: mental health, ωₜ = 0.93). Convergent, divergent and test-retest validity assessments confirmed the scale had acceptable validity. The scale could be used to investigate whether beliefs about the impact of diet on health shape dietary behaviour and investigate the effectiveness of interventions designed to change diet-health beliefs.

items.title: A Source-Specific Approach to Internalised Sexual Prejudice: Scale Development and Initial Validation
items.abstract: Internalised sexual prejudice (ISP) is theorised as the incorporation of social devaluation into negative evaluations of one’s own sexuality. Existing measures, however, generally assess these evaluations without distinguishing the social sources associated with them. We developed the Source-Specific Internalised Sexual Prejudice Scale (SS-ISP), a dual-dimensional 12-item measure assessing negative feelings about one’s own sexuality in response to prejudice from straight people or from other LGBTQA+ people with the same six items presented for each source. Across four studies, we examined its content, structure, invariance across groups, initial validity, and temporal stability. In Study 1, relevance ratings from content experts (n = 15 social psychology researchers) supported retaining six of the eight candidate items under both source frames. Exploratory factor analysis in Study 2 (n = 276 gay men) identified two related source-specific factors. Study 3 replicated this structure in an independent sample (n = 982 LGBTQA+ adults), and supported scalar invariance across cisgender gay men, lesbian women, bisexual men, and bisexual women. Both dimensions demonstrated high internal consistency and positive associations with an established measure of internalised sexual prejudice and concurrent psychological distress. Group differences emerged for LGBTQA+-source ISP, but not for straight-source ISP. Both source-specific dimensions contributed to explaining concurrent psychological distress beyond conventional ISP. An exploratory comparison indicated a stronger adjusted association for LGBTQA+-source ISP than for straight-source ISP. Study 4 (n = 284) indicated moderate 12-month test–retest reliability (ICCs = .65–.68). The findings support distinguishing source-linked manifestations of ISP and retaining their reported social context within its measurement.

items.title: GPT-4 reasons like infants about objects but not agents
items.abstract: Theory of Mind (ToM) is central to human social cognition and is critical for successfully navigating the social world. However, most work to date has explored explicit ToM in AI, particularly with large language models (LLMs), and has found mixed results. In contrast, decades of developmental psychology research with human infants has found remarkable, early-emerging implicit ToM. However, little work has explored implicit ToM in LLMs. The current study investigates implicit social reasoning abilities in GPT-4 using model-facing versions of classic infant experiments. In Experiment 1, we explored GPT-4’s implicit ToM abilities across four social reasoning tasks adapted from infant paradigms. In Experiment 2, we explored whether GPT-4 was capable of physical reasoning to contrast with social reasoning in Experiments 1 and 2. Across these three experiments, our results suggest that there may be domain differences in GPT-4’s reasoning abilities, such that GPT-4 struggled with social reasoning tasks despite performing very well on physical reasoning tasks. These findings highlight the importance of systematic exploration of social reasoning in LLMs and provide insight into potential deficits in GPT-4’s social reasoning abilities.

items.title: Examining Linking Language and Causal Implications in Observational Psychological Capital Research
items.abstract: The present study examines whether the issues with implied causal inference identified by Haber et al. (2022) in observational health research extend to the field of industrial-organisational (IO) psychology. Haber et al. found that causal relationships were implied through the language used to link exposures and outcomes and through recommendations for action. This small-scale conceptual replication applies Haber et al.’s approach to psychological capital (PsyCap), an increasingly popular construct in the domain of IO psychology. Specifically, we evaluate the causal strength of the language used to describe the nature of the connection between given variables when reporting findings and when making recommendations for action in 50 PsyCap articles. The majority of action recommendations were found to have strong causal implications (85% in abstracts, 84% in discussion sections), and most linking sentences implied some level of causality (64% in abstracts, 58% in discussion sections). This was despite very few articles explicitly stating an intention to estimate causal effects (10%) and many explicitly warning against drawing causal inferences (42%). No significant relationship was found between the causality implied in the linking sentences and the strength of causal implication of the action recommendations. These findings have important implications for how research is implemented, and very real consequences for those who are the focus of such implementations. Increased transparency about causal interests and reasoning is needed to uphold the credibility of findings and the integrity of applications of observational PsyCap research.

items.title: Ten Concerns About Personality-Change Interventions—and How to Address Them
items.abstract: Many people want to change their personality in some way and personality traits have been found to predict various important aspects of life, including well-being, health, relationship quality, and work success. As a result, volitional personality interventions designed to elicit personality trait change in desired directions have recently gained momentum in research and public discourse. Although the initial evidence on the effectiveness of these interventions is promising, concerns regarding their benefits, risks, and societal implications remain underexplored. In this review, we discuss 10 concerns regarding methodological, ethical, and practical limitations of volitional personality change interventions. Drawing on research across different areas of psychology, we provide a balanced discussion of each concern and outline directions for future research and practical applications of these interventions. Volitional personality change interventions have the potential to improve people’s life and increase satisfaction with the self. However, realizing this potential requires sustained research efforts, thoughtful study design, and careful implementation of these interventions to maximize benefits and mitigate concerns.

items.title: A Systematic Review and Theoretical Framework of Stress Generation in Daily Life
items.abstract: Stress generation describes processes by which individuals actively contribute to the occurrence of self-generated stressful events. Personal characteristics like neuroticism or psychopathology have been found to predict the occurrence of major life stressors over several months or years. However, a profound understanding of stress generation over shorter time periods in people’s daily lives is still missing. Here, we integrated recent research on person-environment transactions from personality psychology into the clinical stress generation literature to develop a process model of stress generation. This process model posits that stress generation unfolds across multiple timescales and that short-term dynamics between momentary, state-level personal characteristics and daily hassles are the building blocks for established long-term stress generation effects. To evaluate a core aspect of this model, we conducted a systematic literature search on stress generation in daily life (45 studies, Ntotal = 9’818). Results show that both dispositional traits and momentary states predict the occurrence of daily hassles, supporting the existence and relevance of stress generation in daily life. However, future research on stress generation across timescales is needed to test the theorized link between stress generation in daily life and long-term stress generation effects.

items.title: Beyond Understanding Pariwara: A Philosophical Journey Toward Authentic Being
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines the Filipino concept of pariwara and reinterprets it through existential, ethical, and Filipino philosophical perspectives. In common usage, pariwara refers to a person whose life, behavior, or choices have gone astray, often carrying negative judgments of irresponsibility, moral failure, or social disconnection. However, this paper challenges the assumption that being pariwara constitutes a permanent identity. It argues that pariwara is better understood as a condition of existential disorientation that may become a turning point toward self-understanding, moral responsibility, and authentic being. The study employs conceptual analysis and hermeneutic-phenomenological reflection to examine the lived and philosophical meaning of pariwara and to place it in dialogue with Western existentialism, virtue ethics, the philosophy of hope, and Filipino philosophical psychology. The discussion draws from Sartre's concepts of freedom, choice, and responsibility; Heidegger's distinction between inauthenticity and authenticity; Kierkegaard's understanding of becoming oneself; Aristotle's theory of habituation and character formation; and Gabriel Marcel's philosophy of hope. These perspectives are complemented by the Filipino concepts of kapwa and loob, which emphasize that authentic personhood is relational and inseparable from responsibility toward others. The paper proposes a transformative movement from pariwara toward authentic being through recognition, reflection, responsibility, choice, practice, transformation, and renewed relational participation. Such transformation does not erase past wrongdoing or remove accountability but requires confronting the past while refusing to let it determine the future. Ultimately, the study argues that pariwara should not signify the end of a person's moral or existential journey. Rather, it can represent a moment of possibility through which individuals may recover agency, rebuild character, restore meaningful relationships, and consciously pursue a more authentic way of being.

items.title: Social Vulnerability and Suicidal Ideation in Nursing Home Residents: The Mediating Role of Meaning in Life.
items.abstract: Background and ObjectivesSuicidal ideation (SI) in nursing homes remains underexplored. This study examined whether meaning in life mediates associations between social vulnerability, perceived burdensomeness, and SI.Research Design and MethodsThis is a cross-sectional study with 231 residents from Valencian Community, Spain, aged 60 years or older with preserved or mildly impaired cognitive functioning. Structural equation modeling tested direct and indirect associations.ResultsLower meaning in life was associated with higher SI. Perceived burdensomeness and low social support were not directly associated with SI but were indirectly associated through reduced meaning in life, explaining 42.8% of its variance. Loneliness was directly associated with SI, whereas its association with low meaning in life was borderline.Discussion and ImplicationsMeaning in life may play a relevant role in the psychosocial factors examined and SI, although longitudinal research is needed. Interventions enhancing meaning and addressing loneliness may improve suicide prevention in nursing homes.

items.title: A Smartphone-Based Intervention to Decrease Neuroticism: Protocol of the CHILL Study
items.abstract: Many people worldwide want to be less neurotic. As lower levels of neuroticism predict a range of positive life outcomes, including health, work success, and relationship quality, interventions that help people to become less neurotic could have wide ranging impacts. This study protocol describes the rationale and design of the CHILL Study (Changing How I Live Life) that aims to evaluate the effects of a smartphone-based intervention to reduce neuroticism in the general public. The CHILL Study comprises four survey assessments spread over 5 months, a 6-week intervention phase, and two 1-week experience sampling phases without interventions. During the intervention phase, participants who wanted to become less neurotic were randomized to four different treatment groups. These treatment groups differed in the employed intervention strategies that target different aspects and levels of neuroticism. The CHILL Study moves beyond existing research on volitional personality change by testing which strategies most effectively decrease neuroticism and evaluating the longevity and generalizability of intervention-induced neuroticism change via peer-reports, implicit personality assessments, and a 7-week follow-up period. The goals of the CHILL Study are to generate an effective method for decreasing neuroticism and facilitating the development of a comprehensive theory of neuroticism change.
